NEW DELHI: Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman pitched India’s investment opportunities to global institutional investors and financial institutions during a four-day visit to Singapore, highlighting infrastructure, semiconductors, artificial intelligence (AI), renewable energy and financial services as key areas for greater capital flows, the finance ministry said in a statement on Monday.
The visit, from 8 to 11 October, included meetings with Singapore’s political leadership, financial authorities and major global investors, including BlackRock, JPMorgan Chase, Temasek, GIC, Carlyle and the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA).
Sitharaman encouraged investors to explore opportunities through the National Investment and Infrastructure Fund (NIIF) and the Gujarat International Finance Tec-City International Financial Services Centre (GIFT IFSC). The government also highlighted select infrastructure projects for potential investment.
Discussions focused on mobilizing long-term institutional capital for India’s infrastructure and development priorities and strengthening bilateral investment and financial cooperation, the ministry said.
At a business roundtable with global investment firms, participants discussed India’s economic resilience amid global uncertainties, financial market developments and the implications of rapid advances in AI. Investors expressed confidence in India’s growth prospects and called for predictable, fiscally prudent and growth-oriented policies, alongside continued infrastructure investment.
Separate meetings with senior executives of financial institutions and global corporations, including Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group, Standard Chartered Bank, DBS Bank, Wellington Management, TPG, Intel and British International Investment, covered opportunities across several sectors.
Discussions spanned consumer markets, start-ups, financial technology, healthcare, manufacturing, micro, small and medium enterprises, and trade finance. Other areas included data centres, semiconductors, renewable energy, electric mobility and aviation maintenance, repair and overhaul services.
Meetings with Singapore’s financial authorities explored cooperation in emerging financial technologies, including asset tokenisation, digital money, central bank digital currencies and interoperable payment and settlement systems.
The Monetary Authority of Singapore shared its approach to developing the digital asset ecosystem, including asset tokenization. Both sides discussed potential efficiency gains, regulatory challenges and the need for trusted settlement arrangements, the finance ministry said.
The two countries also reviewed progress on the outcomes of the fourth India-Singapore Ministerial Roundtable and discussed ways to deepen their comprehensive strategic partnership. Talks covered capital markets, payments connectivity, digitalization, semiconductors, AI and cybersecurity, as well as stronger India-ASEAN economic cooperation ahead of Singapore’s ASEAN chairmanship in 2027.
Sitharaman also met Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, Deputy Prime Minister and Trade and Industry Minister Gan Kim Yong, and Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan.
India’s exports to Singapore fell 8.57% to $11.86 billion in FY26 from $12.98 billion in FY25, even as the two countries seek to deepen economic and investment ties.
Singapore remains a key trade and investment partner for India. It was India’s largest trading partner within ASEAN in FY25, with bilateral trade of $34.26 billion, and a major source of foreign direct investment. The two countries have a Comprehensive Economic Cooperation Agreement (CECA), in force since 2005, and are working to deepen trade and investment ties.

articles.title: 🌐🤝🏻 Growing commitment: How 12th EU-ASEAN Business Summit builds stronger regional economic partnership - The Southeast Asia Desk
articles.summary: 🌐🤝🏻 Growing commitment: How 12th EU-ASEAN Business Summit builds stronger regional economic partnership  The Southeast Asia Desk
articles.full_text:
🎯 The Main Takeaway
Southeast Asian and European government and enterprise executives have gathered to discuss strengthening the trade agreement between both regions at the 12th ASEAN-EU Business Summit as part of ASEAN’s 58th Economic Ministers’ Meeting in Manila on 22 September 2026.
The meeting focused on five critical long-term growth areas: energy transition, financial inclusion, digital connectivity, AI transformation, and health-nutrition.
The Summit was led by Ditte Juul Jørgensen, European Commission’s Director-General for Trade and Economic Security, and Satvinder Singh, ASEAN Deputy Secretary-General. It was also attended by executives from HSBC, Prudential, SWIFT, FrieslandCampina and Coca-Cola Europacific Partners.
📡 Why It’s on Our Radar
This summit signals a strong commitment to partnership development between the two blocs, particularly in trade and investment.
The European Union has considerably prioritised strengthening its economic partnership with ASEAN in recent years. It has also shown that the EU is trying to diversify markets to reduce excessive dependence on the United States and China.
Southeast Asian countries see the EU as a strategic partner able to hedge against uncertainties from US-China rivalry. ASEAN member states also recognise the EU as a reliable partner associated with a rules-based international order and multilateralism.
📊 By the Numbers
- ✨ Southeast Asian countries’ trust in the EU has reached 55.9%, the second highest amongst ASEAN Strategic Partners.
- 🛡️ The EU (37.7%) remains ASEAN’s most preferred and trusted “third-party” strategic partner to hedge against US-China rivalry.
- 💶 EU total foreign direct investment (FDI) is the largest in ASEAN, valued at US$31.3 billion in 2025, nearly double the previous year.
- 📈 In 2024, EU FDI stocks into ASEAN accounted for €363.4 billion, while ASEAN’s investment in the EU totalled €294.1 billion. The EU remains ASEAN’s third-largest investor, after the US and China.
- 🌐 ASEAN is the EU’s third-largest trading partner outside Europe, with US$313.1 billion in goods trade in 2025. Bilateral services trade amounted to €139.2 billion in 2024.
🔮 What’s the Next Target
Leaders welcomed the EU-Philippines Free Trade Agreement (FTA), expected to be ratified in 2027. Similar deals with Thailand and Malaysia are also expected to conclude next year, adding to existing FTAs with Indonesia, Vietnam, and Singapore.
The two blocs also pursue a broader region-to-region economic framework to mark the 50th anniversary of ASEAN-EU partnership next year. The EU-ASEAN Business Council urged adoption of an ASEAN-EU Economic Framework Agreement allowing advanced economic integration.
According to a release, Jens Ruebbert, Chairman of the EU-ASEAN Business Council, stated that these bilateral deals should not be the endpoint but the foundation for a more ambitious, longer-term goal to establish a region-to-region FTA.
He added that the council strongly believed a regional deal would provide a competitive edge for European and Southeast Asian companies alike, bringing trade and investment to a level that reflects the scale and strategic importance of the ASEAN-EU relationship.
⚖️ EU-ASEAN B2B Opportunity & Challenge
According to the EU-ABC 12th Sentiment Survey, 74% of European businesspeople believe an ASEAN-EU FTA would deliver more benefits than bilateral agreements, and 49% want negotiations for a regional FTA next year.
There is a set of opportunities and challenges for those looking to expand in ASEAN.
🚀 Opportunities
- 📊 ASEAN ranks as the region offering the strongest economic opportunities for the EU for the fourth consecutive year, with 61% choosing it over China and South Asia — up from 56% in 2025.
- 📈 Nearly four in five (78%) EU business representatives expect to increase trade and investment in ASEAN over the next five years.
⚠️ Challenges
- 💰 US tariff policy uncertainty remains a key concern, with 81% saying it has weakened business confidence in ASEAN.
- 🚧 Nearly three-quarters (73%) of European businesses see too many barriers for efficient supply-chain usage, while 67% identified the lack of harmonised regulations as a key challenge.
🌍EU Largest Trade Partners in Southeast Asia
According to United Nations Comtrade data, the largest Southeast Asian-European trade commodity is primarily agricultural and livestock products. Southeast Asia’s strongest export to the EU is coffee, valued at US$3.8 billion**. The most widely accepted European commodity is **milk and cream**, valued at **US$620.9 million in 2025.
- 🇻🇳 Vietnam: US$85.7 billion
☕ Largest export to EU: **Coffee** (US$3.3 billion)
🥛 Largest import from EU: Milk & Cream (US$116 million)
- 🇲🇾 Malaysia: US$54.7 billion
🌴 Largest export to EU: **Palm Oil** (US$1.28 billion)
🥩 Largest import from EU: Meat of Swine (US$206.3 million)
- 🇸🇬 Singapore: US$53.5 billion
⛏️ Largest export to EU: **Copper Ore** (US$256.3 million)
🥩 Largest import from EU: Meat of Swine (US$83.3 million)
- 🇹🇭 Thailand: US$49.6 billion
🍖 Largest export to EU: **Prepared/Preserved Meat** (US$416.8 million)
🌾 Largest import from EU: Wheat & Meslin (US$63.9 million)
- 🇮🇩 Indonesia: US$31.2 billion
🌴 Largest export to EU: **Palm Oil** (US$1.12 billion)
Largest import from EU: Milk & Cream (US$141 million)
🏁 The Bottom Line
The numbers are no longer the question. The EU is ASEAN’s largest foreign investor, its third-largest trading partner outside Europe, and the strategic partner Southeast Asians trust second-most after decades of hedging between Washington and Beijing.
What remains unresolved is architecture. Europe and Southeast Asia are building their relationship one bilateral FTA at a time—the Philippines in 2027, Thailand and Malaysia close behind—while the larger prize, a region-to-region agreement, stays on the drawing board.
Three-quarters of European businesses say they want it. The question is whether governments will move at the same speed as the capital already flowing between them.
If they do, the 50th anniversary next year could mark more than a milestone. It could mark the moment ASEAN and the EU stopped treating each other as alternatives to somewhere else—and started treating each other as the destination.

Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman held meetings with senior executives of five global financial institutions and investment firms in Singapore to discuss expanding their engagement in India across infrastructure financing, private credit, artificial intelligence (AI), renewable energy and housing finance.
Singapore, October 12 (ANI): Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman held meetings with senior executives of five global financial institutions and investment firms in Singapore to discuss expanding their engagement in India across infrastructure financing, private credit, artificial intelligence (AI), renewable energy and housing finance.
According to posts shared by the Ministry of Finance on X, the meetings involved representatives from Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SMBC), Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken (SEB), HPS Investment Partners, B Capital Group and Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group (MUFG).
The ministry's post said she encouraged HPS to explore setting up a fund in GIFT IFSC and collaboration with the National Investment and Infrastructure Fund (NIIF) to "mobilise financing for large infrastructure projects in India".
In talks with MUFG Chief Executive for Asia Pacific Yukinobu Saeki, discussions focused on expanding the bank's presence in India, particularly in "capital markets, infrastructure and project finance, renewable energy and M&A financing".
Sitharaman also encouraged greater engagement with the National Bank for Financing Infrastructure and Development (NaBFID) to support infrastructure financing. The meeting covered financing support for Indian small and medium enterprises and regulatory roadshows to "enhance market transparency and governance".
During her meeting with SEB Chairperson Marcus Wallenberg, discussions covered India's economic outlook and ways to strengthen investment flows from European institutional investors. The SEB team highlighted opportunities across "energy and data centres, IT and tax services, healthcare, financial services and housing finance".
The talks also covered sustainable finance, private equity investments in non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), the green transition and skill development.
Sitharaman also met SMBC Managing Executive Officer and Co-Head for Asia Pacific Rajeev Kannan to discuss opportunities to expand the bank's engagement in India, including "affordable housing finance, financing for NBFCs, trade finance and other priority sectors".
She encouraged the bank to explore investment and financing opportunities through NIIF and GIFT IFSC, particularly in aircraft leasing.
Separately, discussions with B Capital Group Co-founder and CEO Raj Ganguly focused on "Sovereign AI and the broader AI ecosystem". Sitharaman highlighted India's potential to emerge as a leader in AI services and encouraged the firm to explore AI applications in banking and financial services.
The ministry said B Capital emphasised the importance of a "stable currency and predictable, transparent tax policies" for investors.
The discussions covered potential avenues to expand financing for Indian businesses and infrastructure and attract investment across technology, energy and other sectors. (ANI)

articles.title: Credit growth must go hand in hand with improving the capacity to handle bad debts. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Credit growth must go hand in hand with improving the capacity to handle bad debts.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Expanding credit supports economic growth.
 In 2026, with the goal of achieving double-digit economic growth while maintaining macroeconomic stability and controlling inflation, bank credit will continue to be a crucial resource for production, business, and investment. This necessitates ensuring both the supply of capital to the economy and the control of credit quality and system safety.
 During the first nine months of the year, the State Bank of Vietnam (SBV) continued to proactively and flexibly manage monetary policy, coordinating with fiscal policy and other macroeconomic policies. Regarding interest rates, the SBV maintained the policy interest rates, creating favorable conditions for credit institutions to access low-cost capital; at the same time, it required banks to implement solutions to stabilize interest rates, reduce costs, and publicly disclose lending rates to support people and businesses in accessing capital.
 According to Deputy Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam Pham Thanh Ha, with synchronized solutions, the rate of interest rate increase is slowing down and the interest rate level is basically revolving around a new level. By September 20, 2026, the average deposit interest rate for new transactions will be 6.38%/year, an increase of 1.15 percentage points compared to the end of 2025. 
 Along with managing interest rates, the State Bank of Vietnam (SBV) is implementing various credit solutions to meet capital needs for growth. The principles for allocating credit growth targets for 2026 are publicly available to allow credit institutions to proactively implement them; some credit facilities serving important sectors and projects are subject to appropriate mechanisms to facilitate capital supply. Credit programs for social housing, key projects, growth drivers, and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) are also being further promoted.
 By September 30, 2026, total outstanding credit in the banking system is projected to reach VND 20.75 million billion, an increase of 11.59% compared to the end of 2025 and a 16.69% increase compared to the same period last year. This credit expansion provides additional capital for businesses to supplement working capital, fulfill orders, and implement investment projects. However, the increased scale of credit also places higher demands on the quality of loans. The effectiveness of capital flow depends not only on the ability to supply credit but also on where capital is allocated, the ability to absorb capital, the efficiency of production and business operations, and the repayment capacity of customers. Therefore, along with the requirement to meet capital needs for growth, controlling credit quality and proactively handling outstanding debts becomes a crucial part of maintaining the circulation of capital and ensuring the safety of the banking system.
 Increase both the quantity and quality of credit, and control the risk of bad debt arising.
 Credit continues to expand to meet the capital needs of the economy, but the requirements are not only about the growth rate but also about the quality of the capital flow. Increased credit does not necessarily mean a corresponding increase in bad debt; the level of risk depends on the quality of appraisal, the structure of capital allocation, the efficiency of capital use, and the developments in the economic environment. As the scale of credit expands, the amount of capital affected by adverse economic fluctuations also increases. If production and business activities do not go as expected, a segment of customers may face difficulties with cash flow and the ability to repay debts, leading to overdue and bad debts.
 In a highly open economy like Vietnam, businesses are significantly impacted by international markets, from demand for goods and trade policies to fluctuations in exchange rates and raw material prices. A decline in export orders, increased input costs, or supply chain disruptions can all affect a company's revenue, profits, and cash flow. This impact can also spill over into domestic supply chains, thereby affecting the ability of borrowers to repay their loans.
 Risks don't only come from external factors. Slow domestic purchasing power recovery, prolonged debt, or projects delayed in completing legal procedures and commencing operations can also prevent revenue from being generated on schedule, while debt repayment obligations remain due. For businesses using borrowed capital to expand investment, the longer the time from disbursement to the project generating revenue, the more carefully their ability to withstand adverse fluctuations needs to be considered.
 If new capital helps businesses complete orders, bring projects into operation, and improve operational efficiency, their ability to repay debt will be strengthened. Conversely, if the disbursement rate exceeds the capital absorption capacity or risk control capabilities, outstanding debt may increase while repayment sources remain unsecured. Therefore, credit expansion needs to be accompanied by the selection of feasible projects, monitoring of capital utilization, and regular updates on customers' repayment capacity based on actual developments.
 Interest rates are also one of the factors affecting a customer's financial costs and cash flow, alongside revenue, input costs, project progress, and product sales. When business operations are favorable, businesses are able to fulfill their debt repayment obligations. Conversely, when revenue declines, borrowing costs can increase repayment pressure. Therefore, the risk of bad debt needs to be assessed in relation to the overall business conditions, capital utilization efficiency, and the customer's ability to generate repayment sources.
 Another factor to consider is that bad debt often lags behind credit growth. Loans in the investment or principal repayment grace period may not fully reveal their risks. Only when revenue falls short of targets by the repayment deadline does the ability to repay become more apparent. Therefore, during credit expansion, it is necessary to simultaneously monitor the quality of loans and prepare the capacity to handle any bad debts that may arise in the future.
 If the economic environment is stable, the output market is maintained, and projects are implemented on schedule, credit capital will be effective and the 발생 of bad debts will be limited. Conversely, when business operations face difficulties, revenue declines, or projects are delayed in operation, the pressure of bad debts may increase. This is a risk that needs to be proactively managed, rather than assuming that bad debts will increase along with credit. The assessment should be based on indicators such as Group 2 debts, restructured loans, customer cash flow, and newly arising bad debts.
 When non-performing loans increase, banks must allocate more resources to debt resolution, asset management, and provisioning, which can affect profitability, capital replenishment, and credit expansion capacity. Prolonged debt also delays the return of projects, factories, and collateral assets to operation, resulting in lost revenue generation opportunities. Therefore, timely resolution of non-performing loans also contributes to maintaining resources for growth during credit expansion.
 Therefore, addressing bad debts needs to be considered within the same process as expanding credit to support growth. The goal is to recover capital, restore the ability to utilize assets, and limit the prolonged stagnation of resources in debts and projects that have not generated cash flow. When capital is recovered and assets are put back into operation, resources for investment, production, and business are replenished, while simultaneously reducing pressure on the balance sheets of credit institutions.
 In this process, enhancing VAMC's capacity is crucial. As a professional debt resolution agency, VAMC can support credit institutions in selecting recovery options, connecting them with investors, and restoring asset value. Strengthening its financial capacity, legal tools, and market infrastructure will expand its debt resolution capabilities, limit stagnant capital, support the maintenance of capital flows for the economy, and contribute to ensuring the safety of the banking system.
 Enhancing VAMC's resources and role in the new phase.
 The need to both expand credit to support growth and proactively control and manage risks further clarifies the role of VAMC in the new phase. Decisions by the Prime Minister and decrees by the Government have established a direction to enhance VAMC's role, linking bad debt resolution with restructuring credit institutions, restoring asset values, and developing the debt trading market. Through this, VAMC's position, resources, and operational tools are gradually being strengthened to participate more deeply in the process of resolving bad debts and unlocking capital for the economy.
 Decision No. 1413/QD-TTg dated July 27, 2026, identifies the development of VAMC as a central institution in creating and developing the debt trading market, while continuing to be an effective tool of the State in handling bad debts and restructuring credit institutions. Accordingly, VAMC is oriented towards increasing its charter capital according to the approved policy; completing the legal framework for handling bad debts, collateral assets, and debt trading; developing the Debt Exchange into a national market infrastructure; and establishing a database of bad debts and collateral assets. Therefore, VAMC's role is not limited to buying and recovering debts but also extends to organizing the market, connecting stakeholders, and mobilizing resources to participate in debt resolution.
 Furthermore, Decision No. 1809/QD-TTg dated September 18, 2026, further clarifies the development orientation of VAMC into a central institution of the non-performing loan (NPL) trading market. The decision requires the c

Union Finance and Corporate Affairs Minister Nirmala Sitharaman concluded a four-day official visit to Singapore, holding talks with the country’s leadership and global investors to expand investment, strengthen financial connectivity and advance cooperation in emerging technologies.
During the October 8–11 visit, FM Sitharaman called on Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam and Prime Minister Lawrence Wong. She also met Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry Gan Kim Yong and Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan.
The engagements reviewed progress on the outcomes of the fourth India–Singapore Ministerial Roundtable and explored ways to deepen the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership. The two sides also discussed India–ASEAN cooperation and regional economic ties ahead of Singapore’s ASEAN chairmanship in 2027.
FM Sitharaman highlighted India’s macroeconomic fundamentals, growth prospects and policy reforms, encouraging Singapore-based institutional investors and businesses to increase their participation in the Indian economy.
Select infrastructure projects from the National Investment and Infrastructure Fund (NIIF) pipeline were presented for investors’ consideration, with follow-up discussions envisaged with relevant Indian authorities.
The minister also attended a luncheon hosted by President Tharman and International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva. Senior representatives from global financial institutions, investment firms, academia and the Singapore government exchanged views on global economic and financial developments.
At a business roundtable, FM Sitharaman met representatives of JPMorgan Chase, BlackRock, Deutsche Bank, PIMCO, the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, Carlyle, Temasek, Millennium Management, Citadel and Brevan Howard.
Discussions covered India’s economic reforms and resilience amid global uncertainty, financial market developments, the implications of rapid advances in artificial intelligence and opportunities to attract global capital into Indian assets.
Participants expressed confidence in India’s growth prospects and said they looked forward to continued fiscally prudent, predictable and growth-oriented policies, alongside sustained infrastructure development.
FM Sitharaman separately met senior leaders from Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group, Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation, Wellington Management, Standard Chartered Bank, GIC, DBS Bank, Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken, Temasek, TPG, HPS Investment Partners, CapitaLand Investment, Intel, British International Investment, IHH Healthcare and B Capital.
The institutions and corporations expressed investment interest in consumer markets, startups, fintech, deep technology and healthcare. Talks also explored financing for infrastructure, including AI-related facilities, semiconductors and data centres, as well as renewable energy, manufacturing, MSMEs, trade finance, financial services and food supply chains.
Aircraft leasing, treasury centres and greater participation in India’s financial markets were among other areas discussed.
Mobilising long-term institutional capital for infrastructure and development was a central theme. FM Sitharaman encouraged investors to explore opportunities through NIIF and the GIFT International Financial Services Centre. Participants expressed their intention to sustain and expand investments in India.
In meetings with Singapore’s financial authorities, including the Monetary Authority of Singapore, the two sides discussed asset tokenisation, digital money, central bank digital currencies, interoperability and trusted settlement arrangements.
Singapore expressed interest in sharing its experience in asset tokenisation, opening avenues for further cooperation between the countries’ financial authorities.
Business engagements also covered investment under the India Semiconductor Mission, skilled workforce development, industry-linked training, AI skilling and the application of AI in banking and financial services.
Other areas included renewable energy, electric mobility, aviation maintenance, repair and overhaul, food security and processing, sustainable finance and healthcare infrastructure.
Discussions with the Singapore Business Federation focused on targeted business matching and visits by Singapore business delegations to India for engagement with companies and state governments. The federation identified semiconductor supply chains, aviation maintenance, food security and food processing as potential areas for collaboration.
The visit sought to translate policy dialogue into investment and business partnerships, while strengthening channels for follow-up engagement in emerging and strategic sectors.
FM Sitharaman was accompanied by the NIIF chief executive, the chairperson of the International Financial Services Centres Authority and senior officials from the Department of Economic Affairs.

articles.title: Hanoi implements solutions to achieve double-digit growth targets. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Hanoi implements solutions to achieve double-digit growth targets.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Hanoi remains committed to its target of double-digit GRDP growth for the whole year of 2026, without any downward adjustment; at the same time, it has updated its Q4 operational scenario with a growth target of 16.55%.
With that determination, the city is implementing a comprehensive set of solutions, effectively leveraging the driving forces from industry, construction, services, and other economic sectors, creating a breakthrough to achieve double-digit growth targets.
Building on positive results, clearly identifying bottlenecks.
Reporting at the seventh meeting of the Hanoi City Party Committee's Executive Board, 18th term (2025-2030), yesterday afternoon (October 12), Standing Committee member and Vice Chairman of the Hanoi People's Committee Nguyen Xuan Luu stated that the third quarter saw a breakthrough with a growth rate of 10.02%, higher than the national average for the third quarter (9.95%). This is the first time this year that double-digit growth has been achieved and marks the peak of quarterly growth. In the fourth quarter, the city will focus on achieving a growth target of 16.55%.
Alongside this, consumption, transportation, and tourism maintained their growth momentum. Many transportation, urban, housing, and environmental infrastructure projects saw substantial progress, contributing to expanding development space, improving connectivity, and creating further impetus for economic sectors.
These results show that Hanoi still has room and favorable conditions to promote growth. However, to turn potential into concrete results, the city needs to correctly identify the bottlenecks that are hindering the process of transforming resources into added value.
In reality, the GRDP growth for the first nine months has not met the set target, placing significant pressure on the fourth quarter. According to the operational plan, the city needs to achieve a growth rate of 16.55% in the final quarter of the year to meet the annual target. This is a high requirement, demanding greater decisiveness from all levels and sectors in implementation, while clearly identifying areas capable of rapid transformation and making a significant contribution to growth.
Several key economic sectors, such as construction, industry, trade, exports, information and communication, real estate, accommodation, and food services, are still growing at a slower pace than targeted. Science, technology, and digital transformation have not made a significant contribution to growth; private investment and FDI have not been implemented in proportion to the resources mobilized.
In addition, inflationary pressure is also a matter of particular concern. The average CPI for the first nine months increased by 4.91%, higher than the national average by 0.39 percentage points and exceeding the 4.5% control target for the whole year. Specifically, the housing, electricity, water, and construction materials group increased by 7.44%; and the transportation group increased by 6.90%.
These figures show that Hanoi's growth challenge is not simply about promoting investment or expanding economic activity, but also about ensuring efficient resource utilization, improving production capacity, stimulating rational consumption, and controlling factors that put pressure on price levels.
You may also like
Focus efforts on removing bottlenecks, transforming determination into results.
In response to the high growth target in the fourth quarter, Hanoi remains steadfast in its goal of achieving GRDP growth for the entire year of 2026 without any downward adjustment; simultaneously, it is implementing Directive No. 17/CT-UBND dated July 23, 2026, and updating the operational scenario for the fourth quarter, clearly defining the tasks, progress, and responsibilities of each sector and field.
According to this scenario, the fourth quarter needs to achieve a growth rate of 16.55%; of which, industry and construction need to increase by 14.5%; services by 18.42%; agriculture, forestry and fisheries by 3.77%; and product taxes less product subsidies by 11.89%. The targets set show that the city needs to simultaneously promote industries with the potential to create high added value, better exploit the driving force from services, trade, and tourism, and ensure the contribution of all economic sectors.
The primary focus is on removing obstacles and accelerating the progress of investment projects, especially those with the potential to generate significant construction volume and directly contribute to growth. Obstacles related to planning, land, site clearance, resettlement, and technical infrastructure are reviewed and categorized by project, clearly identifying the responsible agency and the deadline for resolution. Promoting public investment must be linked to the quality and efficiency of the projects and the ability to inject capital into the economy, avoiding situations where capital is allocated but projects are slow to implement.
Along with state resources, the city continues to create favorable conditions for private investment and FDI to quickly translate into actual production and business capacity. Improving the investment environment, shortening processing times, supporting businesses in overcoming difficulties, and promoting eligible projects to become operational are crucial to achieving growth targets.
For industries such as construction, trade, and exports that are still growing below targets, specific solutions are needed for each sector and group of businesses. At the same time, it is necessary to continue leveraging the advantages of services, transportation, tourism, and domestic consumption; and improve the efficiency of connections between production, distribution, and markets. Science , technology, and digital transformation also need to be more closely integrated with production, business operations, corporate governance, and public service delivery, thereby creating real added value.
Another important requirement emphasized is controlling inflation, stabilizing the market, and ensuring major balances. With the average CPI increase for the first nine months exceeding the annual control target, the city needs to closely monitor price developments, especially in housing, electricity and water, construction materials, and transportation; strengthen market management, ensure the supply of goods, and limit factors that increase production and living costs.
The double-digit growth target not only requires speed but also demands quality governance. With limited time remaining in 2026, each task must be linked to specific outputs; each department, sector, and locality must proactively handle work within its authority, avoiding prolonged obstacles that could jeopardize development opportunities. Based on the growth results of the third quarter, the city will review the remaining growth shortfall, clearly identify the added value needed to be generated in the fourth quarter, and break down the scenario into three options—high, medium, and low—down to each department, agency, and the People's Committees of communes and wards.
As one of the localities with a low rate of public investment disbursement, Dong Anh commune's total budget revenue has reached approximately 1,767 billion VND, equivalent to 13% of the city's projected target of 13,796 billion VND. The main reason is the low revenue from land use fees. To date, the commune has only collected 156 billion VND from land use fees; other taxes, fees, and revenues have reached approximately 92% of the projected target.
To improve revenue, Nguyen Van Thieng, Deputy Secretary of the Party Committee and Chairman of the People's Committee of Dong Anh commune, said that the locality is urgently completing the dossiers and preparing to organize land auctions; at the same time, focusing on accelerating procedures for land allocation, determining the financial obligations of investors and organizing land use right auctions according to the city's Plan No. 135.
From a data analysis perspective, Hanoi City Statistics Chief Pham Hoai Nam suggested that the city manage growth based on added value and actual contributions; assigning specific scenarios to each sector, key industry, and large enterprise group. Leading indicators such as industrial output, retail sales, transportation, exports, credit, and project progress need to be monitored regularly to promptly identify causes and implement compensation plans when sectors experience lower-than-expected growth.

For public investment, the focus should not only be on disbursement but also on converting capital into added volume and value in 2026. The city needs to prioritize transportation projects, bridges, ring roads, urban railways, and technical infrastructure that have the potential to generate significant volume in October and November; while also quickly resolving obstacles related to land clearance, materials, and infrastructure relocation.
To achieve double-digit growth targets, Vice Chairman of the Hanoi People's Committee Bui Duy Cuong requested that departments, agencies, and localities specify tasks for each month of October, November, and December, and develop concrete plans and solutions for implementation. For outstanding projects, focus should be placed on completing procedures in October, while simultaneously accelerating land clearance, investment implementation, and construction to create further growth momentum.
The Vice Chairman of the City People's Committee also requested that communes and wards expedite land clearance, especially to facilitate land use rights auctions and generate budget revenue. Regarding land along newly opened roads, rural roads, and ring roads, localities must strengthen management and proactively develop appropriate land use plans to effectively utilize land resources while serving socio-economic development.

articles.title: Unlocking resources and creating a foundation for sustainable growth. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Unlocking resources and creating a foundation for sustainable growth.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Ahead of the Second Session of the 16th National Assembly, scheduled to open on October 17th, in an interview with reporters from the People's Representatives Newspaper, Associate Professor Dr. Bui Van Dung, a full-time National Assembly representative on the Economic and Finance Committee, emphasized that to realize the goal of double-digit growth, it is necessary to effectively remove bottlenecks and improve productivity and actual production capacity. The decisions made at the session must create significant changes in improving institutions, unlocking resources, and enhancing accountability in implementation.
High growth must be linked to macroeconomic stability.
- Distinguished delegates, 2026 is the first year of implementing the socio-economic development goals of the new term, with a requirement of GDP growth of 10% or more. Based on the results of the first nine months, how do you assess the likelihood of achieving the full-year target and what are the priority tasks for the final quarter?
- I believe the economy has gained positive momentum, but achieving the full-year target remains a major challenge. According to the General Statistics Office, GDP for the first nine months of 2026 is estimated to have increased by 9.01% year-on-year; the third quarter alone saw a 9.95% increase. Therefore, GDP in the fourth quarter needs to grow by over 12.5% to achieve double-digit growth for the whole year. This is a target that requires significant effort.
The ability to achieve targets depends on converting existing resources into actual output and added value. Therefore, priority should be given to projects that can be completed and put into operation within the year; production facilities capable of increasing capacity; and businesses with orders but facing capital, input, or procedural obstacles. Removing just one bottleneck can simultaneously free up many resources. In addition, each sector and locality needs to update its Q4 growth scenario with specific contributions, clearly identifying projects that can be completed, bases for increasing output, and markets that can be expanded, along with assigned responsibilities and deadlines.
As General Secretary and President To Lam emphasized: "Do things thoroughly to move quickly, don't use caution as a reason for delay." That spirit must be reflected in the quality of decisions and the responsibility for implementation. Applications that meet the requirements but continue to wait will increase business costs and cause missed opportunities for development.
- The double-digit growth target places significant demands on the mobilization and utilization of resources, while the economy is still under pressure from inflation, exchange rates, and external fluctuations. In your opinion, what solutions should be prioritized to both promote high growth and ensure macroeconomic stability?
- The top priority is expanding supply capacity and improving capital efficiency. If resources increase but bottlenecks in energy, infrastructure, human resources, and procedures remain unresolved, the growth impact will be limited, while price pressures may increase.
With the target of achieving GDP growth of 10% or more and average CPI increase of around 4.5% by 2027, it is necessary to quantify the sources of growth and the conditions to ensure its implementation.
First and foremost, fiscal and monetary policies must be coordinated according to actual developments. Budgetary spending should focus on removing obstacles to production, especially in essential infrastructure, energy, logistics, and improving productivity. Simultaneously, it is necessary to facilitate access to capital for businesses with viable business plans, while ensuring liquidity, system safety, and the development of long-term capital channels. Furthermore, it is crucial to proactively develop scenarios to respond to fluctuations in supply, markets, and capital flows, ensuring the major balances of the economy.
I believe that high economic growth must be aimed at improving the people's living standards. The results of governance need to be verified by real income, job quality, and access to essential services. Every dollar invested must create additional production capacity, reduce costs, and enhance the resilience of the economy.
- At the Second Session, the National Assembly is expected to review the implementation of the state budget and public investment plan for 2026 and decide on the plans for 2027. According to delegates, what bottlenecks need to be addressed to accelerate disbursement, improve the efficiency of public investment, and enhance the leading role of state capital? In particular, what mechanisms and policies are needed to more strongly mobilize resources from the private sector?
- As of the end of September 2026, public investment disbursement is estimated to have reached 640 trillion VND, equivalent to 62.6% of the plan. The remaining volume is very large, requiring the proper handling of the causes of delays while ensuring the quality of the projects.
You may also like
I believe it's necessary to clearly distinguish between projects lacking funding and projects that have funding but lack the necessary conditions for implementation. Delays due to land acquisition issues need to be resolved; delays due to design, materials, or coordination issues require addressing those specific stages. Works that meet the requirements should be inspected and paid for promptly; projects that are no longer feasible according to plan must be reviewed and have their funding adjusted according to the appropriate authority.
For 2027, the quality of preparation must be a crucial basis for capital allocation. Investment efficiency needs to be considered from project selection to the exploitation and operation of the project. Disbursed capital will only truly realize its value when the project generates tangible benefits.
For the private sector, it is necessary to implement Resolution 68-NQ/TW and Resolution 198/2025/QH15 effectively, ensuring property rights, freedom of business, and fair competition. Investment opportunities and access to resources must be made public, public-private partnership projects must be well-prepared, and responsibilities and risks must be clearly defined. State capital can only effectively play its leading role when conditions are created for private capital to participate and create new value for the economy.
Institutional breakthroughs must be validated by their effectiveness in implementation.
- To realize the target of an average GDP growth of 10% or more per year during the 2026-2030 period, maintaining traditional drivers is not enough. According to the delegates, what are the decisive breakthroughs to ensure that science , technology, and innovation truly become the driving force for enhancing productivity, competitiveness, and the self-reliance of the economy?
- In my opinion, the decisive breakthrough is building a mechanism to transform knowledge into productivity. The spirit of Resolution 57-NQ/TW must be concretized through changes in research, application, production, and management; effectiveness must be demonstrated in the ability to master technology, product quality, and the competitiveness of Vietnamese enterprises.
First and foremost, research needs to be commissioned based on specific development and business problems. The linkages between businesses, universities, and research institutes must clearly define needs, outputs, and implementation responsibilities. Simultaneously, it is crucial to enhance the capacity of domestic businesses to adopt, improve, and master technology; linking the attraction of high-tech projects with human resource training, supplier development, and production linkages. Another important requirement is to utilize talent according to their assigned tasks and contributions, empowering them genuinely, ensuring resource availability, and evaluating their performance based on the value they create.
To make a significant contribution from the early years of a term, it is necessary to combine long-term investment in strategic technologies with the rapid application of appropriate technologies within businesses. Support programs should be evaluated based on how much productivity is increased, how much costs are reduced, and how much research results are commercialized.
New growth drivers must be demonstrated by higher productivity, greater added value, and better technological mastery, not just by setting targets or implementing programs.
- At the upcoming Second Session, the National Assembly is expected to consider and decide on many important issues concerning socio-economic development, finance, budget, and the improvement of the legal system. What changes do delegates expect from the decisions made at this Session to unlock resources and create a foundation for achieving growth targets in 2027 and the entire 2026-2030 period?
- I expect the Session to bring about three important changes: comprehensively addressing legal obstacles, linking development goals with implementation resources, and clearly defining responsibilities for enforcement.
You may also like
First, it is necessary to review the legal framework throughout the entire investment process, from land access and investment decisions to construction, operation, and fulfillment of financial obligations. Each amendment must clarify the obstacles to be addressed, the responsible agency, and the impact on the time and costs for businesses. Resolving one issue must ensure that the project can proceed through the remaining stages.
Secondly, the socio-economic development plan, budget, and public investment plan for 2027 need to be considered as a unified whole; clarifying sources of growth, projects that create additional production capacity, capital mobilization plans, and resulting financial obligations. articles.title: Entrepreneurs create new drivers of growth. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Entrepreneurs create new drivers of growth.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Continuing the spirit of "serving the nation and benefiting the people" 
|  | 
| Businessman Do Van Ve, Chairman of the Hung Yen Provincial Business Association, Chairman of the Board of Directors, and General Director of Huong Sen Comfor Textile Company Limited. | 
 There are letters, though only a few hundred words long, whose value transcends time and space, enduring forever. This is the letter President Ho Chi Minh sent to the Vietnamese business community on October 13, 1945. He expressed his wish for the business community to contribute to building a strong and prosperous economy and finance, and to invest capital in projects that benefit the nation and its people. The profound truth is that, during a time of immense national hardship, Uncle Ho recognized the crucial role of entrepreneurs in national reconstruction.
 For the entrepreneurs of Hung Yen province, over the past 81 years, the two words "construction" and the four words "benefiting the nation and the people" have retained their value and have been demonstrated very practically: building good businesses, creating more jobs, producing quality products, fulfilling obligations to the State, and sharing with workers and the community.
 October 13th this year holds special significance as it marks the first Entrepreneurs' Day in Hung Yen province after the merger, opening up a new space for larger-scale development, stronger resources, and more opportunities, realizing the aspiration of "The province paves the way - Businesses take flight." This is the action of Hung Yen entrepreneurs today, continuing the spirit of "benefiting the nation and the people" that President Ho Chi Minh instilled in them in the autumn of 1945.
 Attracting more and more high-quality FDI projects. 
|  | 
| Businessman Bui The Long, General Director of Green i-Park Joint Stock Company | 
 Over the past period, Green i-Park has always received attention, support, and favorable conditions from the provincial leadership and the Hung Yen Provincial Business Association. This is both a favorable condition and a responsibility for the company to continue improving the infrastructure quality of Lien Ha Thai Industrial Park (Green iP-1), attracting suitable investors and businesses in the supply chain, and striving to ensure that each FDI project contributes more to businesses, workers, and the locality.
 To implement the Government 's strategic direction of shifting FDI attraction from quantity to selectively attracting high-quality, technologically advanced, and environmentally friendly projects, as a pioneering infrastructure investor in the Thai Binh Economic Zone, we recognize our responsibility to continue working with the province to overcome limitations, leverage advantages and achievements, strengthen competitiveness, and thereby attract more high-quality FDI projects to the province, making a more practical contribution to the development of Hung Yen.
 "The midwife" expands export market share. 
|  | 
| Ms. Nguyen Thi Mau, Chairwoman of the Board of Directors of Pure Global Joint Stock Company | 
 Experience has shown that close support from local authorities is crucial to the survival of businesses. In-depth trade programs organized by the Department of Industry and Trade have provided invaluable opportunities by directly inviting trade attachés and international partners to learn about and assess the capabilities of factories.
 Besides export promotion efforts, businesses are also boosted through programs supporting technological innovation, agricultural extension, and standardization of security and order. The close synergy between the proactive mindset of state management agencies and the aspirations of businesses has created a powerful impetus, helping Vietnamese goods not only dominate the domestic market but also confidently penetrate deeper into the global supply chain.
 Unleashing 2.5 trillion VND from "dormant" projects 
|  | 
| Mr. Le Hoang Chau, Chairman of the Ho Chi Minh City Real Estate Association (HoREA) | 
 Vietnam is shifting its growth focus from cheap labor to a knowledge-based economy, digitalization, and green energy. Opportunities abound, but the risks from geopolitical competition are also extremely fierce.
 The most urgent task now is to unlock investment resources. The policy of definitively resolving 100% of stalled projects within 5 years is a historic turning point. This decision will free up tens of thousands of hectares of land and more than 2.5 trillion VND of capital that has been buried for many years, creating a solid foundation for achieving double-digit GDP growth.
 In Ho Chi Minh City, resolving difficulties for 650 projects has resulted in a supply of 27,374 housing units. However, purchasing power remains weak due to high loan interest rates. The market is severely lacking in social housing and affordable commercial housing. Therefore, policies to address these issues need to be comprehensively institutionalized by the National Assembly into the Land Law, the Housing Law, and the Real Estate Business Law.
 From outsourcing "satellites" to strategic intermediate links 
|  | 
| Mr. Nguyen Van Tien, Vice President of the Vietnam Industrial Real Estate Association (VIREA) | 
 In the current wave of global supply chain restructuring, Vietnamese private enterprises should not only play the role of "satellite" suppliers of components, processing, or logistics, but must become the main force in retaining and increasing domestic value.
 To realize this, the mindset needs to shift from "attracting FDI at low cost" to "supporting FDI with localization capabilities." Businesses must invest heavily in design, research and development (R&D), testing, and smart packaging. From a macro perspective, the State needs to pave the way for private investment in "green, digital, and interconnected" logistics infrastructure.
 "Contracting out 10" for the era of private economy 
|  | 
| Mr. Dinh Hong Ky, Chairman of Secoin, Chairman of SACA Association | 
Resolution 68-NQ/TW represents a turning point in thinking: private enterprises are no longer considered entities needing support, but rather forces that create national growth. The goal of having 2 million enterprises nationwide by 2030, contributing 55-58% of GDP, is a grand ambition.
 However, businesses are struggling with five bottlenecks: policy changes, high compliance costs, inequality in access to land and capital, weak demand, and the fear of legal risks among enforcement officials. A business cannot plan for 10-20 years if fire safety standards or investment procedures are constantly changing.
 Similar to the "Contract 10" system in agriculture , Resolution 68-NQ/TW only becomes effective when it genuinely empowers businesses, protects property rights, and builds an ecosystem that fosters long-term trust.
 Partnering with businesses to create new growth drivers. 
|  | 
| Mr. Luu Trung Thai, Chairman of the Board of Directors of Military Commercial Joint Stock Bank (MB) | 
 As Vietnam aims for high and sustainable growth, the business community continues to play a central role in promoting innovation, enhancing competitiveness, and driving the economy. To realize this aspiration, unlocking and effectively allocating financial resources is of particular importance.
 MB Bank defines its mission not only as providing capital, but also as accompanying businesses in the process of transforming their growth models, expanding production and business, and participating more deeply in the value chain. The bank prioritizes resources for core economic sectors, strategic infrastructure projects, key industries, promoting digital transformation, green transformation, and the circular economy.
 We are committed to a strategy of rapid yet sustainable growth, based on rigorous risk management, technology, and real-time data. MB aims to become a leading financial group, partnering with the Vietnamese business community to seize opportunities and make practical contributions to the country's prosperous development.
 Lowering costs creates breathing room for production. 
|  | 
| Mr. Nguyen Chi Trung, Chairman of Gia Dinh Group | 
 If we want the private sector to become the driving force of growth, we must first ensure that businesses have the "breathing ground" to maintain production from now until the end of the year.
 The biggest challenge is capital flow. High bank interest rates are eroding profits, while credit disbursement conditions remain restrictive. Furthermore, pressure from rising fuel prices is driving up logistics and raw material costs dramatically. For the export sector, global market fluctuations are further shrinking orders.
 Complex administrative and land procedures also hinder businesses from expanding their production lines. In particular, restrictions on overtime hours prevent seasonal industries like textiles and footwear from flexibly increasing working hours when orders are urgent. For businesses to survive and thrive by 2027, the government needs to quickly launch preferential credit packages specifically for exports, while also significantly removing administrative and labor barriers.
 Institutional "green light" and the aspiration for billion-dollar exports. 
|  | 
| Ms. Ton Nu Xuan Quyen, Chairwoman of the Board of Directors of BLUSAIGON Joint Stock Company | 
 The gap between policy and implementation remains the deepest "wound." Businesses bear too many layers of compliance costs, leading to thin profit margins and a loss of room for reinvestment in R&D and human resources. The valuation of intellectual property (brands, expertise) for loan collateral is almost zero.
 In the handicraft sector alone, export turnover is aiming for $5 billion, but 98% of the 5,400 craft villages remain stuck in the household-based model lacking standardized production. articles.title: MAS Tightens Safeguards on Roadshows Selling Financial Products - Fintech Singapore
articles.summary: MAS Tightens Safeguards on Roadshows Selling Financial Products  Fintech Singapore
articles.full_text:
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) will expect financial institutions to hold public prospecting activities, such as roadshows, only within designated areas at commercial premises.
The regulator announced the enhanced safeguards after a public consultation, citing concerns that poorly conducted prospecting can subject consumers to unsolicited or persistent solicitation.
Financial institutions will be expected to appoint suitably qualified individuals to oversee their representatives’ conduct at these events.
At the start of any engagement, MAS expects representatives to tell consumers clearly that they intend to market financial products or services, and to obtain their consent before going further.
Street canvassing and door-to-door prospecting remain prohibited.
“Consumers should not feel pressured or caught off guard when approached about financial products and services,”
said Lim Tuang Lee, Assistant Managing Director (Capital Markets), MAS.
Lim said the safeguards would help ensure financial institutions treat consumers fairly and professionally, while “allowing financial institutions to continue engaging consumers through appropriate channels”.
The safeguards for physical prospecting complement the [safeguards for digital advertising that MAS introduced in September 2025, which cover content produced by influencers and affiliate marketers acting for financial institutions.
MAS said the two sets of measures reinforce its expectation that firms engage consumers responsibly across all marketing and distribution channels.
MAS first proposed tighter controls on prospecting in public places in April 2023, and has published a response paper setting out the feedback it received and the safeguards it plans to implement.
The regulator will incorporate the changes into its Guidelines on Standards of Conduct for Marketing and Distribution Activities, which it plans to issue in 2027.
Financial institutions will then have a nine-month transition period to implement them.

articles.title: Making AI a new growth engine. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Making AI a new growth engine.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
The national strategy on artificial intelligence to 2030, with a vision to 2045, recently issued by the Prime Minister, sets a target for the AI economy to be equivalent to approximately 6% of GDP by 2030.
AI is entering business practice.
According to the National Strategy on Artificial Intelligence to 2030, issued under Decision No. 1671/QD-TTg dated August 28, 2026, Vietnam aims for an AI-driven economy equivalent to approximately 6% of GDP; a minimum 10-15% increase in labor productivity in AI-applied industries and sectors; and an export value of approximately US$5 billion for AI-integrated products, services, and solutions. The strategy also aims for 60% of businesses applying AI to experience increased productivity, reduced costs, or increased revenue.
In fact, some domestic businesses have shifted AI from a support tool into an integral part of their production and business operations. At FPT Software, by 2025, the company will transition to an "AI-First Company" model, integrating AI into the entire software development and operation process. FleziPT is used as the platform for this strategy, contributing to an 8.2% increase in internal productivity in 2025. FPT's revenue in 2025 is projected to reach VND 70,113 billion, an 11.6% increase compared to the previous year.
Speaking at the SANDBOX 2026 International Conference, Professor Tran Thi Thanh Tu, Head of the Science and Innovation Committee and Director of the Science and Technology Development Fund at Vietnam National University, Hanoi, stated that AI and digital transformation are becoming the foundation of productivity, competitiveness, and sustainable development in Vietnam and ASEAN.
From there, Professor Tran Thi Thanh Tu emphasized the directions including value-based innovation, using AI to enhance human capabilities, innovating training, responsible AI governance, and strengthening cooperation between universities, businesses, the government , and international partners.
From AI applications to data problems
Integrating AI into production and business is just the first step; for technology to truly create productivity and efficiency, businesses must solve the data problem. Dr. Vo Tri Thanh, Director of the Institute for Brand Strategy and Competition Research, stated that data has become a "factor of production" in the modern economy, similar to capital, labor, resources, and technology. As an input to the production process, data needs to be allocated efficiently and have relatively free movement to maximize its value. However, unlike traditional factors of production, data is subject to numerous requirements regarding privacy, security, national defense, and sovereignty .
From this perspective, according to Dr. Vo Tri Thanh, when data is considered an asset, it must, in principle, be tradable. However, to achieve this, clear ownership and property rights over the data need to be established. This is a complex issue because data can simultaneously relate to individuals, businesses, organizations, and even nations. For businesses, these issues become increasingly significant as AI is deeply integrated into production and business operations. Data on customers, markets, production, finance, or supply chains can become input for analytical and forecasting systems. But if data is scattered, difficult to connect, or lacks mechanisms for exploitation, the economic value of this resource will be difficult to realize.
Notably, the Strategy aims for total investment in AI to reach 1-1.5% of GDP annually, including resources from the State, domestic and foreign enterprises, investment funds, public-private partnerships, and other legitimate sources, with investment from the state budget for AI reaching approximately 0.6% of total annual state budget expenditure.
These goals demonstrate that AI cannot develop in isolation from the fundamental resources of the economy. For businesses, investing in AI is therefore not just about acquiring more technological tools, but also about reorganizing data, enhancing human resources capabilities, improving processes, and increasing business efficiency.
From the economic target of AI accounting for approximately 6% of GDP by 2030 to the requirement of a 10-15% increase in productivity in AI-applied industries, Vietnam is setting more specific metrics for its transformation. In this context, the value of AI will not lie in how many new tools businesses possess, but in the technology's ability to help the economy create more value with the same amount of resources and gradually move up to higher value-added stages in the value chain.

articles.title: Singapore Logistics Firms Expand Automation and EV Infrastructure - OpenGov Asia
articles.summary: Singapore Logistics Firms Expand Automation and EV Infrastructure  OpenGov Asia
articles.full_text:
Logistics companies in Singapore are investing in automation, digital systems and electric vehicle infrastructure as they respond to land constraints, labour pressures and supply-chain disruptions. Supported by programmes from Enterprise Singapore, firms across the sector are introducing technologies aimed at improving productivity, reducing emissions and strengthening operational resilience. Examples include vertically stacked trailer storage, battery-swapping systems for electric heavy vehicles and digital forecasting platforms designed to improve inventory management. Details of the initiatives were outlined in a recent Enterprise Singapore report.
The developments reflect broader efforts to modernise Singapore’s logistics ecosystem through digitalisation and automation. Similar initiatives can also be seen in projects such as automated parcel sorting systems and wider national discussions around infrastructure resilience and energy security.
Using automation to overcome land and labour constraints
One Singapore logistics operator has introduced a vertical trailer parking system that allows up to eight trailer chassis to be stored within a single parking lot. According to the company, the system reduces the land needed for trailer storage by up to seven times and frees approximately 0.4 hectares of operational space.
The project was supported through Enterprise Singapore’s Enterprise Development Grant, which will transition to the EDGE Grant from 30 September. Alongside the new parking system, the company has digitised container inspections, automated routine processes and moved parts of its workflow online.
Ground staff who previously carried out manual inspections are now trained to oversee automated systems and digital tools. The company has also introduced automated seal dispensers to reduce repetitive manual handling tasks.
“In Singapore, you cannot simply buy more land. Operating in Singapore requires us to be relentless about efficiency.” Lim Kian Chin, Managing Director
The company’s management team participated in Enterprise Singapore’s Enterprise Leadership for Transformation programme in 2021, which focuses on helping business leaders develop long-term growth and transformation strategies.
Battery swapping supports electric heavy vehicles
Another logistics-related initiative focuses on reducing emissions from heavy goods vehicles through battery-swapping technology. In Singapore, charging large electric vehicle batteries can take up to four hours, creating operational challenges for logistics fleets that require high vehicle utilisation.
A local operator has developed a battery-swapping station in Tuas that enables depleted batteries to be replaced with fully charged units in about five minutes. The facility operates under a four-year trial supported by the Land Transport Authority.
The company previously launched a heavy goods vehicle charging hub in 2023 as part of broader efforts to support the transition to electric transport. Enterprise Singapore assisted with regulatory coordination and support for operators participating in electric prime mover trials.
“Without the EnterpriseSG team proactively engaging the regulatory bodies to study and develop standards for swap stations, we couldn’t have done it.” Ryan Woon, Director
The use of data and intelligent systems is also becoming increasingly important in transport and logistics planning. This trend aligns with wider regional efforts exploring how AI and analytics are shaping mobility systems and freight operations, including developments highlighted in AI-driven mobility initiatives.
Digital forecasting improves supply-chain resilience
Supply-chain visibility and forecasting have also become a priority for companies managing temperature-sensitive goods and fluctuating demand. One Singapore food supply-chain operator is developing a digital platform designed to improve stock replenishment monitoring and procurement planning.
The system was developed after disruptions during the Covid-19 pandemic exposed weaknesses in traditional inventory management approaches. Despite holding several weeks of stock, the company faced shortages when demand increased suddenly while supply chains were disrupted.
The digital platform aims to provide earlier warnings of supply risks, recommend stock movements and support faster operational decisions. The company’s leadership team participated in Enterprise Singapore’s Scale-Up programme, which supports high-growth local enterprises in strengthening leadership and growth planning capabilities.
“Resilience requires earlier information, better forecasting and faster coordinated decisions.” Vincent Seo, Director
Long-term shift towards smarter logistics operations
The projects illustrate how Singapore’s logistics sector is adapting to operational pressures through automation, digitalisation and alternative energy infrastructure. Across the industry, firms are seeking ways to improve land use, raise productivity and strengthen resilience against global supply-chain disruptions.
One logistics operator is currently developing an automated logistics and container hub in Jurong that is expected to increase storage capacity by 30 per cent while using approximately 67 per cent less land than its current operations when completed in 2027. Meanwhile, battery-swapping trials and AI-driven forecasting tools continue to be tested for broader operational use across the sector.
Enterprise Singapore said it will continue supporting companies as they develop new capabilities and respond to changing global trade conditions. The agency described these efforts as part of Singapore’s wider strategy to strengthen its role as a reliable regional connectivity and logistics hub.
