articles.title: Asia News Update: China-EU Trade Deal, Indian Protests, North Korean Missiles and Singapore's AI Warning Dominate October 12 Headlines - NetNewsLedger
articles.summary: Asia News Update: China-EU Trade Deal, Indian Protests, North Korean Missiles and Singapore's AI Warning Dominate October 12 Headlines  NetNewsLedger
articles.full_text:
Asia news for October 12, 2026: China-EU trade negotiations, India’s inflation and protests, North Korean missiles, and Singapore’s AI warnings
NetNewsLedger International News | Monday, October 12, 2026
THUNDER BAY, ON — Asia’s largest economies are facing a week of growing political, economic and security challenges as trade disputes, inflation, artificial intelligence and military tensions reshape the region.
For Monday, October 12, 2026, the leading developments across Singapore, China, India and Japan include a new China-European Union trade arrangement, widespread political protests in India, North Korean ballistic missile launches near Japan, and warnings from Singapore’s leaders about the impact of artificial intelligence on employment.
The news matters far beyond Asia. Decisions being made in Beijing, New Delhi, Singapore and Tokyo could influence Canadian manufacturers, Ontario’s critical minerals industry, global investment and the cost of imported goods.
For Northwestern Ontario, where mining, forestry, transportation and international trade remain essential parts of the economy, developments in Asian markets deserve close attention.
Singapore: Artificial Intelligence, Economic Growth and Public Health
1. President Tharman warns artificial intelligence is threatening entry-level jobs
Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam delivered a warning at the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok on Monday.
Speaking about the growing use of artificial intelligence, Tharman said governments need to address a decline in demand for workers entering the labour market.
New university graduates may be among the first to experience the change, as businesses turn to automated systems for tasks previously handled by junior employees.
The Singapore president also warned that AI could widen economic divisions between richer countries and developing nations.
The concern is not simply that existing jobs will disappear. It is that young workers could lose the entry-level opportunities that traditionally allow them to gain experience and advance into better-paying careers.
The issue has become an international economic challenge as companies invest heavily in AI systems that can handle research, financial analysis, customer service and administrative work.
2. Prime Minister Lawrence Wong calls for AI to strengthen society
Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong is also urging businesses and educators to use artificial intelligence without sacrificing the development of human skills.
Wong said Singapore must protect basic learning in schools and ensure employers continue training and mentoring junior employees.
His government’s approach places emphasis on retraining, fair treatment of displaced workers and regional digital cooperation through the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
The message is that Singapore wants to benefit from AI-driven growth without allowing technology to weaken education or eliminate pathways into employment.
3. Singapore faces an important monetary policy decision on October 14
The Monetary Authority of Singapore is expected to tighten monetary policy when it releases its next decision on Wednesday, October 14.
All 10 economists surveyed by Reuters before the meeting expected further tightening.
Singapore’s economy has benefited from strong investment in technology and AI infrastructure, but rising energy prices and food supply risks have created fresh inflation concerns.
Unlike the Bank of Canada, Singapore’s central bank primarily manages monetary conditions through the exchange rate rather than a conventional policy interest rate.
Economists are watching whether the authority will allow the Singapore dollar to appreciate more quickly to help control the cost of imported goods.
4. Smoke and haze raise health concerns
Singapore is also dealing with unhealthy air quality linked to regional haze.
The government has activated medical subsidy measures beginning October 12 to help eligible residents seek treatment for haze-related health problems.
The environmental problem has affected transportation, with Malaysian carrier Firefly cancelling flights between Seletar and Subang airports as a safety precaution.
The situation illustrates how air pollution crossing international borders can affect public health, business operations and transportation across Southeast Asia.
Why Singapore matters to Canada: Singapore is a major financial, shipping and technology centre. Its experience with AI, inflation and regional trade offers an early view of challenges that Canadian businesses and governments are also confronting.
China: European Trade Negotiations, Taiwan and Growing Economic Pressures
1. China and European Union reach arrangement on hybrid vehicle exports
One of Monday’s biggest international business developments comes from trade negotiations between Beijing and Brussels.
China’s Ministry of Commerce announced the outcome of extensive consultations with the European Union over trade in hybrid and electric vehicles.
The arrangement addresses European concerns about the growing volume of Chinese-made vehicles entering its markets while attempting to provide Chinese exporters with greater certainty.
European officials have indicated the measures could sharply reduce Chinese hybrid vehicle shipments to the EU. China says the arrangement must avoid discrimination and provide a predictable framework for exporters.
The outcome follows three months of negotiations involving senior trade officials.
However, the agreement does not resolve every trade dispute between China and Europe.
The broader issue remains competition between China’s rapidly expanding automotive industry and European manufacturers facing significant pressure from lower-cost imports.
Why this matters to Ontario
Ontario’s automobile manufacturing industry is closely linked to the North American market, but competition from China has become a major international issue.
Chinese electric vehicle manufacturers have developed substantial capacity in battery technology, vehicle assembly and supply chains.
The European arrangement could influence how other governments consider tariffs, import restrictions and industrial policy.
For Northern Ontario, the longer-term implications include investment in nickel, lithium, graphite and other minerals used in batteries and advanced manufacturing.
A significant shift in where electric vehicles are manufactured can influence which mining and processing projects attract investment.
2. Beijing imposes sanctions on officials from two countries that recognize Taiwan
China announced sanctions Monday against officials from Paraguay and Belize over their countries’ diplomatic relationships with Taiwan.
The sanctions target Paraguay’s Communications Minister Gustavo Villate and Belize’s Foreign Minister Francis Fonseca.
Measures include travel restrictions covering Hong Kong and Macau and prohibitions on cooperation with Chinese organizations.
Taiwan condemned the move as interference in the sovereign foreign-policy decisions of other countries.
Beijing considers Taiwan part of China and has worked for years to reduce the number of countries maintaining official diplomatic relations with Taipei.
The sanctions are largely symbolic, but they underscore continuing diplomatic tensions surrounding Taiwan’s international recognition.
3. China’s growing debt raises questions about its economic model
A separate economic analysis published Monday by The Wall Street Journal examines the mounting debt associated with China’s investments in manufacturing, technology, infrastructure and local government projects.
China has continued to prioritize industrial expansion and technological leadership, even as weak domestic demand and difficulties in the property market put pressure on economic growth.
High borrowing levels have raised concerns about whether some investments will generate enough revenue to repay their costs.
The challenge for Beijing is balancing support for strategically important industries with the need to strengthen household consumption and financial stability.
China’s ability to manage its debt will affect global demand for minerals, construction materials and industrial equipment.
4. China continues investing in artificial intelligence infrastructure
Chinese companies and governments are accelerating investment in computing facilities designed to support large-scale AI applications.
State news agency Xinhua reported Monday on the development of so-called token factories, facilities that provide the computing capacity required to run AI services at scale.
The expansion reflects China’s ambition to compete with the United States in artificial intelligence and the infrastructure behind it.
Such growth requires advanced chips, electricity, cooling systems, data centres and substantial capital investment.
For Northwestern Ontario, the important question is whether this global technology expansion creates sustainable demand for copper, nickel and other mineral inputs, and how much of that opportunity Canadian producers can capture.
India: Mass Protests, Rising Inflation and Renewed Canada-India Diplomacy
1. Political protests challenge India’s election authorities
One of India’s biggest stories Monday is a growing protest movement challenging the country’s election authorities.
Thousands of demonstrators marched in New Delhi demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
The protests centre on allegations that changes to electoral rolls removed large numbers of voters and unfairly benefited Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party.
Opposition groups and youth activists have accused election officials of undermining democratic accountability.
The allegations are serious, but they should not be treated as proven findings of electoral misconduct.

articles.summary: Union Finance Minister Smt. Nirmala Sitharaman concludes successful visit to Singapore, focusing on strengthening investment and financial cooperation  पीआईबी
articles.full_text:
Union Minister for Finance and Corporate Affairs Smt. Nirmala Sitharaman concluded her official visit to Singapore from October 8 to 11, 2026, after a series of high-level bilateral engagements and meetings with leading global investors, financial institutions and businesses aimed at strengthening India–Singapore economic and financial cooperation.
During the visit, the Union Finance Minister called on H.E. Mr. Tharman Shanmugaratnam, President of Singapore, and H.E. Mr. Lawrence Wong, Prime Minister of Singapore, and met H.E. Mr. Gan Kim Yong, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade & Industry, and H.E. Dr. Vivian Balakrishnan, Minister for Foreign Affairs.
The engagements provided an opportunity to review progress in advancing the outcomes of the 4th India–Singapore Ministerial Roundtable (ISMR) and explore avenues to further deepen the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership. The two sides also exchanged views on strengthening India–ASEAN cooperation and regional economic ties, including in the run-up to Singapore’s ASEAN Chairmanship in 2027.
Smt. Sitharaman also participated in a luncheon meeting hosted by H.E. Mr. Tharman Shanmugaratnam, President of Singapore, and Ms. Kristalina Georgieva, Managing Director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF). The luncheon brought together senior leaders from global financial institutions, investment firms, academia and the Singapore Government, providing an opportunity for exchanges on global economic and financial developments.
Discussions with Singapore’s leadership focused on expanding bilateral investment, strengthening financial connectivity and advancing cooperation in emerging technologies. The Union Finance Minister highlighted India’s strong macroeconomic fundamentals, growth prospects and ongoing policy reforms, and encouraged greater investment by Singapore-based institutional investors and businesses in India’s growth story. Select infrastructure projects from the National Investment and Infrastructure Fund (NIIF) pipeline were highlighted for consideration by investors, with a view to facilitating follow-up discussions and engagement with relevant Indian authorities.
As part of the investment outreach, Union Minister for Finance and Corporate Affairs Smt. Nirmala Sitharaman participated in a business roundtable with senior representatives of leading global financial institutions and investment firms, including JPMorgan Chase, BlackRock, Deutsche Bank, PIMCO, the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA), Carlyle, Temasek, Millennium Management, Citadel, and Brevan Howard. The discussions covered India’s continued commitment to economic reforms and resultant economic resilience amidst global uncertainties, developments in global and domestic financial markets, the implications of rapid advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI), and opportunities to attract greater global capital into Indian assets. The participants expressed confidence in India’s growth story. They remarked that they look forward to continued progressive, fiscally prudent, predictable, growth-oriented policies of the government along with a focus on infrastructure.
The Union Finance Minister also held separate bilateral meetings with senior leadership of major institutional investors, financial institutions, and global corporations, including Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group (MUFG), Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SMBC), Wellington Management, Standard Chartered Bank, GIC (Government of Singapore Investment Corporation), DBS Bank, Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken (SEB), Temasek, TPG, HPS Investment Partners, CapitaLand Investment, Intel, British International Investment (BII), IHH Healthcare, and B Capital.
The senior leadership of these financial institutions and global corporations expressed strong investment interest in key sectors, including consumer markets, start-ups, FinTech, Deep-tech, and healthcare. These engagements also explored investment and financing opportunities across infrastructure, especially AI and AI related infrastructure including semiconductors and data centres, renewable energy for India’s energy transition and energy security, manufacturing, MSMEs and trade finance, financial services, food supply chains and other growth-oriented sectors.
Opportunities relating to aircraft leasing, treasury centres and greater participation by global investors in India’s financial markets were also explored. Mobilising long-term institutional capital and expanding avenues for financing India’s infrastructure and development priorities were key themes of the investment discussions. Smt. Sitharaman encouraged investors to explore opportunities through the NIIF and GIFT International Financial Services Centre (GIFT IFSC). The participants reaffirmed their strong commitment to the Indian market and expressed their intention to sustain and expand their investments in India, reflecting continued confidence in the country’s long-term growth prospects.
The visit also advanced dialogue on financial connectivity and emerging financial technologies. In meetings with Singapore’s financial authorities, including the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), both sides exchanged views on frontier technologies such as tokenisation of financial assets, digital money, central bank digital currencies (CBDCs), interoperability and trusted settlement arrangements. Singapore expressed its keenness to share its experience in asset tokenisation. The discussions provided an opportunity to explore further cooperation between the financial authorities of the two countries on emerging technologies and their application in financial markets.
Engagements with businesses also covered opportunities arising from India’s expanding semiconductor and AI ecosystems. Discussions included investment under the India Semiconductor Mission, development of skilled manpower, industry-linked training and AI skilling initiatives, and the application of AI in banking and financial services. Other areas included renewable energy, electric mobility, aviation maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO), food security and processing, sustainable finance, and healthcare infrastructure.
Engagement with the Singapore Business Federation (SBF) focused on strengthening business-to-business linkages through targeted business matching and visits by Singapore business delegations to India for meaningful interactions with Indian businesses and State Governments. SBF highlighted potential areas for collaboration, including semiconductor supply chains, MRO, food security and food processing.
The visit reaffirmed the depth of the India–Singapore partnership and the shared interest in translating ongoing policy dialogue into greater investment, business engagement and financial cooperation. The wide-ranging interactions with Singapore’s political leadership, institutional investors, financial institutions and businesses helped showcase India’s growth and investment opportunities, identify areas of mutual interest and strengthen channels for follow-up engagement. The discussions are expected to support continued efforts to mobilise long-term capital, deepen financial connectivity and advance cooperation in emerging and strategic sectors.
Smt. Sitharaman was accompanied by the CEO of the National Investment and Infrastructure Fund (NIIF), the Chairperson of the International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA), and senior officials of the Department of Economic Affairs.

articles.title: Chinese drivers stopped buying cars, so China’s automakers shipped them abroad: exports are up 64% while domestic sales fell 27% - Fortune
articles.summary: Chinese drivers stopped buying cars, so China’s automakers shipped them abroad: exports are up 64% while domestic sales fell 27%  Fortune
articles.full_text:
China’s passenger car exports surged 64% in September from the same month in 2025, an industry association reported Monday, as Chinese automakers increasingly focus on exports to drive growth amid sluggish domestic sales.
China exported around 919,000 passenger vehicles in September, lifted by overseas demand for plug-in hybrids and pure electric vehicles, data from the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers showed. In the first nine months of 2026, China exported over 7.1 million passenger cars, up more than 70% from the same period last year.
Meanwhile, domestic passenger car sales in China fell for most of the year as automakers faced weaker consumer confidence at home and scaled-back government subsidies. They fell 27% year-on-year in September to over 1.6 million units, according to the association.
China is the world’s largest vehicle exporter, but is facing increasing skepticism from trade partners who fear it’s undermining their domestic industries and trade balance.
The EU is capping Chinese hybrid vehicle imports at 350,000 a year, officials say.
Chinese car sales grow in regions including Europe
In recent months, Chinese automakers have more aggressively targeted rapid growth in overseas markets such as Europe, Latin America, Southeast Asia and Africa. Canada is also opening its doors to Chinese EV exports under a tariff cut deal with China.
The industry increasingly relies on overseas markets for sales and profit growth as players seek to offset weakness in the domestic market, analyst Stephen Chan of S&P Global Ratings said.
Consultancy AlixPartners and some auto analysts expect Chinese automakers to export nearly 10 million vehicles globally in 2026.
In Europe, Chinese automakers are increasingly challenging the European auto industry with lower costs and prices. AlixPartners’ analysis found, for example, that a Chinese-branded EV costs around $20,000 to produce, compared with $31,000 for a European equivalent.
EU to cap Chinese hybrid vehicle imports at 350,000 annually
The EU has already imposed higher tariffs on pure electric vehicles from China. Recent policy discussions have also focused on the rapid rise in sales of Chinese hybrids in Europe.
Amid growing pressure on the EU to rebalance trade with China, EU trade chief Maroš Šefčovič said Friday that the two sides had reached an interim deal that could halve Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to the bloc.
The agreement sets an annual import quota of 350,000 hybrid vehicles made in China, including plug-in hybrids, two senior EU officials said Monday. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity, in line with European Commission policy.
Starting as early as December, customs authorities across the 27-nation bloc will coordinate monitoring of these imports and halt further shipments once the annual quota is reached, one official said. The limit excludes cars made in Europe by Chinese companies.
Analysts said protectionist measures would likely continue to cloud Chinese automakers’ overseas outlook.
“You can’t expect BYD or the other OEMs (manufacturers) to export too many cars without facing tariffs or pushbacks from the foreign governments,” Xiao Feng, head of Hong Kong and China industrials research at investment group CITIC CLSA, told reporters recently.
Geopolitics is the biggest challenge to BYD’s overseas expansion, executive vice president Stella Li, who leads the Chinese EV giant’s global growth, acknowledged at an event this month.
BYD has therefore been expanding overseas production, including setting up plants in Thailand, Indonesia, Brazil and Hungary, she told the Milken Institute Asia Summit in Singapore.
More overseas production limits impact from trade curbs
Chinese automakers will likely continue to expand overseas production to reduce exposure to tariffs and other risks, said Ming Lee, head of Greater China automotive and industrial research at BofA Global Research, a unit of Bank of America.
“More and more volume will be made locally,” he said.
Meanwhile, the U.S. has effectively shut Chinese EVs out of its market with hefty tariffs. President Donald Trump’s meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping during Xi’s state visit to Washington last month yielded no deal on access for Chinese EVs.
Experts say continued political uncertainty likely makes the U.S. market a lower priority for Chinese automakers.
___
McNeil reported from Brussels.

 The program, attended by representatives from the Solana Foundation, opened up opportunities for discussions on potential collaborations with the global technology ecosystem.
 Connecting resources and expanding opportunities for international cooperation.
 The signing ceremony took place at FUTA Residence (196–198 Vo Nguyen Giap Street, Da Nang City), marking the beginning of a cooperative relationship between FUTA Land and DISSC. It also demonstrates the company's proactive approach to networking in the context of Da Nang's efforts to promote digital transformation , innovation, and attract international investment. 
|  |

 According to the memorandum of understanding, the two sides will focus on three key areas of cooperation.
 In this collaboration, FUTA Land and DISSC will strengthen connections between investment funds, financial institutions, strategic investors, and international partners with investment opportunities and project development by FUTA Land.
 Both sides will collaborate to build a service ecosystem to support businesses, experts, and international investors coming to work and live in Da Nang; and at the same time, research and access new technologies in the fields of digital finance, blockchain, and real estate management.
 The presence of Solana Foundation at the program facilitated discussions among the parties regarding the potential application of blockchain technology in business operations, asset management, and the development of new investment models.
 Some areas of research interest include digitizing transaction processes, enhancing transparency in asset management, and exploring the possibility of digitizing economic rights associated with real estate.
 These are directions that need further research and evaluation regarding feasibility, economic efficiency, and compliance with Vietnamese law before being considered for implementation in practice.
 Within the framework of the program, representatives from both sides spoke about cooperation opportunities, performed signing ceremonies, and exchanged views on areas with potential for future development.
 Both sides expect the cooperative relationship to gradually materialize through practical research programs, initiatives, and activities that are consistent with each party's capabilities and development orientation.
 FUTA Land aims for development based on technology and strategic partnerships.

 In addition to developing land reserves and project portfolios, the company focuses on applying technology to improve management efficiency, operations, and customer experience.

 Connecting with international innovation support organizations and technology partners is seen as an opportunity for FUTA Land to access new knowledge and solutions, while also seeking applications that suit practical needs.
 Against the backdrop of Da Nang's efforts to develop an International Financial Center, a Free Trade Zone, and an innovation ecosystem, FUTA Land expects this collaboration to contribute to expanding its partner network, creating more investment opportunities, and enhancing its long-term competitiveness.

articles.full_text:
BUSAN — The Busan-Jinhae Free Economic Zone Authority is stepping up efforts to draw investment from Southeast Asia and expand its network of global companies through a partnership with Vietnam's largest industrial park developer and operator.
The authority said on the 12th that it signed a memorandum of understanding at the headquarters of Vietnam Singapore Industrial Park (VSIP) to strengthen cooperation on industrial park development and investment promotion.
Park Sung-ho, commissioner of the authority, and Nguyen Phu Thinh, VSIP's chief executive, attended the signing along with other senior officials from both organizations. They discussed a broad range of joint measures covering investment promotion and support for resident companies.
VSIP was established in 1996 on the basis of economic cooperation between the Vietnamese and Singaporean governments and ranks as Vietnam's premier industrial park developer and operator. It currently runs 30 projects across Vietnam and has attracted about 1,000 global companies from 30 countries.
An official at the authority said the agreement is aimed at linking the leading global manufacturers based in VSIP parks with the advanced logistics and industrial infrastructure centered on Busan New Port, building a practical bridge between Korea and Vietnam.
The two organizations agreed to flesh out cooperation in several areas, including sharing know-how on industrial park development and operation, exchanging investment information and networks, identifying and connecting potential investors, and supporting resident companies in their local operations.
Using the partnership as a springboard, the authority plans to actively promote the free economic zone's investment environment to Korean companies operating in Vietnam as well as global manufacturers. Its strategy is to identify early and attract firms weighing a return to Korea or the establishment of new production bases in the country.
The authority also plans to highlight Busan New Port's world-class port and logistics infrastructure and the competitiveness of its industrial parks to companies based in VSIP parks, broadening the scope of trade and investment.
"VSIP is a key institution that has led Vietnam's growth by drawing large-scale investment from global companies," Park said. "By closely sharing the experience the two organizations have built up in industrial park development and investment promotion, and by continuing to exchange corporate and investment information, we will create new business opportunities linking the two countries."

articles.title: Opening new avenues for development: From urbanization to 'urban economy' - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Opening new avenues for development: From urbanization to 'urban economy'  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
TOD cities, multi-centered cities, port cities, airport cities, creative cities, data cities… are not only places to live but also become new growth drivers for Vietnam in this era of self-development.
When next-generation urban models move beyond the blueprints.
In just about two months, the Long Thanh International Airport will officially join the world aviation map. Planned to be built on an area of approximately 5,000 hectares and applying leading-edge technologies, Long Thanh is envisioned to become the largest international air hub airport in Vietnam and on par with the region. For Dong Nai City, Long Thanh Airport is not simply a transportation infrastructure project but is considered a "blockbuster" creating a powerful boost to socio-economic development. Because, while Long Thanh Port is considered a breakthrough project in transportation infrastructure, the Long Thanh airport city is expected to create a breakthrough in opening up new development opportunities for the entire region. Resolution No. 16 dated July 21, 2026, of the Politburo on the construction and development of Dong Nai City until 2035, with a vision to 2065, also sets out the task of comprehensively developing the Long Thanh airport city and its surrounding areas within the network connecting the Southeast region, the Mekong Delta region, the South Central coastal region, and the Central Highlands, to become an important driving force for the development of Dong Nai.
Accordingly, the airport city is not a standalone project surrounding Long Thanh Airport, but rather a multi-centered urban area encompassing the digital economy , aviation industry, high technology, and inter-regional logistics. This means the urban area is being shaped as a "global economic gateway," not simply an airport terminal. The area surrounding Long Thanh Airport will be divided into specialized functional zones such as a duty-free zone, an international exhibition center, high-speed air logistics, a high-tech zone, and a system of satellite service cities. Thus, international businesspeople can fly in, hold meetings, sign contracts, shop, and fly out within a single day without experiencing the congestion of the old inner city.
It can be said that Vietnam's first complete airport city model is finally being realized after decades of conceptualization.
Furthermore, the TOD (Transit-Oriented Development) model is expanding beyond the narrow confines of inner-city metro lines like Ben Thanh - Suoi Tien (Ho Chi Minh City) or Cat Linh - Ha Dong ( Hanoi ), elevating them to "TOD economic corridors." A prime example is the Ho Chi Minh City - Can Tho high-speed railway line, over 170 km long, or the future North-South high-speed railway line. At each transfer station passing through localities such as Tay Ninh, Dong Thap, Vinh Long, and Can Tho, the area within a 1-2 km radius around the station is not just a passenger pick-up and drop-off point, but is being directly planned as a compact TOD mini-city – integrating commercial centers, logistics services, office buildings, and research areas. The train not only carries people but also capital and labor productivity, redistributing them throughout the Mekong Delta region. Localities with metro and railway lines are making TOD a central pillar in their new urban redevelopment strategies.
Facing the sea, the coastal city of Can Gio, with its Vinhomes Green Paradise mega-project, is attracting significant attention as a candidate in the global "7 Wonders of Future Cities" campaign, initiated by the world- renowned New7Wonders organization. Wonders are no longer just massive structures confined to stone and steel, but cities that "breathe" in harmony with nature, powered by human intelligence and emotion. These are places that transform sustainable thinking into a lifestyle, and technological achievements into energy for happiness for each resident. Vinhomes Green Paradise closely meets most of the stringent criteria of the world's urban design award. The project presents a perfectly balanced green economic challenge: developing a world-class ecological, financial, and tourism mega-city while preserving the Can Gio Mangrove Biosphere Reserve intact. From the "dream" of generations of policymakers, the Can Gio reclaimed land megacity is not only gradually taking shape but is also becoming the first urban development project planned, designed, and developed by Vietnamese people to confidently step onto the global stage.
Even in the heart of major cities like Ho Chi Minh City or Hanoi, the definition of "housing" in new urban areas has completely changed. No longer are these monotonous apartment blocks serving only the purpose of "going to work and sleeping." New-generation urban areas like Thu Duc (Ho Chi Minh City) or Hoa Lac and Vinhomes Ocean Park (Hanoi) are designed as ecosystems for living, working, and creating. They integrate R&D centers, co-working spaces, universities, international hospitals, and green public spaces. Residents, especially the knowledge workforce and creative youth, find an environment that stimulates thinking, minimizing unnecessary commuting time so they can focus all their energy on creating added value.
Across the country, new-generation urban models are gradually emerging alongside mega-projects that are shaping the identity of Vietnam in the new era.
You may also like
These are "maximum productivity machines".
The models that Vietnam is launching are the development trends of leading cities around the world. A city that is properly planned for its intended function can become a "blockbuster" that stimulates a massive surge in GDP.
One of the most successful examples is the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region with its "railway + real estate" model, pioneered by the Hong Kong Metro Rail Corporation (MTR Corporation) since the 1970s. Instead of relying entirely on state funding, MTR acquired the rights to develop elevated spaces and areas surrounding stations from the government at the value of undeveloped land. After the railway line was completed, land values skyrocketed, and MTR partnered with private investors to build compact mixed-use urban complexes including high-rise apartments, shopping malls, and offices right on top of the depots or connected to the metro stations. Classic landmarks such as the International Finance Centre (IFC) at Hong Kong Station or the Kowloon Station complex (including the 118-story ICC building) are vivid proof: profits from TOD (Transit-Oriented Development) not only offset a large portion of railway construction costs but also helped MTR become one of the few urban rail companies in the world to operate profitably for decades.
For example, in the case of Incheon Airport City, South Koreans don't view it simply as a tourist airport. Instead, they've planned the entire surrounding area as the Incheon Free Economic Zone (IFEZ), comprising three cores: Songdo Smart City (an international R&D and education center), Yeongjong (a tourism, resort, and aviation commercial city), and Cheongna (a financial and service center). The IFEZ has become a magnet attracting tens of billions of USD in FDI, making Incheon one of the most powerful high-tech growth engines in South Korea.
According to urban planning expert and architect Ngo Viet Nam Son, modern models such as TOD (Transit-Oriented Development), airport cities, port cities, free trade zones, or international financial centers are concepts that have absolutely no practical precedent in Vietnam. We have never had a true TOD, an airport city, or a properly designed free trade zone. All of these are only in their initial stages, outlining the first steps, so it's too early to confirm their success and contribution to the economy. However, looking at the transformation of the southern part of Ho Chi Minh City, starting with the Phu My Hung urban area, architect Ngo Viet Nam Son affirms that an urban area, if planned and implemented systematically, creating a "complete urban ecosystem," not only brings significant economic value but also has immense social and welfare implications.
"Starting in 1993 through a joint venture model between foreign enterprises and state-owned enterprises of Ho Chi Minh City, Phu My Hung is a clear example of a successful urban economic model. The best thing about Phu My Hung at that time was that the State did not spend a single penny of budget on infrastructure. From the 17 km long Nguyen Van Linh Boulevard to the entire complete internal technical infrastructure, everything was invested in by private companies and then handed over to the State. It was a true urban ecosystem ensuring a cycle of living and working for residents within a short travel radius (about 15 minutes). Looking back at Nguyen Van Linh Boulevard, one end is the Tan Thuan Export Processing Zone creating tens of thousands of jobs; the other end is a logistics center, a hub for goods for the entire region; in the middle is a chain of services, commerce, healthcare , major universities and residential areas. Residents living there not only live there, but they also have jobs, high incomes and full access to amenities. A prime example." "This is how very strong growth was achieved," architect Ngo Viet Nam Son pointed out.
Turn urban planning into a "money-printing machine".
In fact, the way Hong Kong, Singapore, and others have turned urban planning into a "money-making machine" for their budgets and a driver of labor productivity growth lies in their strategy of closely integrating five key links: infrastructure, transportation, real estate, labor productivity, and urban finance. A prime example is the decision by Hong Kong's MTR Group not to build independent public transportation but instead to implement a "Rail plus Property" model. When the urban rail line connecting Hong Kong Island with Chek Lap Kok Airport and Kowloon was laid, the foundations of the stations were designed to be directly integrated with the bases

articles.title: MAS Plans Next Phase of Wholesale CBDC Settlement With Tokenised Bills - Fintech Singapore
articles.summary: MAS Plans Next Phase of Wholesale CBDC Settlement With Tokenised Bills  Fintech Singapore
articles.full_text:
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) plans to use wholesale central bank digital currency (CBDC) to settle tokenised MAS Bills.
MAS Managing Director Chia Der Jiun outlined the plans at the INSEAD Digital Finance & Agentic AI Summit on 9 October.
The initiative aims to bring tokenised assets and digital central bank money onto common infrastructure to support settlement finality.
MAS made wholesale Singapore dollar CBDC available through its Singapore dollar Test Network in 2025.
Its first successful trial involved the settlement of interbank overnight lending transactions between DBS, OCBC and UOB.
“As usage of private digital money scales, CBDCs will ultimately be needed to anchor monetary stability,”
Chia said.
Through its BLOOM initiative, MAS is working with the industry on domestic and cross-border settlement using tokenised bank deposits and regulated stablecoins.
The regulator has also consulted on legislative amendments to implement its Single-Currency Stablecoin framework, covering reserve backing, capital requirements, redemption and disclosure.
MAS Pushes for Wider Adoption of Tokenised Assets
The regulator is working to expand commercial tokenisation through Project Guardian, with adoption still largely confined to smaller ecosystems.
Its Global Layer One (GL1) initiative is also developing common standards to improve interoperability between digital financial networks.
MAS recently published Version 1.1 of its Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime (SAFR) white paper.
It also released an open-source reference implementation to support controls over AI agents executing financial transactions.

articles.title: From Vietnam's new position, opening the space for next-generation technology investment flows. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: From Vietnam's new position, opening the space for next-generation technology investment flows.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
|  | 
| KNIC Nam Long Thanh covers an area of 1,000 hectares and is located 5km south of Long Thanh International Airport. | 
 From advantageous location to infrastructure capacity
 In a world constantly changing due to technology, trade, and new demands for sustainable development, global capital flows are not disappearing, but rather becoming more cautious, selective, and demanding in terms of where they will invest. For Vietnam, this shift is occurring precisely as the country enters a "new era of growth," when its new position needs to be transformed into new competitive advantages and foundations strong enough to retain capital in the long term.
 Amidst the ongoing restructuring of international supply chains, Vietnam is also crossing a new development threshold to participate more deeply in links with high technology, data, and added value content. The opportunity therefore lies not only in attracting more capital, but also in the ability to attract projects that can create long-term value for the economy .
 This new status also sets a new set of standards. Beyond location and cost, investors are increasingly looking deeper into the stability and scalability of power sources, access to clean energy, water quality, digital infrastructure, logistics, skilled workforce, and the ability to meet ESG standards.
 In other words, new capital is looking for more than just a location. They are seeking certainty. This is also a view repeatedly emphasized by Mr. Nguyen Tuan Anh, Deputy General Director of KN Holdings Group and Vice President of the Vietnam Real Estate Association, when discussing the future of industrial real estate. “Investment incentives may open the door, but the reliability of infrastructure and management capacity are what keep the supply chain running smoothly behind that door,” Mr. Tuan Anh said.
 In semiconductors, precision electronics, data centers, or medical devices, even small fluctuations in electricity, water, or data can result in enormous costs. Investors therefore need a system where backup infrastructure, clean energy, monitoring capabilities, data security, and support services do not exist in isolation, but operate as parts of a single structure.
 Industrial parks must prepare for ever-changing industries.
 Based on that vision, KN Holdings developed KN Industrial City (KNIC) as a new-generation industrial city, with two key projects in Dong Nai : KNIC Nam Long Thanh and KNIC Dong Long Thanh.
 This orientation is inherited from KN Holdings' nearly half-century foundation in real estate, tourism and services, renewable energy, and industrial real estate. In particular, its experience in energy provides the basis for KNIC to integrate green energy and sustainable operational solutions into its industrial park infrastructure. KNIC aims for an ecosystem connecting energy, logistics, digital infrastructure, operational technology, and investor support services.
 An industrial park built today may operate for decades. When project lifecycles are much longer than technology cycles, infrastructure cannot simply meet current demands. It needs sufficient room to adapt to industries that are changing faster than ever before.
 KNIC Nam Long Thanh and infrastructure platform for semiconductors and data centers.
 Spanning 1,000 hectares and designed by Nippon Koei, KNIC Nam Long Thanh is located 5 km from Long Thanh International Airport, 25 km from the Cai Mep - Thi Vai deep-water port complex, and enjoys convenient connections to Ho Chi Minh City and the inter-regional expressway network.
 For industries with high operational demands, such as semiconductors and data centers, location advantage is only part of the equation. Particularly for hyperscale data centers, access to high-capacity, stable, redundant power supplies and room for expansion are crucial factors in assessing the feasibility of an investment location.
 Building on KN Holdings' energy platform through KN Energy, the energy roadmap at KNIC Nam Long Thanh is oriented towards four 110 kV substations, with the potential to expand to approximately 800 MVA; rooftop solar power up to approximately 600 MW; and a BESS energy storage system of approximately 60 MW.
 From that foundation, KNIC Nam Long Thanh aims to develop a high-tech cluster where data infrastructure, energy, logistics, R&D, supplier networks, and technical human resources are connected within a single ecosystem, thereby supporting the development of AI, data centers, smart manufacturing, and data-driven industries.
 When ESG becomes an operational competency
 While KNIC Nam Long Thanh clearly demonstrates a high-tech and digital infrastructure orientation, KNIC Dong Long Thanh adds a crucial piece to the KNIC ecosystem with a focus on green manufacturing and sustainable supply chains. The 1,000-hectare project, designed by Nikken Sekkei, targets industries such as electric vehicles , mechanical engineering, electronics, renewable energy, pharmaceuticals and medical equipment, food, and beverages.
 For KNIC, ESG is not just a commitment but needs to be translated into measurable operational capabilities. From renewable energy and BESS to resource management, water treatment and reuse, solutions are integrated into infrastructure to support businesses in gradually meeting the increasingly stringent standards of the global supply chain.
 Ultimately, the value of a green industrial park lies not only in what is promised in the planning, but also in resource efficiency, risk reduction capabilities, and verifiable results during operation.
 Prepare for requirements that do not yet exist.
 The shift toward high-tech industries has also made human resources an integral part of industrial competitiveness. With semiconductors, data centers, and advanced manufacturing, the ability to attract experts, skilled workers, and retain a stable workforce is increasingly tied to the quality of the living and working environment and skill development opportunities surrounding the industrial park.
 From that perspective, KNIC develops the Work-Live-Learn model, connecting production with living spaces, services, and vocational training, integrating human infrastructure into the industrial ecosystem. Because as technology and investment standards constantly change, long-term value lies not only in the ability to meet current needs but also in the capacity to address those needs that are yet to materialize.
 And perhaps, the opportunity in change lies precisely in that ability to prepare. No one can accurately predict what investors will need in 20 or 30 years. But we can prepare today a foundation that is flexible enough so that when requirements change, infrastructure does not become a limitation to development.

This article first appeared in The Edge Malaysia Weekly on October 12, 2026 - October 18, 2026
The tabling of Budget 2027 by Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim last Friday will be followed by policy-level debates in parliament starting on Monday. Invariably, tax experts will also go through the proposals with a fine-tooth comb and analyse its impact on the country and businesses and consumers alike.
Advance data for Malaysia’s third quarter (3Q) 2026 gross domestic product (GDP) will be released on Oct 16.
In the palm oil sector, the Malaysian Palm Oil Board will be releasing production, trade and stock numbers for September on Monday, Oct 12. All eyes will be on whether the total palm oil stocks will breach the three million tonne level amid elevated prices, higher production and declining exports. In August, total stocks came in at 2.82 million tonnes.
The Monetary Authority of Singapore’s (MAS) Monetary Policy Statement will be released on Oct 14 together with the Ministry of Energy, Trade & Industry’s issue of advance 3Q GDP data.
“Our economist, Jester Koh, expects the MAS to tighten monetary policy further in this meeting via another ‘very slight’ slope-steepening move (+25 basis points [bps]), taking the S$NEER slope to 1.5% per annum, although he acknowledges that the decision will be a very close call,” says UOB Global Economics & Markets Research economist Alvin Liew in a report last Friday, adding the next major data release will be September non-oil domestic exports on Oct 16.
There are no major Asia-Pacific central banks with monetary policy decisions over the week; however, the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) will release the minutes of its September meeting on Oct 13 and September jobs report on Oct 15.
China will release a slew of economic data including September money supply, aggregate financing and yuan new loans data from Oct 9 to 15. It will also put out September external trade, Consumer Price Index (CPI) and Producer Price Index (PPI) data on Oct 14.
India is due to release its September CPI on Oct 12 and September external trade data from Oct 14 to 16. Japan’s key data will be its PPI for September on Oct 13. and final August industrial production and core machine orders on Oct 15.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank will hold their 2026 annual meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, from Oct 12 to 18, with US Federal Reserve (Fed) chairman Kevin Warsh attending with other central bank chiefs from major and regional economies.
The IMF will release the updated World Economic Outlook and Global Financial Stability Report on Oct 14 and the Fed will release the latest Beige Book report the following day. Thereafter, the Fed will enter the external communications blackout period from Oct 17 (Sat) to Oct 30.
A key focus in the US will be the corporate earnings reporting season with 38 S&P 500 companies among 364 US companies reporting during the week of Oct 14 to 17, with major US banks reporting from Oct 13 onwards.
There is a substantial US economic data docket next week, including the preliminary University of Michigan consumer sentiment for October on Oct 9; National Federation of Independent Business small business optimism for September and US existing home sales on Oct 13; federal budget balance for September from Oct 13 to 20; US September CPI and core CPI on Oct 14; as well as import and export price indices for September and September industrial production on Oct 16.
Over at the courts, the civil suit over a land deal brought by the Federal Land Development Authority (Felda) and Felda Investment Corporation Sdn Bhd (FIC) against Synergy Promenade Sdn Bhd and 21 former directors and officials — including former chairmen Tan Sri Mohd Isa Samad and Tan Sri Shahrir Samad — will continue over Monday to Thursday at the KL High Court.
On Oct 13, the High Court will hear Perikatan Nasional’s leave application for judicial review of the Registrar of Societies’ order suspending the political coalition’s activities.
The next day, the High Court will hear Datuk Seri Najib Razak’s urgent application to stay the execution of his 15-year prison sentence and RM11.38 billion fine in the 1Malaysia Development Bhd-Tanore Finance Corp case. Najib is seeking to pause the penalties until all avenues of appeal are exhausted. The application is scheduled to be heard before Judge Noor Ruwena Md Nurdin.

articles.title: Direct Indexing: From Wall Street to Vietnam - Theinvestor
articles.summary: Direct Indexing: From Wall Street to Vietnam  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
In the United States, Direct Indexing is gradually becoming a familiar approach to wealth management. In Vietnam, the model is beginning to take shape in practice. But bringing technology into everyday investing requires more than algorithms. What matters is whether it can help people build wealth steadily and with discipline, without having to spend their days watching trading screens.
In the book "The Intelligent Investor", Benjamin Graham introduces "Mr. Market", a character who comes calling every day. When euphoric, he offers to buy shares at an exorbitant price; when gripped by pessimism, he is willing to sell his own holdings at a steep discount. Investors are free to listen to him, but they are under no obligation to accept his offers. Prices change every day; the underlying value of a business does not necessarily move at the same pace.
Warren Buffett, Graham's legendary disciple, has frequently returned to this metaphor when discussing investing. Yet perhaps his most accessible piece of advice has little to do with a multibillion-dollar deal.
In his 2013 letter to Berkshire Hathaway shareholders, Buffett devoted part of his discussion to how ordinary people should invest when they lack the time to become stock market experts. Rather than trying to predict which stocks will outperform, he advocated owning a broad collection of businesses through a low-cost index fund and allowing time to do much of the work.
That conviction is also reflected in the arrangements Buffett made for his own family. He instructed the trustee responsible for money left to his wife to invest 90% in a low-cost S&P 500 index fund. One of the world's most successful investors chose a remarkably simple principle for someone close to him: it is possible to participate in the growth of many businesses without constantly having to identify the best individual stocks.
When investing does not have to become a second job
As an economy grows wealthier, the way its people think about their financial future also changes. With rising incomes, savings are no longer intended solely as protection against unexpected expenses. They increasingly serve a broader purpose: building wealth over the long term.
According to UOB's ASEAN Consumer Sentiment Study 2026, 89% of Vietnamese respondents save more than 10% of their monthly income, the highest proportion among five ASEAN markets surveyed. Meanwhile, 63% allocate more than 10% of their annual income to investments. The appetite for long-term wealth accumulation is expanding alongside the economy.
At the macroeconomic level, this aspiration intersects with another need: businesses require long-term capital to invest in technology and expand production. The stock market can connect household savings with businesses, allowing the benefits of economic growth to become a foundation for family wealth.
Yet the desire to invest does not necessarily come with the time or expertise needed to manage a portfolio independently. Someone may want to own shares in promising companies while still devoting most of their day to work and family. Long-term investing therefore calls for convenient approaches that do not turn the stock market into a second job.
Individual stocks offer investors greater control over their decisions. Open-ended funds provide professional management, while exchange-traded funds (ETFs) offer exposure to index-tracking portfolios. Direct Indexing adds another option: investors own individual shares directly, while technology and investment professionals support portfolio allocation, monitoring and rebalancing according to a consistent set of rules.
A survey of 400 U.S. financial advisors published by FTSE Russell in September 2026 found that the proportion using Direct Indexing had risen from 33% to 41% over the previous year. Some 83% were either using the approach or planning to adopt it.
For Vietnam, Direct Indexing brings together direct share ownership and disciplined portfolio management. Rather than replacing individual stocks, open-ended funds or ETFs, the model could complement existing investment products, making long-term investing more accessible to a society with a growing capacity to accumulate wealth.
Bringing a new investment approach closer to everyday Investors
Making a modern investment model accessible to the wider public involves more than applying algorithms. The greater challenge is to turn methods that traditionally demand considerable knowledge, time and effort into an investment experience simple enough for people to sustain over many years.
Launched in August 2026, VPS Smart Indexing (VSI) is among the pioneering products applying Direct Indexing in Vietnam. Under VSI, clients directly own the shares in their portfolios, while VPS Securities Joint Stock Company manages their investments on their behalf according to their chosen strategies.
The product combines the expertise of investment professionals with quantitative technology, aiming to help investors establish and maintain the habit of making regular contributions towards long-term wealth accumulation.
How the model works was explained at an online discussion titled "Market Upgrade: A Turning Point Opening Up New Investment Opportunities", held in early October 2026 by VPS.
Responding to a question about allocating VND1 billion ($38,590) across a portfolio of 20 stocks, Le Thi Le Hang, CEO of Saigon Capital, explained that the money would not simply be divided equally among the holdings. Instead, portfolio weights are calculated based on each stock's contribution to risk, combined with an assessment of price trends, rather than being determined by fixed allocations.
The VSI01 model portfolio is reviewed and rebalanced monthly. When unusual developments affect an individual company or the broader market, investment professionals can conduct additional assessments and make adjustments outside the regular rebalancing schedule.
Algorithms handle tasks requiring extensive data processing and consistency, while investment professionals contribute experience and judgement when circumstances demand it. Both serve the same purpose: ensuring that portfolio management follows a defined methodology, rather than allowing every investment decision to be driven by emotional reactions to price movements.
VSI01 allows investors to start with VND50 million ($1,930), although VPS recommends an initial investment of at least VND200 million ($7,720) to help their actual portfolios track the model portfolio more closely. Together with a mechanism for regular additional contributions, this structure is designed for people seeking to build wealth gradually rather than simply pursuing short-term trading opportunities.
VSI will not be the only product applying Direct Indexing, nor is it intended to replace individual stocks, open-ended funds or ETFs. What is more significant is the decision by VPS, an established securities firm with a substantial brokerage presence and a large client base, to pursue this approach.
By committing resources to developing VSI, the company is demonstrating its confidence in the potential of Direct Indexing as a long-term wealth management approach, rather than merely another application of new technology.
For Direct Indexing to become a familiar investment choice, the market will need more time, trustworthy products and service quality proven through real-world experience.
Nevertheless, the involvement of established financial institutions such as VPS represents a meaningful step forward. It brings disciplined, rules-based investing closer to people who would rather devote their time to work and family, while allowing their savings to pursue a longer-term journey towards wealth accumulation.

| Ms. Luc Kim Thanh, Director of Digital Business, Kafi Securities Joint Stock Company | 
 Assets are increasing rapidly, but management services haven't kept pace.
 According to Ms. Luc Kim Thanh, Vietnam is in a transitional phase between asset creation and asset management. The difference between the two phases is evident in the rate of increase in personal financial assets and the still modest size of the fund management industry.
 Citing McKinsey's forecast, she said that the total personal financial assets of Vietnamese people could reach approximately $600 billion by 2027, up from about $360 billion at the end of 2022. Meanwhile, the total net asset value of domestic securities investment funds is currently only about 93 trillion VND, equivalent to 0.7% of GDP.
 The target set for 2030 is to raise this ratio to 5% of GDP. This means the fund industry would have to expand approximately sevenfold in four years, highlighting the gap between market potential and current service delivery capacity.
 "I believe that Vietnam has been very good at creating assets, but we are only just beginning to learn how to manage them," Ms. Thanh remarked.
 According to the expert, the current bottlenecks are concentrated in three factors: insufficient diversity of financial products, a limited number of specialized service providers, and the lack of widespread public habit of entrusting assets to professional management units.
 Placing Vietnam within the development process of markets such as Singapore , Thailand, and Malaysia, Ms. Thanh argued that the asset management industry typically goes through four stages. It begins with the accumulation of tangible assets, primarily through real estate and savings deposits. This is followed by the emergence of standardized financial products such as open-ended funds, bonds, and investment-linked insurance.
 In the third stage, asset management advisory services gradually emerged, charging fees per asset. A more advanced stage of development was estate planning and the transfer of assets across generations.
 According to experts, Vietnam is currently in the latter half of the second phase and beginning to transition to the third phase. This is not necessarily a sign of misguided development, as earlier markets also had asset portfolios focused on real estate and deposits at similar times.
 However, Vietnam has two notable advantages: technology and the speed of asset growth. While more developed markets took years to build branch networks and consulting teams, the current digital platform allows for widespread service delivery at a lower access cost.
 Citing a BCG report, Ms. Thanh stated that financial assets in Vietnam are increasing by over 9% annually. According to Knight Frank data she cited, the number of individuals with a net worth of $30 million or more has increased by approximately 29% in five years and is projected to increase by nearly 60% in the following five years.
 Another factor is the upgrade of the Vietnamese stock market to a secondary emerging market by FTSE Russell, effective September 21, 2026. According to Ms. Thanh, the long-term value of the upgrade lies not only in its ability to attract foreign capital, but also in the requirement to raise operational standards, information transparency, and risk management in the domestic market.
 Knowing the need to diversify while remaining focused on traditional assets.
 The gap between individual investors' perceptions and actions is reflected in their asset portfolio structure. Citing a 2026 survey of over 1,000 individual investors, Ms. Thanh stated that savings deposits accounted for an average of 37% of the portfolio, real estate 36%, and gold 14%. Thus, these three traditional channels accounted for 87% of the total assets of the surveyed group.
 Notably, 86% of survey participants agreed that it's not advisable to concentrate a large portion of assets in a single channel. However, 76% still preferred real estate or gold, primarily because these are assets they feel more familiar with and understand better. This reflects the gap between recognizing the benefits of diversification and actually implementing them in their investment portfolios.
 Tangible assets provide a sense of security because they are visible, while financial products are limited and trust in professional asset management takes time to develop.
 Over-concentrating on a few traditional assets can lead to an unbalanced portfolio, low liquidity, and dependence on a market cycle. When the cycle reverses, many assets can be affected simultaneously, especially at times when investors need cash.
 Nevertheless, the market has already shown initial changes. According to data, the number of investors holding fund certificates is currently around 733,000, a 1.6-fold increase compared to the end of 2024. This number is still small compared to nearly 14 million securities accounts, but it shows a growing trend towards accessing investment through funds.
 Another issue is the distinction between asset trading and asset management. According to her, many investors currently make decisions based on individual opportunities, judging success by the profit or loss of each transaction, rather than on progress toward long-term financial goals. This approach can increase transaction costs, opportunity costs, and leave investment decisions heavily influenced by short-term market fluctuations.
 Conversely, asset management requires defining objectives, capital utilization timelines, risk tolerance, and portfolio allocation principles before selecting products.
 According to Ms. Thanh, the role of an asset management firm is not only to seek investment opportunities but also to help clients maintain financial discipline, especially when the market is volatile.
 This need is projected to become increasingly evident as the first generation of property owners in Vietnam enters the asset transfer phase. At that point, the concern will not only be annual profits but also how to preserve, manage, and transfer assets to future generations.
 To develop asset management, the consulting profession must be standardized.
 Along with changing needs, technology and artificial intelligence are opening up the possibility of making asset management services more accessible to a wider range of investor groups.
 According to Ms. Thanh, technology can help reduce service costs, allowing investors with around 100 million VND to access asset management methods previously reserved primarily for clients with large assets.
 Technology platforms can continuously monitor portfolios, support rebalancing according to predetermined principles, and personalize services for multiple investors with different goals and risk tolerance levels.
 However, technology cannot completely replace humans. Understanding family circumstances, explaining things to clients during periods of market volatility, and handling unprecedented situations still require the role of a consultant.
 Technology can also amplify risks if there is a lack of data governance and internal controls. A flaw in a model deployed on a large scale can simultaneously affect many users.
 Regarding the conditions for developing the asset management industry in Vietnam, Ms. Thanh proposed four groups of solutions.
 First, the market needs to expand its asset classes and investment products, including voluntary pension funds, index funds, and themed investment funds, while also perfecting the legal framework for alternative asset classes.
 Secondly, the personal financial advisory profession needs to be standardized through a professional certification framework, ethical standards, and mechanisms for transparency regarding fees and conflicts of interest.
 According to Ms. Thanh, this is a crucial requirement because asset management activities depend heavily on customer trust. If practitioners are not standardized, expanding products and services will lack a solid foundation.
 Thirdly, it is necessary to develop the depth of the bond market, enhance transparency and liquidity to form a reliable fixed-income component in a balanced investment portfolio.
 Fourth, Vietnam needs to gradually improve the legal infrastructure for long-term estate planning, including family trust structures, asset transfer mechanisms, and related tax policies.
 Ms. Thanh believes that the establishment of an International Finance Center in Ho Chi Minh City could create opportunities to test and standardize new products and services according to international practices. In her assessment, when products are diversified, the consulting profession is standardized, and the market has a suitable risk management framework, the Vietnamese asset management industry will be able to transition from asset accumulation to professional asset management.

articles.title: Corporate bonds: Pressure to mature is increasing again. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Corporate bonds: Pressure to mature is increasing again.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
|  | 
| The image is an illustration created by AI. | 
 With increased issuance, capital flows remain concentrated.
 According to the recently released Q3 report by Vietnam Investment Credit Rating Joint Stock Company (VIS Rating), the value of new bond issuances reached VND 172 trillion, a 9.7% increase compared to the same period last year. However, this improvement mainly comes from secondary bank bonds and some real estate companies, and does not reflect a uniform recovery across all issuance groups.
 There are some noteworthy figures: Bank bonds accounted for 66% of the total issuance value in the quarter, while real estate bonds accounted for 26%; privately placed bonds accounted for 83%, while public offerings accounted for 17%.
 A notable driving force came from subordinated bonds issued by banks to increase Tier 2 capital, meeting capital adequacy ratio requirements. State-owned banks and some private banks, including Sacombank , intensified this activity. Conversely, the issuance of regular bonds by banks decreased by 22% year-on-year, as banks shifted towards long-term certificates of deposit to raise capital from individual investors.
 In the real estate sector, issuance value increased by 29% year-on-year, but was concentrated in Vinhomes and businesses related to Masterise. Some bond issues had maturities of three to seven years, aimed at raising capital for large-scale projects.
 The list of the largest bond issuances of the quarter clearly shows differentiation. Agribank issued bonds to the public worth VND 14,673 billion on July 31st, with a ten-year maturity and an initial interest rate of 7.9%, classified as secondary. Vinhomes issued VND 8,000 billion privately on September 24th, with a two-year maturity and an initial interest rate of 12%. Three other private placements, each worth VND 7,000 billion, belonged to Hung Long, Masterise Lumiere Office, and Thanh Quang.
 By the end of the quarter, the total value of outstanding bonds reached VND 1,535 trillion, equivalent to 10.9% of nominal GDP. Of this, privately placed bonds accounted for VND 1,340 trillion, and public bonds VND 195 trillion. Banks accounted for VND 699 trillion and residential real estate VND 475 trillion in the sector-specific outstanding bond structure.
 On the secondary market, the average daily transaction value reached VND 7.2 trillion, an increase of 12.2% compared to the same period last year. However, the increase in transactions and improved issuance have not yet resolved the issue of principal and interest payments for businesses facing financial difficulties.
 While late payments decrease, pressure to meet deadlines increases.
 A positive aspect of the third quarter was the reduction in the rate of new bond defaults over the past 12 months to approximately 0.2%, compared to 0.38% in the previous quarter. The value of new defaulted bonds in the quarter was around VND 300 billion, significantly lower than in previous periods. The report noted that one issuer within the Novaland ecosystem defaulted for the first time in the quarter.
 Despite a decrease in new cases, VIS Rating notes that payment pressure remains high for businesses within the Novaland ecosystem. Stagnant real estate sales, high interest rates, and limited cash flow continue to impact their ability to meet due obligations. This is a risk inherent in the financial condition of each organization and cannot be assessed solely by the overall default rate of the entire market.
 Some businesses choose to extend bond maturities to reduce short-term pressure. Van Huong Investment and Tourism Joint Stock Company and SMC Investment and Trading Joint Stock Company have extended their maturities by one to two years. Postponing the payment date can help reallocate debt obligations, but it does not mean the debt has been fully settled.
 On the positive side, the process of handling overdue payments has improved. The cumulative debt recovery rate reached 51.5%, an increase of 3.8 percentage points compared to the previous quarter; more than VND 11 trillion was repaid to investors during the quarter. The payments mainly came from issuers related to Hung Thinh and Sunshine.
 Specifically, Hung Thinh Land repaid 5,380 billion VND of overdue principal debt during the quarter. Construction Business Development Company 3 repaid 1,210 billion VND; Nova Real Estate Investment Joint Stock Company repaid 968 billion VND; and Nova Thao Dien Company Limited repaid 965 billion VND. These figures reflect the progress of debt resolution at each company, while remaining outstanding debts still need to be monitored.
 The bigger challenge lies in the upcoming maturity dates. Approximately 252 trillion VND of bonds will mature in the next 12 months, compared to 157 trillion VND in the most recent 12 months. A significant proportion of these are previously overdue or restructured bonds from financially distressed issuers.
 Specifically for the fourth quarter of 2026, the value of maturing bonds is expected to be around 75 trillion VND, of which 39 trillion VND is for residential real estate, 18 trillion VND for banking, and 18 trillion VND for other sectors. Approximately 26 trillion VND of this total consists of bonds that have defaulted or been granted extensions.
 In 2027, the maturities continue to be concentrated in the largest quarters: approximately 83 trillion VND in Q2, 64 trillion VND in Q3, and 84 trillion VND in Q4. The pressure lies not only in the total amount to be repaid, but also in the ability of each enterprise to access new sources of capital as borrowing costs increase and liquidity is limited.
 In the list of non-banking enterprises with the largest maturing assets over the next 12 months, Vingroup tops the list with 23,000 billion VND, followed by Hung Phat Invest Hanoi with 12,650 billion VND… These are figures for maturing obligations, not a list of organizations with delayed payments.
 Regarding the outlook, VIS Rating forecasts stable primary bond issuance in Q4 2026, mainly driven by the demand for project development capital and refinancing from real estate developers. However, limited fundraising capacity and high capital costs continue to put pressure on companies with weak credit profiles, especially those that have previously defaulted on or restructured bonds.
