articles.title: The cornerstone of China's economic resilience. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: The cornerstone of China's economic resilience.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Despite challenges from the international environment and domestic restructuring, the Chinese economy continues to demonstrate resilience thanks to its solid industrial foundation, the boom in artificial intelligence (AI), and timely fiscal and monetary support packages.
China's GDP growth in the first quarter of 2026 is projected to reach 5% before slowing to 4.3% in the second quarter due to energy supply disruptions related to the conflict in the Middle East. Overall, in the first half of 2026, China's GDP is expected to grow by 4.7% year-on-year.
Exports remain a crucial driver of economic growth. Despite global economic fluctuations, China's export performance has seen impressive growth.
According to a World Bank report published in October 2026, the country's exports in the period from April to July 2026 increased sharply by 21.1% compared to the same period last year. The main drivers of this increase came from high-tech goods, notably electric vehicles (EVs), the green industry, and products related to artificial intelligence (AI).
Khám phá thêm
Tìm hiểu lịch sử
Đọc Mẹo Du Lịch
Khám phá ĐNA
Amidst the global AI boom, China has solidified its central position in the supply chain. World Bank analysis shows that China is the largest supplier of AI-related goods among the East Asian economies studied, with exports in this sector reaching $785 billion between May 2025 and April 2026. Notably, components and intermediate inputs used in the production of finished products account for nearly three-quarters of the country's total AI exports.
Besides its export capabilities, China also possesses a comprehensive AI ecosystem. Albert Park, chief economist at the Asian Development Bank (ADB), believes that China has a complete ecosystem for AI development, leading the world from the semiconductor manufacturing value chain and data center systems to large-scale language modeling (LLM).
At the same time, the Chinese government 's "AI Plus" initiative is being vigorously implemented to deeply integrate AI into all aspects of the economy and social life, thereby creating momentum to promote high-quality development.
Technological strengths have positively impacted market sentiment. ADB Chief Economist Albert Park points out that investor confidence in the Chinese stock market has rebounded significantly, stemming from the recognition of the country's leading position in digital transformation and AI.
You may also like
Furthermore, signs of easing geopolitical tensions and a more stable US-China relationship are also creating a favorable environment for attracting international investment.
Besides the impetus from the AI wave, China's economy continues to demonstrate considerable resilience thanks to its inherent capabilities. Albert Park emphasized that the Chinese economy maintains positive growth potential due to its high-quality workforce, coupled with the superior competitiveness and innovative spirit of its leading enterprises. The vast and diversified industrial scale further strengthens the economy's resilience against external fluctuations.
Furthermore, the ability to mitigate the impact of energy risks is also a key positive point. According to the ASEAN+3 Macroeconomic Research Office (AMRO) and the World Bank, although the conflict in the Middle East disrupted global energy supplies in Q2 2026, the impact on China was significantly reduced.
This stability is achieved thanks to China's diversified energy sources, abundant strategic oil reserves, high proportion of renewable energy, and flexible control measures over domestic gasoline prices.
Furthermore, the proactive policy management of the Chinese government plays a crucial role in stabilizing the economy. Albert Park highly praised the recent enhanced support policies, particularly the focus on boosting domestic consumption. Solutions such as reallocating support resources to low-income households and expanding the social security system not only stimulate consumption but also create a sustainable safety net.
In particular, China recently announced a nationwide interest rate subsidy policy for home loans to reduce the burden of interest payments for families buying their first home, expected to take effect within one year. Analysts believe this policy will bring more significant benefits to the new housing market in second, third, and fourth-tier cities; properties serving first-time homebuyers and basic housing needs are likely to benefit the most.
Regarding fiscal and monetary policy, AMRO stated that accelerating the disbursement of public funds and the issuance of government bonds will positively support economic activities in the second half of 2026. At the same time, monetary policy and financial conditions will continue to be maintained in an accommodative state to support capital flows.
Thanks to positive factors from high-tech exports and timely support policies, the World Bank, in its October 2026 East Asia and Pacific Economic Update report, raised its 2026 GDP growth forecast for China to 4.5%, up from the previous forecast of 4.2%. Similarly, AMRO also projected China's economic growth at 4.5% for both 2026 and 2027.
You may also like
While the overall outlook is positive, both AMRO and the World Bank note short-term risks. Externally, a prolonged or renewed escalation of conflict in the Middle East could continue to drive up energy costs and undermine China's trade.
Trade tensions with the US and the European Union (EU) could disrupt supply chains and restrict exports. In addition, a sudden drop in global AI investment is also a significant risk, given that global demand for Chinese electronics and electrical equipment has contributed significantly to the country's recent export and manufacturing growth.
Domestically, the prolonged adjustment of the real estate market could continue to undermine construction activity, household confidence, and consumption, while increasing credit risk for real estate developers and related financial institutions. The labor market's lack of significant recovery could reinforce a cautious saving mentality among the population and slow the transition to a consumption-driven growth model.
Despite facing some short-term headwinds from the international environment and domestic structural adjustments, the Chinese economy has maintained stable growth. High-tech exports, comprehensive AI infrastructure, strong industrial production capacity, and flexible governance policies are the core drivers keeping the economy on a positive trajectory.

articles.title: Deputy Prime Minister Pham Gia Tuc chaired the meeting of the Central Steering Committee on Housing Policy and Real Estate Market. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Deputy Prime Minister Pham Gia Tuc chaired the meeting of the Central Steering Committee on Housing Policy and Real Estate Market.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
(Chinhphu.vn) - On the morning of October 13, at the Government Headquarters, Politburo member and Standing Deputy Prime Minister Pham Gia Tuc, Head of the Central Steering Committee on Housing Policy and Real Estate Market, chaired the first meeting of the Steering Committee after its restructuring.
The meeting was held in a hybrid format, combining in-person and online participation, connecting with several provinces and cities. Attendees included leaders from ministries, departments, and localities, as well as representatives from associations and businesses operating in the real estate sector.
Rental housing should be given priority in development.
In his opening remarks at the meeting, Deputy Prime Minister Pham Gia Tuc stated that, in recent times, the Central Committee, the Politburo , the Government, and the Prime Minister have issued many important resolutions, conclusions, and directives aimed at perfecting the mechanisms and policies for housing development and the real estate market.
In particular, following the directives of General Secretary and President To Lam, the Government has focused on implementing housing development policies that prioritize both social housing and rental housing, identifying rental housing as a strategic segment requiring focused development.
The Prime Minister also directly worked with 13 localities on the implementation of socio-economic development tasks, the pilot implementation of investment in rental housing, and other housing support programs and objectives.
Assessing the current situation, the Standing Deputy Prime Minister stated that, despite achieving positive results, the housing sector and real estate market are still facing many difficulties and challenges, focusing on three major issues.
First, the results of implementing targets for the development of social housing and rental housing are still low. While the target for social housing development assigned to localities in 2026 is over 97,000 units, in the first nine months of the year, the whole country only completed nearly 47,000 units, reaching about 48% of the plan.
Secondly, housing prices remain unaffordable for the vast majority of people, especially workers and laborers, including a segment of civil servants. Meanwhile, the inventory of unsold properties tends to increase, and access to credit remains difficult, affecting purchasing power and the market's absorption capacity.
The Prime Minister has directed the Ministry of Construction to conduct a thorough review of the inventory of unsold real estate to find appropriate solutions; and at the same time, focus on removing difficulties regarding credit sources, especially policy credit sources serving housing development.
Thirdly, many real estate projects remain stalled and face long-standing obstacles, mainly related to legal issues, land, and finance, which need to be resolved soon to unlock social resources.
Assigning a task to only one agency, individualizing responsibility.
Discussing the tasks of the newly restructured Steering Committee, Deputy Prime Minister Pham Gia Tuc requested that its members uphold a sense of responsibility and determination to seriously and effectively implement the policies, resolutions, and directives of the Central Committee, the Government, and the Prime Minister.
Specifically, it is necessary to clearly define the key tasks for the remaining months of the year, and assign specific responsibilities to each ministry, sector, and locality according to their functions and authority.
You may also like
The Deputy Prime Minister emphasized the principle of "one task assigned to only one agency or organization," while also stressing the need for individualized responsibility in implementation.
Regarding projects that are stalled, facing difficulties, or have long-standing obstacles, the Deputy Prime Minister emphasized the direct responsibility of the local Party secretary in directing these matters, as assigned by the competent authority.
Issues falling under local jurisdiction must be proactively resolved by the local authorities; issues falling under the jurisdiction of ministries and agencies must be handled by those ministries and agencies; and matters falling under the authority of the Prime Minister or exceeding the authority of the Prime Minister must be compiled and reported for consideration and resolution.
Regarding institutional reform, the Deputy Prime Minister stated that the Government is promoting the amendment of legal regulations on land, housing, and real estate business to remove current obstacles and create favorable conditions for the implementation of new projects.
The Deputy Prime Minister affirmed that the Government is ready to listen to and incorporate reasonable and valid opinions from associations and businesses to improve mechanisms, policies, and laws.
Emphasizing that the ultimate goal of policies and guidelines is national development and continuously improving the material and spiritual lives of the people, the Standing Deputy Prime Minister stated that ensuring housing needs are met is an extremely important issue that requires attention and resolution through practical policies and solutions.
Real estate transactions are decreasing, and inventory levels are trending upwards.
Reporting at the meeting, Deputy Minister of Construction Nguyen Van Sinh stated that in the first nine months of 2026, the Government, the Prime Minister, and the Ministry of Construction issued 48 directives aimed at improving the institutional framework and resolving difficulties and obstacles in the housing sector and real estate market. The Ministry of Construction also issued two official dispatches and organized 18 working groups to inspect and urge localities to develop social housing and rental housing.
Regarding the market situation, the whole country has 2,221 real estate projects recorded with a total investment capital of approximately 6.87 million billion VND. In the third quarter of 2026, the country recorded about 92,004 successful real estate transactions, equivalent to 92% compared to the previous quarter.
Apartment and land prices in the secondary market tend to decrease compared to Q2/2026, but still remain high in major cities. Market liquidity remains low, with transactions mainly concentrated in projects with complete legal documentation and convenient locations.
According to reports from 27 out of 34 localities, the inventory of real estate in the third quarter of 2026 was approximately 51,950 units/plots/land parcels, showing an upward trend compared to the previous quarter.
Deputy Minister Nguyen Van Sinh noted that this is only the amount of unsold real estate reported by developers. In addition, there is a large volume of unfinished investment capital in projects, while transactions in the secondary market are also facing many difficulties.
Regarding the development of social housing, according to a report by the Ministry of Construction, to date, the whole country has 947 projects with a scale of 910,933 units that have been completed, are under implementation, or have received investment approval, equivalent to about 91% of the target of the Project to invest in the construction of at least 1 million social housing units.
Of these, 363 projects have been completed with 216,626 units; 293 projects are under construction with 363,065 units; and 291 projects have received investment approval with 331,242 units.
In the first nine months of 2026 alone, the whole country completed 46,962 social housing units.
Regarding rental housing, by the end of Q3/2026, the whole country had completed 8,314 units, reaching 48% of the annual plan. The Ministry of Construction anticipates that the total number of rental housing units completed in 2026 could reach 18,049, achieving 105% of the plan.
You may also like
Notably, from June 2026 to the present, the whole country has started construction on 29 projects with a scale of 85,594 units, of which 33,886 are rental housing units, accounting for about 40%.
Reporting on the real estate credit situation, Deputy Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam Nguyen Ngoc Canh stated that by the end of August 2026, outstanding real estate credit reached approximately 5.23 million billion VND, accounting for more than 25% of the total outstanding credit to the economy.
For social housing loan programs, outstanding loans reached over 51,000 billion VND, of which the Social Policy Bank accounted for over 26,000 billion VND and commercial banks over 25,000 billion VND.
The preferential credit program for social housing development under Resolution No. 33/NQ-CP has been expanded from VND 120,000 billion to over VND 153,000 billion, with the participation of 11 commercial banks.
By August 31, 2026, the committed loan amount will reach approximately VND 50,300 billion; disbursed funds will reach approximately VND 17,500 billion, an increase of about 2.3 times compared to the end of 2025, of which approximately VND 15,000 billion will be allocated to developers and VND 2,500 billion to homebuyers.
According to Deputy Governor Nguyen Ngoc Canh, real estate investment is long-term in nature, while the capital mobilized by the banking system mainly has shorter maturities, posing liquidity risks. Therefore, it is necessary to diversify capital mobilization channels and create sustainable medium and long-term capital sources for the real estate market.
Based on the reports, the meeting continued to focus on discussing and clarifying difficulties and obstacles related to legal issues, credit sources, housing prices, and the development of social housing and rental housing. Deputy Prime Minister Pham Gia Tuc requested that ministries, sectors, localities, associations, and businesses specifically identify shortcomings, propose solutions to address them, and clearly define responsibilities and authority for resolution, as a basis for implementing key tasks in the coming period.

articles.title: How do Vietnamese tycoons transfer power? - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: How do Vietnamese tycoons transfer power?  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
TP - The biggest obstacle for the succeeding generation is not generational conflict in management, but rather the core issue of their ability to lead the next phase of the family business's development. Therefore, the strategy needs to harmonize the old foundation while being innovative in the new context, as well as aiming for sustainable development for the family business instead of falling into a cycle of rivalry and conflict.
Currently, the F1 generation, consisting of the children of the founders, are entrusted with running the company to maintain its reputation in the market and uphold investor confidence.
Recently, Mr. Pham Nhat Quan Anh (33 years old) - Chairman of VinFast Global - also assumed the position of General Director of VinFast Global, replacing Mr. Pham Nhat Vuong, who was appointed as Chairman and General Director of VinFast Vietnam. Meanwhile, Mr. Pham Nhat Minh Hoang (26 years old) became the General Director of GSM Global and General Director of GSM Vietnam.
Mr. Pham Nhat Quan Anh and Mr. Pham Nhat Minh Hoang are the sons of Mr. Pham Nhat Vuong - Chairman of the Board of Directors of Vingroup and Mrs. Pham Thu Huong - Permanent Vice Chairman of the Board of Directors of Vingroup.
Thus, Mr. Pham Nhat Quan Anh and Mr. Pham Nhat Minh Hoang taking on new roles is seen as a transfer of leadership power within the businesses of the Vingroup ecosystem.
Similarly, within the Vietnamese business community, power transitions have been and are taking place in influential family-owned corporations such as Novaland,ACB , TTC AgriS, REE, etc., with pivotal shifts in mindset.
At Novaland Group's 2026 shareholders' meeting, Mr. Bui Cao Nhat Quan was elected Chairman of the Board of Directors of Novaland for the term 2026-2031. Mr. Bui Cao Nhat Quan, 44 years old, is the son of Mr. Bui Thanh Nhon, the former Chairman of the Board of Directors of Novaland. He previously served as Deputy General Director of the Investment and Trading Division of Novaland for 10 years, from 2007 to 2017.
Refrigeration and Electrical Engineering Corporation (REE) has also made a notable shift in its leadership transition. Accordingly, REE has appointed Mr. Nguyen Ngoc Thai Binh as General Director and legal representative. Mr. Binh is the former Deputy General Director of REE and has been with the company for 18 years. He is the son of Ms. Nguyen Thi Mai Thanh, the former Chairwoman of the Board of Directors of REE.
In the banking sector, Mr. Tran Hung Huy is a notable figure, having inherited the business from both his parents. In 2013, at the young age of 34, Mr. Huy assumed the position of Chairman of the Board of Directors of Asia Commercial Bank (ACB). After 13 years of leadership, Mr. Huy has guided ACB through numerous challenges, regained market share, and maintained positive growth in profits and scale.
In the agricultural sector, Ms. Dang Huynh Uc My, Chairwoman of the Board of Directors of Thanh Thanh Cong - Bien Hoa Joint Stock Company (TTC AgriS), has also been continuously buying shares to increase her ownership. Ms. My is the next generation, having received the management rights of TTC AgriS from her mother, Ms. Huynh Bich Ngoc, the former Chairwoman of the Board of Directors of TTC AgriS.
Sacombank also appointed Mr. Nguyen Xuan Thai (23 years old) as an assistant to the Board of Directors, and Ms. Nguyen Ngoc My Anh (25 years old) as an assistant to the General Director. Notably, Ms. My Anh and Mr. Thai are the two children of Mr. Nguyen Duc Thuy - the Standing Vice Chairman of the Board of Directors of STB.
A power shift is also underway within the family of Mr. Do Quang Hien, Chairman and CEO of T&T Group. Accordingly, Mr. Do Quang Vinh (37 years old), Mr. Hien's eldest son, holds the position of Vice Chairman and Deputy General Director of SHB Bank. His younger brother, Do Vinh Quang, became Chairman of Hanoi Football Club at the young age of 25. By 2026, Mr. Quang will hold the position of Vice Chairman and Deputy General Director of T&T Group.
Leadership skills are needed.
Speaking to Tien Phong newspaper, Dr. Huynh Phuoc Nghia - Director of the Center for Economics, Law and Management (UEH School of Economics, Law and State Management, Ho Chi Minh City University of Economics) said that the driving force of family businesses is formed by the founders having an entrepreneurial spirit.
However, to overcome difficulties and gather initial resources, support from within the family is needed, including spouses, siblings, and close relatives. Together, they build the business, possessing unique business values and secrets, and creatively guide it through challenges. The first crucial element is using the family as a pillar of development; family trust and unity make management easier and allow for shared risk within the family business.
Currently, most family businesses in Vietnam are entering a generational transition phase, grappling with concerns about the pressures of the times and cultural differences. However, according to PwC research, only 15% of family businesses have a plan for transferring management control.
The biggest challenge for the next generation is the enormous "shadow" of the founder. To continue the legacy successfully, the first generation (F1) needs to skillfully implement the five pillars of business and family, including protecting the core business processes, products, and innovations of the family; and safeguarding the family name in business operations and social relationships.
Demonstrate leadership capabilities through practical application. Develop cross-generational human resource management skills. Optimize business relationships between family and company.
You may also like
According to Mr. Nghia, succession planning should begin 10 years in advance, depending on the company's size and the complexity of the leadership generations. This plan includes a rigorous process from capacity building and job testing to delegation of authority and seeking support from outside the family.
Currently, some large family businesses in Vietnam have adopted a more systematic and even stricter approach compared to some other countries in the Asian region.
The next generation inheriting family businesses in Vietnam must be aware of the challenges they face, primarily the business environment, building a talent pool of peers, and applying leadership skills in a new environment.
These changes must be understood by the founding generations themselves, who must realize that failure to adapt will inevitably lead to difficulties and failure for the succeeding generations.
"Many people believe that the biggest obstacle for the next generation is generational conflict in management. In reality, that's not the case; the core issue is the ability to lead the next phase of the family business's development."
Therefore, the strategy is to reconcile the old foundations while being innovative in the new context, as well as aspiring for sustainable development for the family business instead of falling into a cycle of competition and conflict,” Mr. Nghia said.
Currently, only 20% of family businesses are able to plan for a smooth succession process, with the majority having to cope with succession crises.
Therefore, Vietnamese family businesses are currently having to manage many relationships and adjust their business models to adapt to changes. In doing so, they have established a code of conduct for all family members involved in or related to the company's interests. This code governs the distribution of authority, the legal basis for assets, and how to act when the family business faces difficulties.
"Not all Vietnamese family businesses successfully transition to the next generation, but it's crucial to establish rules that prioritize business development and gain the consensus of all relevant family members."
Furthermore, the influence of family culture on business also needs to be carefully considered, prioritizing management transition for the next generation to absorb new cultures, create value, build employee solidarity, and adapt to changing times,” Mr. Nghia said.
Overcoming the F0 syndrome
Meanwhile, economist Tran Anh Tung, Head of Business Administration at the Faculty of Business Administration, Ho Chi Minh City University of Economics and Finance, stated that there are three easily observable scenarios when power is transferred from the first-generation (F0) to the second-generation (F1) of family businesses in Vietnam.
The best-case scenario is a well-prepared transition, where F1 is assigned to individual business units before ascending to the top position. In this scenario, power comes with responsibility, and results are measurable.
The second scenario involves nominal transfer of power, where F1 holds the titles of CEO and Vice President, but F0 still makes decisions regarding investment, personnel, and cash flow. This model easily creates "two centers of power," making it difficult for the organization to rely on the founder's opinion and for F1 to build its own credibility.
The third scenario is to professionalize management, with the family retaining ownership but the CEO potentially being an outsider. This is often a reasonable option when the first child (F1) lacks the necessary skills or is unwilling to manage the company.
PwC previously noted that only 36% of Vietnamese family businesses had a documented succession plan; a subsequent survey revealed that approximately 42% of businesses acknowledged a low level of trust between NextGen and CurrentGen.
Therefore, Vietnam's challenge over the next 10 years is not whether the son will inherit the father's business, but whether businesses can shift from governance based on the personal reputation of the founder to governance based on institutional principles. A successful transition is achieved when the company can function effectively even when the founder is absent from the boardroom.

articles.summary: IMF: AI Investment Lifts Global Growth Despite War, Debt Risks  Global Banking & Finance Review
articles.full_text:
IMF: AI Investment Supports Global Growth as Debt and War Raise Risks
By David Lawder
IMF World Economic Outlook: AI, Energy Shocks, and Diverging Growth
BANGKOK, Oct 13 (Reuters) - The global economy will still manage to top 3% real GDP growth this year as strong AI investment offsets the energy shock from the war in the Middle East, but downside risks are mounting and more countries are being left behind and vulnerable to rising debt loads, the International Monetary Fund said on Tuesday.
Despite a more protracted conflict that has kept oil prices above $100 a barrel, the IMF is forecasting 2026 global growth at 3.1%, a slight uptick from the 3.0% it predicted in July.
The World Economic Outlook forecast, released as global economic and finance leaders gather in Bangkok for the IMF and World Bank annual meetings, is about even with the most optimistic scenario issued in April but below 2025 global growth of 3.5%.
For 2027, the IMF predicts 3.4% global growth, flat with the July forecast and up 0.2 percentage point from April.
AI Investment Drives Growth in Key Economies
The slight improvement is largely due to continued strong investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure, prompting growth upgrades for key advanced economies building AI platforms and especially for countries supplying AI hardware, including South Korea, Malaysia, Mexico and Thailand, which is hosting the meetings this week.
"The global economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits, so we need to move from just coping to rebuilding," the IMF's chief economist, Silvana Tenreyro, told a news conference. "We need to restore fiscal space. We need to rebuild supply-side resilience."
Risks to Global Growth
She said major downside risks to growth include a prolonged, intensified war in the Middle East that spikes inflation pressures, rising bond yields that raise government borrowing costs, El Nino-driven extreme weather events and a reassessment of AI profitability that craters investment and asset prices.
Mitigating the Oil Price Shock
Countries and companies moved quickly to mitigate the oil price shock, drawing down reserves, substituting other suppliers and energy sources and cutting oil demand, Petya Koeva Brooks, the IMF's deputy research director, told Reuters in a separate interview. She said global growth would have fallen to 2.5% this year without these measures, but their effect is fading as the war drags on.
Divergence and Downward Revisions
The IMF noted a growing divergence between countries benefiting from AI and those bypassed by it. Just 32 countries now account for 95% of global growth, compared to 54 countries in April.
Downward growth revisions have become more widespread, with the IMF downgrading 47% of economies since the April forecasts were issued, including several energy importers outside AI value chains.
Gulf Economies Hit Hardest
Hardest hit by downgrades were the Gulf countries directly impacted by the US-Israeli war against Iran, with Saudi Arabia's GDP now forecast to contract 3.3% this year compared with the 1.7% growth predicted in July.
Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates are also expected to fall into deep recessions, with 2026 contractions of 7.6%, 16%, 16.7%, 15.6% and 3.9%, respectively.
Major Economies: United States, Europe, China, and India
United States and Europe
UNITED STATES FLAT, IMPROVEMENT IN EUROPE
Among major economies, the IMF forecast US growth of 2.3% for both 2026 and 2027, unchanged for this year and 0.1 percentage point higher for next year. The US economy is expected to be supported by robust private consumption, tax cuts and AI investment, though the boost from AI will be offset by its large import content.
Euro zone growth for 2026 was upgraded to 1.1% from 0.9% in July due to stronger investment in AI, participation in AI value chains such as chemical production in Germany, and higher defense spending in EU countries. Britain's 2026 growth forecast also was upgraded by 0.3 percentage point from July to 1.3% due to larger AI investment.
China and India
The IMF forecast China's growth at 4.5% for 2026 and 4.0% for 2027, both down 0.1 percentage point from July, as higher oil prices exacerbate weak domestic demand despite strong exports.
India remains the world's fastest-growing major economy at 7.0% for both 2026 and 2027, up 0.6 percentage point this year and 0.3 percentage point next year compared with the July forecasts amid robust domestic demand, services activity and AI investment.
Inflation Outlook
The AI investment surge is projected to keep upward pressure on prices, with global headline consumer price inflation forecast at 4.7% in 2026 and 4.1% for 2027.
Energy Prices and AI: Uncertainties Ahead
Oil Price Scenarios
ENERGY PRICE, AI RISKS
Participants at the IMF and World Bank meetings in Bangkok will be assessing a precarious outlook. The IMF forecasts are based on assumptions that the Strait of Hormuz will reopen in March 2027 with a broad return to pre-war shipping conditions occurring by October 2027. The IMF assumes an average oil price of $96 per barrel for 2026 and $87 in 2027.
But under an adverse scenario highlighted in the report, in which a worsening war pushes oil prices to $130 per barrel through the first quarter of 2027, growth would be reduced by 0.2 percentage point in 2026 and 0.5 percentage point in 2027. Inflation in 2027 would surge by another 1.1 percentage point to 5.2%.
AI's Double-Edged Sword
AI is also a huge source of uncertainty, with major downside and upside risks, the IMF report said. Under a scenario of faster adoption of the technology and accelerated investment, global GDP could rise a further 0.6% by 2029, with the bulk of the benefits going to the US and China.
Potential Downside: Weak Productivity Gains
But if productivity gains from AI fail to materialize, prompting a sharp decline in investment, US GDP could fall by 0.8% directly, causing spillovers to Asian technology exporters with a total direct GDP impact of as much as 0.4% by 2028.

articles.title: When scale arrives before proof: Singapore’s capital allocation question in Southeast Asia - Asian Business Review
articles.summary: When scale arrives before proof: Singapore’s capital allocation question in Southeast Asia  Asian Business Review
articles.full_text:
In Singapore, financial capacity can be created before the return on that capacity is known.
Singapore occupies an unusual position in Southeast Asia. It is not the region’s largest market, but it is one of its most important centres for capital formation, structuring, and allocation. Banks, institutional investors, listed companies, and regional headquarters based in Singapore routinely make decisions whose economic consequences are realised elsewhere across the region.
That position creates an advantage. It also creates a recurring capital-allocation problem. Capital can create capacity long before it proves value.
In Singapore, that problem can appear at the financial layer. One major bank recently executed a synthetic securitisation referencing a US$1b ($1.278b) corporate-loan portfolio whilst operating from a position of considerable strength, with quarterly net profit close to S$3b, return on equity around 17%, deposits above $600b and a common-equity Tier 1 ratio close to 15%.
The transaction creates regulatory capacity. That is real. But regulatory capacity is not yet an economic return.
The value still has to travel through a second chain. Capital relief must become deployable balance-sheet capacity. That capacity must support additional lending. The lending must generate adequate spreads. Credit losses must remain acceptable. The resulting activity must ultimately produce sufficient economic profit.
The transaction can therefore succeed mechanically before its full economic value has been demonstrated.
This is not a criticism of capital management. It is a distinction between creating the ability to deploy capital and proving that the subsequent deployment creates value.
The same expression can appear elsewhere in Southeast Asia in a very different form. In Indonesia, one healthcare investment involved roughly Rp1.9t ($135m) for a 40% stake, alongside explicit plans to improve procurement, reduce material costs, strengthen partnerships, and develop digital capabilities.
These were not vague aspirations. They were identifiable operating levers. But capital entering the business did not itself prove that those interventions would translate into better economics.
Within roughly 18 months, significant financial problems had emerged. By late 2025, the business had entered a long-dated restructuring agreement with five banks.
The important point is not that the original investment thesis was necessarily wrong. Nor does the later restructuring prove that the capital should never have been deployed. The point is narrower.
Capital created the opportunity for the operating thesis to work. It did not establish that the operating thesis had already worked. The economic chain still had to move from capital, to intervention, to better operating performance, to stronger cash generation, and ultimately to sustainable equity value.
Singapore and Indonesia are very different markets, and the two examples sit at different points in the capital-allocation process. But the underlying expression is similar.
In Singapore, financial capacity can be created before the return on that capacity is known. In Indonesia, operating capacity can be funded before the return on those interventions has been realised. In both cases, an intermediate achievement risks being mistaken for the final result.
That distinction matters across Southeast Asia because the region increasingly rewards visible scale. Companies expand into new markets, acquire assets, extend distribution, build digital platforms, increase lending capacity, and assemble regional footprints. Investors can point to larger balance sheets, wider market presence and greater strategic reach.
Those achievements are meaningful. They are not the same thing as value creation.
Capital committed is evidence of funding access. Assets assembled are evidence of execution capacity. Operating capability shows that a larger system can function. Sustainable value creation requires something more demanding: recurring cash generation, improved productivity, stronger returns on capital, or a durable economic advantage.
The analytical error occurs when evidence from the earlier stages is treated as proof of the final one.
Southeast Asia is particularly exposed to this problem because its growth opportunities are real, but often unevenly developed. The region combines large addressable markets, infrastructure requirements, fragmented geographies, rapid formalisation, and increasingly deep pools of institutional capital.
Those conditions create legitimate reasons to invest ahead of maturity. They also make it possible for physical or financial scale to arrive faster than economic validation.
Stores can be opened. Assets can be acquired. Loans can be originated. Customers can be added. Market presence can be counted. Returns take longer.
Working-capital requirements may rise. Integration costs can persist. Utilisation can disappoint. Pricing may prove weaker than expected. Revenue can increase while returns on incremental capital deteriorate. This creates a simple but important asymmetry: the evidence of expansion usually becomes visible before the evidence of value creation.
For boards and investors, the relevant question is therefore not whether capital was successfully deployed. It is what changed economically because that capital was deployed.
Did margins improve? Did utilisation rise? Did working-capital intensity fall? Did cash conversion strengthen? Did returns on capital improve? Did the enlarged platform produce economics superior to the available alternatives?
Those are the measures that convert capital allocation from strategic narrative into economic results.
For Singapore, this question is especially important because its regional advantage is increasingly one of capital allocation rather than capital scarcity. Singapore already has financial capacity.
The harder test is whether capital deployed from, through or by Singapore into Southeast Asia is consistently converted into adequate incremental returns.
The Indonesian example matters not because it is a Singapore transaction, but because it shows the same underlying inference error at a different point in the chain. In one market, capital creates financial capacity before value is proven. In another, capital funds operate intervention before value is proven.
The expression changes. The underlying discipline does not. Southeast Asia does not suffer from a shortage of capital. The harder problem is knowing when capital has actually earned the right to be called value.
Capital can fund the proof. It should not be mistaken for the proof.

articles.title: Singapore Central Bank Chief Says CBDCs Needed As Digital Money Scales - Crowdfund Insider
articles.summary: Singapore Central Bank Chief Says CBDCs Needed As Digital Money Scales  Crowdfund Insider
articles.full_text:
Singapore’s central bank will step up work on wholesale central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) and stablecoin regulation as tokenised financial markets develop, with the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS)’s managing director saying central bank money will ultimately be needed to anchor monetary stability.
Chia Der Jiun said preparations for central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) could begin while tokenised assets and private forms of digital money remain at an early stage of development.
As the use of privately issued digital money expands, CBDCs will play a role in preserving monetary stability and providing certainty in settlement, he said.
“Tokenised transactions will only scale if they are settled using safe and trusted digital money,” Chia said in a keynote address at the INSEAD Digital Finance & Agentic AI Summit on Friday.
MAS has made wholesale Singapore dollar central bank digital currency available through its Singapore dollar Test Network, which became operational in 2025.
The first successful trial involved the settlement of interbank overnight lending transactions between DBS, OCBC, and UOB.
The central bank is now preparing to use wholesale CBDC to settle tokenised MAS bills, bringing tokenised assets and central bank digital currency together on common infrastructure.
The initiative aims to provide greater certainty and finality in transactions.
MAS has also consulted on legislative amendments to implement its proposed Single-Currency Stablecoin framework.
The framework includes safeguards covering reserve backing, capital requirements, redemption at par and disclosure, while addressing cross-border issuance and recognition of foreign stablecoins regulated under comparable regimes.
Chia said tokenised bank deposits, regulated stablecoins and CBDCs could serve different purposes, depending on the needs of users and markets.
Deposit tokens may be suited to banking-related activities such as cash management and payments, while stablecoins could gain wider adoption on cryptocurrency exchanges and in fintech payments.
However, privately issued digital money must remain anchored in a trusted monetary system.
Commercial bank deposits maintain parity with central bank money through their convertibility into central bank reserves, while stablecoins depend primarily on the transparency and adequacy of their reserve assets.
Chia said additional regulatory requirements and access to central bank reserves could be considered for stablecoins that eventually become systemically important.
Tokenisation faces challenge of commercial adoption
Beyond digital money, MAS is working with financial institutions to move asset tokenisation from experimentation towards wider commercial use.
Through Project Guardian, the central bank has worked with industry participants to test tokenisation across asset classes and develop common standards and practices.
Chia said adoption would require financial institutions to coordinate their approaches to asset servicing, disclosure, interoperability and risk management.
Although tokenisation has advanced in areas such as bond issuance, private credit, corporate debt, equities, precious metals and money market funds, activity remains small relative to conventional markets for these assets.
Repo transactions offer a potential use case, as tokenisation could coordinate securities transfers, cash movements, collateral valuation and other processes on compatible infrastructure, reducing repeated reconciliation between participants.
The challenge is extending these benefits beyond individual institutions and closed networks. Chia said customers, counterparties, and financial market infrastructure would need to move together for tokenised markets to achieve scale.
MAS is also working through Global Layer One, an industry collaboration platform intended to support cross-border transactions in tokenised assets.
Its initiatives include a Market Infrastructure Toolkit to assess digital financial infrastructure against international standards and a Programmable Compliance Toolkit to embed regulatory requirements into digital infrastructure.
Chia said financial markets were unlikely to converge on a single global ledger. Instead, the industry would need to connect multiple platforms and networks while maintaining appropriate governance, resilience, risk controls, and regulatory compliance.
MAS advances safeguards for AI-driven finance
Chia also highlighted the implications of artificial intelligence agents that could act on behalf of individuals and institutions, including initiating and executing financial transactions.
Such agents could increase the speed at which money moves in response to relatively small differences in benefits and incentives, requiring financial institutions to sharpen their value propositions and improve how they communicate with both customers and their AI agents.
The technology also raises questions around authority, permissions, identity, accountability and governance, particularly where agents can execute transactions within financial institutions’ systems.
Earlier this year, MAS and industry participants published the Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime (SAFR) white paper, setting out a framework for governing AI agents during execution.
The framework covers agent identity and authorisation, checks against a user’s mandate before actions are executed, and mechanisms for accountability and auditability.
MAS has since published version 1.1 of the white paper, incorporating contributions from a broader group of financial institutions and AI developers.
The Future of Finance Institute has also released an open-source reference implementation to support industry testing and development.
Chia said public-private collaboration would remain essential as digital finance evolves, with common standards, sound regulation and trusted infrastructure needed to support adoption across tokenised assets, digital money, and AI-enabled financial services.

articles.title: Prospects For A Political Solution To The Myanmar Crisis – OpEd - Eurasia Review
articles.summary: Prospects For A Political Solution To The Myanmar Crisis – OpEd  Eurasia Review
articles.full_text:
Key Takeaways:
- Min Aung Hlaing’s 100-day peace initiative was rejected by major resistance groups, while his visits to India, China, Russia and selected ASEAN states aim to ease isolation, secure arms and economic support, and gain legitimacy despite ongoing air strikes and civilian casualties.
- In Rakhine, military blockades and Arakan Army operations have created shortages and disrupted trade with Bangladesh, yet limited border commerce offers relief and could revive roughly $260 million in annual exchanges if formalized under stable conditions.
- Diplomatic and military advantages will not end the conflict without a negotiated political settlement; resistance unity could block further offensives, while compromise would improve prospects for peace, Rohingya returns and regional connectivity.
A peaceful resolution to Myanmar’s prolonged conflict remains uncertain. Despite repression, displacement, economic hardship, and immense sacrifice, peace has not returned. The popular struggle against military rule has continued for more than five years, demonstrating the resilience of the resistance. The authorities continue to confront armed resistance groups without making meaningful progress toward compromise or a political settlement. The peace and stability promised after the elections have yet to materialize. Even amid the civil war, the authorities have sought to improve relations with neighboring countries, expand diplomatic engagement, enhance international acceptance, and strengthen the economy. Peace and stability in Myanmar, particularly in Rakhine State, are essential to resolving the Rohingya crisis. If the government can combine its international initiatives with credible measures to restore domestic peace, relations between Bangladesh and Myanmar could improve, supporting regional development and security.
The United Nations’ independent investigative mechanism has reported a continuing rise in the number and severity of serious crimes in Myanmar, alongside intensified military air strikes against civilians. Military forces have reportedly struck homes, schools, hospitals, religious buildings, and shelters for displaced people. Human rights organizations say violence against civilians continues in areas controlled by resistance groups through air strikes, arson, and forced displacement. Both the military and the ethnic armed group Arakan Army have been accused of widespread and systematic abuses against the Rohingya minority. Illicit economic activities, including illegal mining, drug production, human trafficking, and scam centers, help finance the conflict and deepen the human rights crisis.
After assuming the presidency, Min Aung Hlaing announced a 100-day initiative and called for peace talks with armed resistance groups. Major resistance organizations, including the Kachin Independence Organization, the Karen National Union, the Chin National Front, and the Arakan Army, rejected the proposal. Despite maintaining regular contact with the military, the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) did not participate in the 100-day peace initiative. Under pressure from China, the MNDAA is now engaged in talks with the Myanmar authorities. Because the group controls important border trade routes with China, the government, with Beijing’s support, is seeking greater influence over these routes.
If the main armed resistance groups agree to separate ceasefires, their combined effect could alter the balance of the conflict. The Myanmar military could then reposition its forces and launch new offensives, potentially prolonging the war. Critics therefore argue that the government’s 100-day peace initiative is primarily a political strategy designed to strengthen regional and international acceptance of the new electoral system.
Since taking office as president, Min Aung Hlaing has visited India, China, Russia, and several ASEAN countries. His visit to India appeared intended to reduce Myanmar’s heavy dependence on China by strengthening ties with another major regional power. During the visit, Myanmar pledged that its territory would not be used to threaten India’s security. Both sides emphasized the need to advance stalled connectivity projects, including the Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project and the India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway, and set a bilateral trade target of US$5 billion.
The main subjects of Min Aung Hlaing’s visit to Russia were military cooperation, nuclear energy, space, digital technology, special economic zones, and energy projects. Relations between Russia and Myanmar now extend across defense, nuclear energy, infrastructure, and other strategic sectors. The multibillion-dollar arms trade remains central to the relationship. Diplomatically, the visit was intended to strengthen the government’s international legitimacy and strategic position through ties with a key ally, despite continued Western sanctions and isolation.
Although ASEAN has declined to formally recognize Myanmar’s military rule and continues to exclude the country from high-level meetings, Min Aung Hlaing’s recent visits have helped improve bilateral ties with individual member states. The Myanmar authorities have exploited divisions within ASEAN by cultivating relations with each member separately as part of a broader effort to break their international isolation. Official receptions in Laos, Thailand, Vietnam, and Cambodia have helped advance these ties. Analysts argue that such bilateral engagements give the military government an appearance of diplomatic influence and legitimacy, weakening ASEAN’s joint peace framework, the Five-Point Consensus. Min Aung Hlaing also urged the Thai prime minister to stop support and arms supplies from reaching Myanmar’s resistance forces.
At the same time, Myanmar and Thailand discussed border security measures to counter the smuggling of drugs and prohibited chemicals. Bangkok’s decision to restore ties amid allegations of widespread atrocities and war crimes against civilians has drawn strong criticism from Thai politicians and international human rights organizations.
During his visit to Belarus, Min Aung Hlaing held talks aimed at attracting investment. He argued that Belarusian businesses operating in Myanmar could gain access to ASEAN and the wider Asian market, while Myanmar’s exports could reach the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) through Belarus, creating reciprocal opportunities. The Myanmar authorities have long sought EAEU observer status and have held extensive discussions with EAEU representatives on cooperation in energy, agriculture, education, and transport.
The Myanmar military has maintained a prolonged blockade of roads and waterways connecting Rakhine State with the rest of the country. As a result, many civilians in Rakhine face shortages of medicine and other basic necessities. Communities have therefore sought food, medicine, fuel, and essential goods from Bangladesh and India. Military operations, the activities of the Arakan Army, restrictions on movement, and widespread insecurity have largely halted cross-border trade and made humanitarian access increasingly difficult, disrupting local livelihoods. Conditions improved somewhat when limited trade resumed along the Teknaf-Kanyin Chaung border route during the conflict. Border trade therefore serves both economic and humanitarian needs. Much of it is conducted through informal arrangements; a stable and formal framework could expand trade and strengthen economic relations between the two countries.
Before the conflict in Rakhine disrupted regional commerce, official statistics placed the annual trade volume along the Bangladesh-Rakhine border at approximately US$260 million, demonstrating the economic complementarity of the two neighboring regions. Agriculture, fisheries, marine products, livestock, forestry, and small-scale industries once formed the backbone of local livelihoods. Revitalizing these sectors could support a two-way trading relationship that benefits people on both sides of the border. Greater market access for local entrepreneurs would encourage investment and create jobs in border communities. A normalization of conditions in Rakhine would also improve the prospects for addressing the wider crisis between Bangladesh and Myanmar.
The Bangladesh-Rakhine border could become more than a simple crossing point. Realizing its potential will depend on sustained stability, investment in infrastructure, simpler trade rules, and durable cross-border cooperation. With expanding regional connectivity through the route linking Paletwa in Myanmar to Mizoram in India, the area could emerge as an important economic corridor in the Bay of Bengal region. The challenge for the Government of Bangladesh and the authorities in Rakhine is to ensure that border trade supports a more prosperous, connected, and peaceful frontier and contributes to lasting peace between the two countries.
The Myanmar authorities have yet to take effective steps to end the internal conflict. Experience over recent decades suggests that the crisis will remain difficult to resolve without a political settlement. The government is currently seeking greater international acceptance through diplomacy while maintaining its military capabilities and expanding trade and economic relations. It is also deepening ties with neighboring countries, particularly China and Russia. Myanmar has encouraged investors by emphasizing its access to wider markets and the strategic importance of its geographic position, presenting these factors as opportunities for increased investment and trade.
These initiatives are unlikely to succeed unless peace returns to the country. It remains unclear whether pressure on the resistance groups can produce a compromise. If the groups remain united and coordinate their actions, the government’s strategy may fail. If their unity fractures, however, the military could regroup and attack them separate

articles.title: Final article: Connecting to create new value - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Final article: Connecting to create new value  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Beyond supply chains, operational capabilities, and industrial symbiosis, the next question facing industrial parks is how to connect with what lies outside the factory fence. Many argue that Vietnam is shifting from a low-cost manufacturing destination to a strategic regional manufacturing hub, where demand is no longer limited to traditional industrial land but has expanded to integrated development models.
 To clarify these changes, a reporter from the News and Nation newspaper interviewed Ms. Trang Le, General Director and Senior Director of Research and Consulting at JLL Vietnam.
 Madam, what new opportunities are emerging for Vietnam's industrial real estate sector due to the influx of investment capital?
 Vietnam continues to have a favorable foundation for attracting investment. In the first two quarters of 2026, total registered foreign investment reached approximately US$34.7 billion, a 61% increase compared to the same period last year; implemented capital reached approximately US$13 billion, an 11% increase. During the same period, GDP increased by approximately 8.2%, and export turnover increased by 21%. These indicators show that investment, production, and trade continue to support the market. 
 Ms. Trang Le, General Director and Senior Director of Research and Consulting at JLL Vietnam, shared this information at the Industrial Real Estate Forum 2026 held at the end of September.
 Opportunities also arise from shifts in industries. Beyond traditional manufacturing, demand is expanding into high technology, pharmaceuticals, research and development, and data centers. These activities require investment locations that align with the company's long-term strategy.
 Vietnam has advantages in terms of geographical location, a network of free trade agreements, and a domestic market. Coupled with infrastructure upgrades, these factors help businesses integrate their operations into regional production networks. Therefore, developers need to view opportunities by identifying which industry sectors and functions their location best suits.
 Investors now have more location options, but why do industrial land rental prices still vary so significantly between regions, Madam?
 The differentiation is linked to the conditions of each location, especially connectivity. Within the key markets surveyed by JLL, the North has approximately 13,000 hectares of operational industrial land in 75 industrial parks, with an occupancy rate of 82.4%. The South has approximately 28,100 hectares in 141 industrial parks, with an occupancy rate of 84.1%. These figures are for the surveyed markets, not for all industrial parks nationwide.
 Industrial land lease prices in the North range from approximately 120-180 USD/m², while in the South they range from 100-320 USD/m², calculated for the entire lease term. Areas near international seaports, airports, or major transportation routes still command higher prices than the average.
 Such a price range indicates that businesses have multiple options, but each option comes with different conditions. Therefore, the price needs to be considered in relation to location and accessibility to transportation networks and markets. For investors, the advantages of the location must be demonstrated by the actual connections that the business can utilize.
 With expanding transportation infrastructure creating opportunities for production, what should these new locations do to become long-term choices for FDI investors?
 First, it is necessary to determine the role of the location within the overall development network. With the addition of expressways, ring roads, or transportation hubs, businesses may consider areas outside of traditional industrial centers. However, the prospects of a location must be viewed in conjunction with existing conditions and long-term development directions. 
 In the South, Long Thanh International Airport, Ho Chi Minh City's Ring Road 3, the Ben Luc - Long Thanh expressway, and other logistics hubs are expected to expand regional connectivity. (Illustrative image)
 By 2030, JLL forecasts that surveyed markets in the North could add approximately 5,000 hectares of industrial land, while the South could add over 6,000 hectares. In the North, Hai Phong leads in future supply, with four industrial parks already under construction in May 2026 alone. Hanoi also commenced construction on two new industrial parks, adding to the development space.
 In the South, Long Thanh International Airport, Ho Chi Minh City's Ring Road 3, the Ben Luc - Long Thanh expressway, and logistics hubs are expected to expand regional connectivity. These changes create more options while also requiring industrial parks to be viewed within a broader economic context.
 New land plots need to be connected to transportation networks and have conditions that support long-term operations. The attractiveness of a location comes from these factors, not just from the added land area.
 Many projects combine industrial, residential, and commercial elements. Why, despite having all these components, has a complete ecosystem not yet been created, Madam?
 The issue lies in whether the components truly fit together. Bringing industry, housing, and commerce into a single project creates spatial cohesion. To become an ecosystem, these components must meet the needs of the relevant user groups.
 Developers need to understand the income, housing needs, and affordability of workers in industrial zones. In reality, there is still a gap between factory workers and the target customer group for residential and commercial properties.
 If the residential area is developed for a different customer group, workers may still not find suitable housing, even if the housing is right near their workplace. In that case, the buildings stand next to each other but do not truly complement each other.
 This is one of the reasons why some integrated models have not been as effective as expected. Whether a project is complete or not should be judged by its ability to meet real needs, not just by its list of works.
 According to her, what should developers consider to ensure that housing and services are truly suitable for people working in industrial zones?
 In my opinion, the first step is to identify who the product is for. Workers, skilled laborers, and professionals have different living needs. Analyzing the characteristics of the workforce, income, and ability to pay will help investors choose the right product. 
 The attractiveness of investment locations lies not only in having modern production facilities but also in the connectivity between the production site, transportation networks, and suitable living conditions. (Illustrative image)
 Housing near the workplace may not necessarily solve the needs if workers lack access to it. The same applies to commercial amenities; they may be available but not meet their needs. Therefore, the development of these components must be linked to the very people who will work and live in the area.
 Workers' housing, expert apartments, and community amenities are part of the "soft infrastructure" that helps attract and retain workers, especially those from other localities and foreign experts.
 Understanding the users correctly is essential for investors to arrange the components appropriately. Only when the workplace and living conditions are integrated can the integrated model effectively meet long-term needs.
 Furthermore, developers need to consider the existing infrastructure, amenities, and services in the surrounding area to connect with and support the project. Some areas already partially meet the living needs of workers. Recognizing this helps investors understand what is lacking in the area before deciding to invest further.
 If each industrial park builds its own self-contained system without integration with the broader economic space, investment efficiency and synergy will be limited. Placing the project within the context of the entire area will help to better define the role of each component.
 For new industrial zones, attractiveness needs to be built on the connection between production facilities, transportation networks, and suitable living conditions. When these components serve the right needs and support each other, the new investment location has a foundation for long-term business and worker development.
 Thank you very much, Madam!
 Hai Yen (News Report)

articles.summary: Indonesia's new police chief moved fast to shake up the force. Can he change its culture?  CNAOf the 242 police chiefs nationwide, 118 (49%) were replaced. Major positions in the audit and inves..  매일경제Making police reform work  The Jakarta PostInterpreting the Meaning Behind General Suyudi's Mass Reshuffles  Kompas.comIndonesia’s police chief makes 70 appointments and promotions — Channel NewsAsia  UA.NEWS
articles.full_text:
analysis Asia
Indonesia's new police chief moved fast to shake up the force. Can he change its culture?
New Indonesian Police Chief Suyudi Ario Seto began overhauling the force just two days after getting the job. Experts ask whether his sweeping personnel changes are indicators of wider change.
JAKARTA: Within two days of taking charge of Indonesia’s national police, Suyudi Ario Seto began reshaping the force.
Seventy officers were promoted or given new appointments on Oct 3, while 18 others received new remits, as part of wide sweeping changes, which also saw many others reassigned to make way for the newly promoted officers.
Among the major changes, the police chief of the Riau Islands province, which is south of Singapore, was appointed head of the national criminal investigation agency.
The Jakarta police chief has been appointed chief of the National Police’s General Supervision Inspectorate and the Riau province police chief, who was previously with the police’s counterterrorism unit Densus 88, has been tasked to oversee public security and order.
Political watchers and former senior officers whom CNA spoke to suggested several different reasons for the speed and scale of the reshuffle.
Several said it was part and parcel of generational renewal and an attempt to better match key appointments with officers with specific expertise. Others suggested that the moves were to disrupt established hierarchies and remove centres of influence associated with Suyudi’s predecessor.
The question some are asking is whether these personnel changes will lead to a change in the culture of the institution.
Suyudi, 53, who was sworn in as national police chief by President Prabowo Subianto on Oct 1, is a 1994 police academy graduate whose career has included criminal investigation, cybercrime, regional command and narcotics enforcement.
He has indicated that he wants the police to become more responsive to the public. As part of that, a new tagline was unveiled on Oct 5: “Polisi Bersama Masyarakat”, or “Police Together with the Community”.
Public expectations are high for a change in the way the police operate after Suyudi's immediate predecessor, Listyo Sigit Prabowo, became embroiled in a number of controversies.
These included tensions between the police force and the Attorney General’s Office over graft and money laundering probes implicating senior officials at both institutions, and allegations against the police of abuse of power and brutality, culminating in protests last August when a delivery driver was fatally struck by an armoured police vehicle.
The sudden changes have cast a spotlight on the issues Suyudi intends to address and whether moving people at the higher levels will translate into deeper reform.
But analysts told CNA that the real test is whether his personnel changes will alter how officers behave towards the public.
“We have to see whether these changes alter the culture and change public services,” said Bambang Rukminto, an analyst from Jakarta-based think tank Institute of Security and Strategic Studies (ISESS).
“If not, this is just changing the players.”
“Police Together with the Community” is not the first new tagline that Suyudi has rolled out.
During his tenure as police chief of Banten - a province bordering Jakarta - from June 2024 to August 2025, Suyudi called on officers to be humane but firm, promoting the motto “Polisi HEBAT” - Humanis, Eksis, Bermanfaat, Antisipatif dan Tegas (“humane, present, beneficial, anticipatory and firm”).
That approach faced a high-profile test in January 2025, after officers at Cinangka subdistrict police station in Banten failed to respond appropriately to a request for police assistance by a car-rental owner, who was fatally shot after making the call.
Suyudi publicly acknowledged the failures and removed the local police chief and two officers from their posts pending an internal professional standards investigation into alleged unprofessional conduct.
His most recent role was head of the national narcotics agency (BNN), from August 2025, where he pursued what the agency called a “war on drugs for humanity”, combining enforcement against traffickers with rehabilitation for drug users.
In one nationwide operation in November 2025, BNN and other agencies raided 53 drug hotspots across 34 provinces and detained 1,259 people.
Following further investigations, 37 people were named suspects while 369 underwent rehabilitation, according to BNN.
His record points to an approach that combines firm enforcement with an emphasis on public service, experts said.
However, whether the initial quick personnel changes and his track record indicate an appetite for deeper reforms of the national police force is another matter, they said.
“After this overhaul at the elite level, the question is whether it will also be followed by changes to the lower levels,” Bambang said.
SWIFT CHANGES
The police overhaul that Suyudi ordered reached some of the most powerful positions in the national police hierarchy.
Asep Safrudin, formerly the police chief of the Riau Islands province, was appointed head of the national criminal investigation agency. His predecessor Syahardiantono has been reassigned to the presidential staff office.
Meanwhile, former Jakarta police chief Asep Edi Suheri has been appointed chief of the National Police’s General Supervision Inspectorate. He succeeds Wahyu Widada, who has been moved to serve as a high-ranking officer at the ministry of agrarian affairs and spatial planning.
Riau province police chief, Herry Heryawan, who has prior experience in criminal investigation, the police’s counterterrorism unit Densus 88, and regional command roles, was appointed to oversee public security and order. He replaces Karyoto, who will retire at the end of this month and who, like some Indonesians, goes by one name.
Dedy Kusuma Bakti, who previously held a senior intelligence and security role, was promoted to take the overall lead in those functions.
Former national police commissioner Poengky Indarti said these key appointments represented a natural progression for them given their relevant prior experience.
“The (police’s) professionalism will be strengthened, and this signals a positive trend for the enhancement of the national police's performance,” she added.
The changes also extended well beyond national headquarters.
Nineteen of Indonesia’s provincial police chiefs were rotated on Oct 3, including commanders responsible for Jakarta and several of the country’s most populous provinces in Java, as well as resource-rich provinces in Sumatra and Sulawesi.
Suyudi also changed the leadership of Densus 88 by promoting its deputy chief, Tubagus Ami Prindani, to head the unit.
He appointed a new cybercrime director, Suhermanto, who had previously been assigned to the national narcotics agency.
In all, 70 senior and mid-ranking officers were promoted or given new appointments.
“He wants to make radical changes,” Bambang said, arguing that the speed could be intended to signal the necessity of reform. He described the overhaul as unusually fast and likened its scale to “bedol desa”, an Indonesian expression referring to moving an entire village.
He said one possible explanation was that Suyudi wanted both generational renewal and also to disrupt established structures within the police.
Head of non-governmental organisation (NGO) Indonesia Police Watch (IPW) Sugeng Teguh Santoso said the reshuffle was designed partly to remove centres of influence associated with Suyudi’s predecessor.
Suyudi has strong political backing to make such changes as he was President Prabowo’s sole pick to become the police chief.
“It appears the strategy is to completely overhaul the personnel at national police headquarters first, and only then consolidate the programmes,” Sugeng said.
“This is so the new police chief can control the institution under one command.”
But not all experts saw the speed as particularly significant.
Former national police commission commissioner Poengky said that while the turnaround appeared quick, early reshuffles by incoming police chiefs are not unusual.
Former police chief Tito Karnavian, who is now home affairs minister, moved 110 personnel nine days after becoming police chief in July 2016, she noted, while Idham Azis transferred 170 personnel seven days after taking office in November 2019.
“There is nothing strange or problematic with this reshuffle,” Poengky told CNA, describing such rotations as part of “regeneration, renewal and organisational strengthening”.
She also argued that several appointments matched officers with their expertise, citing Dedy’s appointment to lead intelligence and Herry’s move to the security maintenance agency following experience in criminal investigations, counterterrorism and regional policing.
“Essentially, professionalism is being strengthened,” she said.
CHANGING MORE THAN THE LEADERSHIP
Suyudi’s bigger task now is whether he can change the police’s military culture, experts said, followed by other challenges such as tackling narcotics, online gambling and even terrorism.
Bambang from ISESS said that police often treat protests as security threats rather than events where police should protect peaceful demonstrators while isolating those who might be committing violence.
At the end of August last year, a motorcycle taxi driver was killed by an armoured police vehicle in Jakarta, triggering nationwide protests. It became the most serious unrest of Prabowo's presidency so far since his appointment in October 2024.
Jakarta-based NGO KontraS recorded 561 incidents of police violence between July 2025 and June 2026. Although this is lower than previous years, where KontraS recorded 602 incidents between July 2024 and June 2025 and 641 cases between July 2023 and June 2024, the police have continued to come in for public criticism.

IMF-WB Conference: Policymakers Face Difficult Choices: The annual IMF-WB conference in Bangkok is seeing global policymakers facing difficult choices in the face of a range of economic challenges. The energy shock from the Middle East conflict, public debt pressures, and rising inflation are creating uneven impacts, particularly affecting developing countries. While the IMF is calling for the creation of fiscal buffers, development organizations warn that cuts to support could derail development goals and push more people into poverty.
2. China's economy continues to thrive in Q3 2026 thanks to consumption and technology: Chinese economic data for Q3 2026 shows clear signs of improvement, driven by a recovery in domestic consumption and a strong increase in investment in new technologies such as AI and humanoid robots. Spending at stores increased by 2.6%, while investment in AI and robotics surged by 184.1% year-on-year. Both manufacturing and services PMI indices exceeded 50 points, confirming continued economic expansion and supporting Beijing's 4.5-5% growth target for this year.
3. OPEC sharply lowers its 2026 oil demand growth forecast: On October 12, the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) decided to sharply lower its forecast for global oil demand growth in 2026 to 400,000 barrels per day, but expects demand to surge again in 2027 due to pent-up demand. OPEC Secretary General Haitham Al Ghais said the new adjustment is a significant reduction from the 1.4 million barrels per day forecast made earlier this year, reflecting the actual developments in the global energy market over the past period.
4. IMF Managing Director: AI Investment Wave Fuels Global Economic Growth: IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva stated that the massive wave of investment in artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure is creating a "demand shock," helping the global economy maintain a 3% growth rate despite challenges from the energy supply chain. This boom particularly benefits Asian economies that supply AI hardware. However, she also warned that AI could cause profound changes in employment and inequality, requiring governments and international organizations to develop appropriate response strategies.
5. Record demand from China provides support for gold prices: Strong demand from the People's Bank of China (PBoC) and its citizens is becoming a crucial support for global gold prices, helping them withstand pressure from high US bond yields. The PBoC has been continuously buying gold for 23 months to diversify its foreign exchange reserves and reduce its dependence on the US dollar. Along with this, the sluggish domestic real estate and stock markets have also prompted Chinese citizens to seek gold as a safe asset. As a result, the country's gold imports in the first eight months of 2016 reached a record high of over 1,000 tons.

Renault, Stellantis, Volkswagen, Mercedes, and Asian brands all took advantage of the event to introduce new products, focusing on battery technology, performance, and charging speed.
7. China and EU reach agreement to maintain hybrid vehicle export growth: China and the European Union (EU) have reached an agreement to limit imports of hybrid vehicles from China to 350,000 units per year. This agreement was reached after three months of negotiations, aiming to maintain stable export growth for Chinese businesses while avoiding escalating bilateral trade tensions. The agreement is seen as a step towards protecting practical interests and creating a more predictable trade environment, although this new limit represents a significant reduction from China's previous export forecasts.

The US electric vehicle charging market is experiencing record growth: Despite a sharp decline in electric vehicle (EV) sales in the US following the removal of tax incentives, the charging station industry is still recording record expansion. This growth is also driven by soaring gasoline prices due to geopolitical conflicts, causing some consumers to reconsider using electric vehicles. 9.
