This initiative aims to address the challenges arising from the boom in new tourism forms such as ecotourism and camping, while ensuring sustainable development and efficient resource use. The guidelines encourage the development of supporting infrastructure in rural and natural areas, and consider planning specific ecological zones dedicated to suitable tourism activities.

articles.title: Singapore Sets New AI Risk Rules for Finance. What They Mean for Brokers - Finance Magnates
articles.summary: Singapore Sets New AI Risk Rules for Finance. What They Mean for Brokers  Finance Magnates
articles.full_text:
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has drawn a clearer regulatory line around the use of artificial intelligence in financial services. On 7 October 2026, the regulator published its Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence Risk Management, establishing supervisory expectations for financial institutions using AI, from traditional machine-learning models to Generative AI and increasingly autonomous AI agents. The guidelines follow a public consultation launched in November 2025 and will begin taking effect on 7 October 2027.
AI is increasingly moving beyond chatbots and productivity tools into areas that can influence financial decisions, customer interactions, compliance, risk management and potentially execution itself. MAS specifically warns that AI agents with access to tools could autonomously perform erroneous or unauthorised actions. It also identifies financial, operational, conduct, financial crime and reputational risks arising from AI, alongside security, privacy and third-party risks associated particularly with Generative AI.
- FinancialMarkets.media Strengthens Its AEO Offering as AI Reshapes Financial Search
- What AI Can and Cannot Replace in Trading Technology Development
- Finance Firms Keep 87% of AI Use Cases Internal as EU Rules Take Effect
A Framework Built Around Risk, Not a Ban on AI
The framework is not designed to slow the adoption of AI. Its central idea is proportionality. MAS expects financial institutions to understand where AI is being used, determine how important and risky each application is, and then apply controls that match that risk. A tool used to proofread an internal email clearly does not require the same controls as an AI model influencing investment recommendations or customer risk assessments.
This distinction is important when considering whether the framework is "mandatory". These are guidelines setting out MAS' supervisory expectations, rather than a standalone piece of legislation imposing identical technical requirements on every company. Yet regulated firms should not interpret this as optional guidance. MAS states that all financial institutions should adhere to its high-level expectations when deploying AI, while implementation should be proportionate to their size, activities and AI risk exposure. The guidelines also complement existing MAS requirements and principles, including Fairness, Ethics, Accountability and Transparency, known as FEAT.

| 7 October 2026 | AI guidelines published | 
| 7 October 2027 | AI oversight, risk management and policies | 
| 7 October 2028 | AI lifecycle controls, capabilities and infrastructure | 
This gives firms roughly one year to establish the core governance layer and another year to complete the broader operational framework. MAS has also said that it intends to consult the industry in 2027 on whether further guidance specifically addressing agentic AI would be useful.
Who Needs to Follow the Guidelines?
The scope is broad. MAS says the guidelines apply to all financial institutions and all forms of AI technology. The categories listed by the regulator include banks, fund managers, financial advisers, insurers, payment institutions, exchanges, clearing houses, custodians, credit rating agencies and firms dealing in capital markets products. Exempt futures and OTC derivatives brokers are also explicitly included among the categories covered.

articles.full_text:
(Dan Tri Newspaper) - With his achievements in business management and operations, along with his positive contributions to the community, Mr. Do Vinh Quang - Vice Chairman of the Board of Directors of T&T Group, Chairman of the Board of Directors of T&T Homes - was honored as "Outstanding Vietnamese Entrepreneur - Saint Giong Cup" in 2026.
On the evening of October 11th, at the National Convention Center ( Hanoi ), the Vietnam Chamber of Commerce and Industry (VCCI) held a ceremony to celebrate Vietnamese Entrepreneurs' Day (October 13th) and to honor and award the title of "Outstanding Vietnamese Entrepreneur - Saint Giong Cup" for 2026. Entrepreneur Do Vinh Quang was one of 100 outstanding entrepreneurs honored at the event.
"Outstanding Vietnamese Entrepreneur - Saint Giong Cup" is an award periodically selected by the Vietnam Chamber of Commerce and Industry (VCCI) since 2006, to recognize entrepreneurs with outstanding achievements in production and business; pioneering innovation; fulfilling social responsibility; building corporate culture; complying with the law ; and making positive contributions to the socio-economic development of the country.
According to Mr. Ho Sy Hung, Chairman of VCCI, the evaluation for the 2026 award will not only be based on scale, revenue, or profit, but also consider the business's performance and leadership capacity over the past five years, starting from 2021; its ability to maintain competitiveness, overcome difficulties, and contribute to the country's development.
The group of entrepreneurs selected for recognition in 2026 are leading and managing businesses with total revenue in 2025 of approximately 1.34 trillion VND, pre-tax profit of nearly 248,000 billion VND, tax contributions of approximately 97,000 billion VND, and job creation for approximately 273,000 employees.
Speaking at the event, Politburo member and Standing Deputy Prime Minister Pham Gia Tuc affirmed that the Government acknowledges the efforts and contributions of the business community to socio-economic development, job creation, budget contributions, improving people's lives and Vietnam's position.
The Deputy Prime Minister emphasized that the Party and the State have always considered businesses as the core force of the economy ; strong businesses lead to a strong economy, and thriving businesses lead to a prosperous nation.
Management and operational imprint at a diversified enterprise.
You may also like
Sharing his thoughts on receiving the award, businessman Do Vinh Quang said that the award is a recognition of his and his company's contributions and efforts to the socio-economic development of the country and their social responsibility activities for the community.
"This award is also a great source of motivation for me and the team of young entrepreneurs nationwide to continue to affirm our capabilities, constantly innovate, dare to think and act, actively contribute to the sustainable development of the community, the prosperity of the nation, and elevate Vietnam's position on the international stage," Mr. Do Vinh Quang emphasized.
Mr. Do Vinh Quang currently holds the positions of Vice Chairman of the Board of Directors and Deputy General Director of T&T Group, Chairman of the Board of Directors of T&T Homes, Chairman of the Board of Directors of Vietravel Airlines, Chairman of Hanoi Football Club, and is directly involved in the management and operation of many other member companies within the T&T Group ecosystem.

The group focuses on seven core areas, which are also key sectors of the national economy, including finance and investment; real estate; industry and trade; energy; infrastructure, logistics, and aviation; forestry and high-tech agriculture; healthcare, education, and sports…
During his time managing and operating T&T Group, businessman Do Vinh Quang focused on developing multi-sector management capabilities, connecting investment resources, and expanding strategic partnerships with domestic and international partners. These orientations are clearly demonstrated in the areas he directly oversees, such as finance and investment, aviation, real estate, and sports.

Besides his activities at the company and in the community, the Vice Chairman of T&T Group was trusted and elected as the youngest entrepreneur to be elected as a representative to the Hanoi City People's Council for the 2026-2031 term; he also holds the positions of Vice Chairman of the Hanoi City Small and Medium Enterprises Association, Chairman of the Vietnam Young Entrepreneurs Association Committee (8th term), Vice Chairman of the Global Data Experts Network, and Member of the Executive Committee of the Vietnam Association for the Protection of Children's Rights…
Previously, in 2023, Mr. Do Vinh Quang was honored as an Outstanding Asian Entrepreneur at APEA 2023. He has also received numerous commendations from central and local ministries and agencies for his business activities, sports, and social work.

articles.title: Philippine President Hails Diplomatic Engagement with Myanmar’s Regime - The Irrawaddy
articles.summary: Philippine President Hails Diplomatic Engagement with Myanmar’s Regime  The Irrawaddy
articles.full_text:
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has hailed recent visits by Myanmar coup leader Min Aung Hlaing to fellow ASEAN countries as part of a “new approach” to resolving the country’s crisis.
In an interview with The Straits Times published Saturday, Marcos claimed credit for a recent engagement by various ASEAN governments with the putschist regime of Min Aung Hlaing.
Marcos conceded that ASEAN’s previous insistence on its Five-Point Consensus peace plan for Myanmar and refusal to engage with Myanmar’s regime at the political level were “absolutely correct.” But he added they were “not working.”
“Nothing’s happening, so we had to do something else,” he told the daily.
This prompted the Philippines during its 2026 chairmanship of the bloc to propose a “new approach” at the ASEAN Summit in Cebu in May, he said without going into detail.
He then pointed to coup leader Min Aung Hlaing’s recent visits to Malaysia and Cambodia as signs of progress, describing them as “shoots coming out of the ground” that had “not happened before” and would eventually lead to a “complete resolution.”
“Asked if ASEAN was moving towards recognizing the Myanmar government, Marcos said the grouping has to move towards that if it is going to play a part in resolving the conflict in the country,” the Straits Times wrote.
Since appointing himself president in April and rebranding his regime, Min Aung Hlaing has also visited ASEAN members Thailand, Laos and Vietnam, while reportedly being invited to Indonesia and Brunei.
However, the diplomatic engagement Marcos cited has yet to lead to any reduction in violence on the ground. In some cases, Min Aung Hlaing’s trips coincided with aerial massacres on civilians at home.
In the latest major atrocity, a military airstrike on a crowded market in Rakhine State on Sept. 28 killed at least 50 people, while further air raids in the state targeted locations where displaced people were sheltering. A week later the putschist leader was being welcomed in Kuala Lumpur.
ASEAN’s Five-Point Consensus consist of ending violence, beginning dialogue among all parties, appointing an ASEAN special envoy, and ensuring that humanitarian assistance those in need. It was adopted in April 2021 in response of the military coup. However, the regime led by Min Aung Hlaing has since ignored the framework, and most recently the regime’s new rubber-stamp Parliament rejected it altogether.
The conflict since the 2021 coup has killed an estimated 100,000 people and internally displaced about 3.8 million as of June 2026.
“Shaking hands with war criminals is a threat to humanity,” Thinzar Shunlei Yi, a Myanmar democracy and human rights activist, told The Irrawaddy. “We are watching to see whether the ASEAN leaders will show accountability if their re-engagement with the regime does not work out.”
Some ASEAN members are standing firm. Timor-Leste, the bloc’s newest member, has supported Myanmar’s pro-democracy movement and initiated legal proceedings against the military regime in February over alleged war crimes. And Singapore, which stands to take over the rotating chairmanship at year-end, affirmed this summer that there can be “no political representation” for Myanmar at ASEAN meets.

articles.title: Palace confirms Muhriz will skip Malaysia’s rulers council amid tussle over Negeri Sembilan throne - The Straits Times
articles.summary: Palace confirms Muhriz will skip Malaysia’s rulers council amid tussle over Negeri Sembilan throne  The Straits TimesTuanku Muhriz denies receiving invite to Conference of Rulers meeting, says not attending  MalaysiakiniWho rules Negeri Sembilan? Royal row tests Malaysia’s constitutional order  South China Morning PostBackdating is taboo in law — Hafiz Hassan  Malay MailNegeri Ruler, Tuanku Muhriz, invited to Conference of Rulers meeting tomorrow &nbs...
articles.full_text:
AI generated
KUALA LUMPUR – Negeri Sembilan ruler Muhriz Munawir will skip the Oct 13 to 15 Conference of Rulers, the latest development in an escalating palace feud that has dragged the federal Malaysian government into a brewing constitutional crisis.
“His Royal Highness has elected not to attend the Conference of Rulers and focus on matters in Negeri Sembilan,” the state palace said in a brief statement on Oct 12, referring to the Oct 14 installation of Jelebu’s new territorial chieftain or Undang.
This confirms The Straits Times’ report earlier on Oct 12 that the embattled Negeri Sembilan ruler will not be attending the formal meetings on Oct 14 and 15, and will instead preside over the new Undang’s appointment, according to official sources who spoke on condition of anonymity given the sensitivity around royal affairs.
This would give Yang di-Pertuan Besar, or Yamtuan, Muhriz a clear majority in the state’s Dewan Keadilan dan Undang, the highest authority of the state’s Adat Perpatih, a centuries-old custom governing its feudal hierarchy.
Of the four Undang, empowered under the state’s unique Constitution to elect or depose a ruler found unfit to reign, Jelebu’s chieftain will now be the third seen to be loyal to Muhriz.
The appointment gives him more leverage against a coup led by his cousin, Nadzaruddin Ja’afar, who wants to replace him.
Sources with knowledge of the discussions had told ST that the uncertainty over the rightful ruler of the small central state has split the nine state sovereigns over whether Muhriz should attend the upcoming Conference of Rulers meeting, which will be held at Istana Negara in Kuala Lumpur.
This was the same reason the June enclave was cancelled, given concerns over the validity of deliberations if Muhriz attended.
But with outstanding issues that must be discussed before the end of the year, including constitutional amendments that Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s administration hopes to pass in Parliament, the October edition must go on.
Typically, the nine royal houses are not invited but attend the conference as established members. However, the ruler chairing the conference sends out informal invitations to a pre-council the day before formal proceedings.
The Negeri Sembilan palace statement added that Muhriz “did not receive a formal invitation letter from the conference chairman, His Royal Highness the Sultan of Perak, to attend the pre-council meeting”.
Nadzaruddin – proclaimed by three former and one current Undang as the new Yamtuan – has aligned himself with the rebel chieftains and UMNO, which reclaimed the state from Anwar’s Pakatan Harapan after forcing snap polls held in August.
The bruising crisis has damaged the constitutional monarchy and left Negeri Sembilan without a functioning government since September.
The Undang proclaimed on April 19 that they had removed Muhriz from the throne, but the Constitution explicitly requires an inquiry into the Yamtuan’s alleged transgressions. Such a panel was never convened.
Malaysia’s Attorney-General has repeatedly stated that Muhriz’s claimed dismissal was unconstitutional and affirmed his legitimacy as Negeri Sembilan’s ruler.
Muhriz has taken a public stance against corruption and abuse of power – in particular, over the appointment of judges – that has sparked murmurs among Malaysia’s elite.
These include UMNO leaders who are spearheading the move to pardon former prime minister Najib Razak.
He was due to chair the June conference, when the issue of a renewed pardon bid by former UMNO chief Najib – currently serving a six-year term for graft involving the multi-billion-dollar 1MDB saga – was a key talking point among the rulers, according to sources close to several royal houses.
Najib was granted a conditional house arrest in September by the Federal Territories Pardons Board chaired by Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar of Johor as Malaysia’s King – a role rotated in five-year terms among the nine monarchs.
Muhriz has so far kept silent despite the cloud over his legitimacy. However, the fact that he has presided over the removal of three Undang speaks volumes.
“He may make his feelings clear during the appointment of the Jelebu Undang on Oct 14,” a source close to the Negeri Sembilan palace told ST.
This comes even as Negeri Sembilan UMNO chief Jalaluddin Alias has been forced to deny reports that he plans to oust his party colleague Ismail Lasim as chief minister.
On Sept 17, Ismail claimed that his state Cabinet – formally known as executive councillors or exco – affirmed Muhriz’s removal as Yamtuan based on an April proclamation by the Undang.
This is despite Ismail being sworn in as Menteri Besar before Muhriz, the day after UMNO won the Aug 1 snap polls.
But the state secretary – the top civil servant in the state bureaucracy – has cited the Attorney-General’s legal opinion in refusing to gazette the Ismail administration’s decision to unseat Muhriz.
On Sept 20, Muhriz sacked the exco, and the bureaucracy subsequently barred them from entering the offices of the executive council.
The Menteri Besar has shifted allegiances between the two claimants to the throne, deepening the palace crisis.
He filed two police reports earlier in September, seen by ST, stating that he was forced to sign a proclamation under duress on Aug 3 that Muhriz was no longer Yamtuan and denying that he supported the dethroning of Muhriz.
UMNO’s key role in deepening the palace crisis flies in the face of the party’s stance that politicians should not interfere with royal matters.
It was the principle it invoked when withdrawing support for the previous chief minister Aminuddin Harun, which led to the state assembly being dissolved in June.
UMNO had accused Aminuddin, a vice-president in Anwar’s Parti Keadilan Rakyat, of interfering with Negeri Sembilan’s Adat Perpatih when he refused to sign off on the proclamation by the Undang ousting Muhriz.
The belief in UMNO is that, having criticised Aminuddin for gainsaying the Undang, the public expects the party to put the matter to bed now that it has taken power in Negeri Sembilan.
Party vice-president Johari Ghani was reported as saying UMNO must clear the air on Negeri Sembilan before the campaign for the Nov 14 Melaka state polls.
“We must explain and tell the public that the parties that want to sack Muhriz is not UMNO,” he told reporters on Oct 11.

articles.title: Reasons why floating interest rates have risen to 16-17% per year. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Reasons why floating interest rates have risen to 16-17% per year.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Lending interest rates are under upward pressure as many banks adjust their base interest rates and reference rates applied to floating-rate loans. At some banks, the base interest rate has reached 13.5% per year, significantly increasing borrowing costs after loans expire their preferential period or enter the interest rate adjustment period.
 The base interest rate is as high as 13.5% per year.
 Specifically, from October 1st,ACB adjusted its base interest rate to 9.5% per annum across the entire system. Compared to the 9.2% per annum rate applied by the bank from August 1st, this base interest rate has increased by 0.3 percentage points.
 Previously, from September 18th, VPBank also applied a new base VND interest rate schedule for secured loans of individual customers. The interest rate is divided according to the disbursement time, loan purpose, loan term, and adjustment cycle.
 For real estate, consumer, auto, and business loans disbursed after November 15, 2024, the base interest rate, adjusted monthly, will fluctuate between 11-13% per annum. If adjusted every three months, this base interest rate will increase to 11.8-13.5% per annum.
 Meanwhile, the remaining loan categories have lower base interest rates, ranging from 9.4% per annum for one-month terms, 10.6% per annum for 12-month terms, and 11.4% per annum for loans over 15 years.
 At Techcombank , the base/reference interest rate schedule applied to individual customers borrowing for real estate purchases, secured consumer loans, and car loans was also adjusted last month. The standard base interest rate is 9% per annum, while some products have their own reference rates.
 Specifically, the base interest rate for VinFast car loans is 8.5%/year, for Thaco car loans is 9.5%/year, and for secured business loans for household businesses is 8.8%/year. For unsecured consumer loans adjusted according to the standard base interest rate, such as overdrafts, MyCash/F2, or installment loans, the base interest rate is 13%/year.
 At VietBank, the base VND interest rate is currently 9.7%/year for loans up to 6 months, 10.3%/year for loans up to 12 months, and 10.7%/year for medium and long-term loans over 12 months. The 10.7%/year rate is also used as a benchmark for some loans linked to 13-month VND savings deposit interest rates. 
|  | 
|  Rising base interest rates mean borrowers who reach the floating interest rate phase will face higher costs. Photo: Nam Khanh . | 
 The base/reference interest rate is the benchmark interest rate that banks apply to loans during the floating interest rate period. Accordingly, the actual interest rate will be equal to the base/reference interest rate plus a margin as agreed in the loan contract. Typically, this interest rate spread margin ranges from 3-3.5%.
 For example, if the base interest rate is 9% per year and the margin is 3%, the actual lending interest rate will be 12% per year. Similarly, if the base interest rate is 13.5%, the actual floating interest rate could reach 16.5% per year.
 However, a base interest rate of 13.5% per year at some banks does not mean that all customers will have to pay interest at this rate; it depends on the specific loan product and contract terms.
 Pressure on banks to raise capital.
 Behind the adjustment of the base interest rate is the pressure to balance the capital sources of the banking system. When credit grows faster than deposits, credit institutions must increase their efforts to attract deposits to meet lending needs, while simultaneously ensuring liquidity and a suitable capital structure.
 According to data from the General Statistics Office, as of September 28th, capital mobilization by credit institutions increased by 9.78% compared to the end of 2025, while credit to the economy increased by 10.89%. At the same time last year, these two indicators increased by 9.99% and 13.37% respectively.
 Thus, although credit growth is lower than the same period last year, this indicator is still growing faster than capital mobilization. The growth gap between the two indicators shows that the pressure to supplement capital remains present in the banking system.
 This pressure is even more evident in the deposit market. Currently, savings interest rates for terms of 6 months or more have exceeded 9% per year at many banks; in fact, some deposit products offer interest rates above 10% per year, depending on the deposit amount, the initial deposit amount, or the deposit method. 
| A SERIES OF BANKS OFFER SAVINGS INTEREST RATES OVER 9% PER YEAR FOR DEPOSITORS WHO HAVE DEPOSITED FOR 6 MONTHS OR MORE. | 
| Bank | Request | Interest rate/year | 
| Cake by VPBank | Send online from 500 million VND | 9.6% | 
| Vicki Bank | Send online from 500 million VND | 9.6% | 
| SHB | From 300 million VND or more | 9.1% | 
| HDBank | From 2 billion VND or more | 9.3% | 
| Sacombank | From 500 million VND | 9% | 
| NCB | From 500 million VND to less than 1 billion VND | 9.6% | 
| MBV | No specific deposit amount required. | 9% | 
| GPBank | From 100 million VND or more | 9.1-9.3% | 
| OCB, Bao Viet Bank | From 100 million VND or more | 9% | 
| VPBank | From 300 million VND or more | 9% | 
| Note: The interest rates shown in the table are the maximum rates a depositor can receive when additional incentives are added. | 
 According to experts at Vietcombank Securities Company (VCBS), the gap between credit growth and deposit mobilization is forcing banks to step up efforts to mobilize stable medium-term capital, especially in the 6-13 month maturities.
 As funding costs rise, the ability to maintain low lending interest rates also narrows. Banks must balance the need to compete on deposit interest rates to attract capital with the goal of ensuring business efficiency. This pressure may be reflected in new lending rates or benchmark rates for floating-rate loans, depending on each bank's policy and contract terms.
 Besides the supply and demand for capital, exchange rate movements, inflation, and year-end payment demands also affect the room for maneuver in interest rate management. According to VCBS, increasing exchange rate pressure, inflation close to the target of 4.5%, and high payment demands at the end of the year are factors that limit the room for lowering the policy interest rate.

articles.title: Bac Ninh seeks to develop housing market for foreign residents - Vietnam Economic Times
articles.summary: Bac Ninh seeks to develop housing market for foreign residents  Vietnam Economic Times
articles.full_text:
Bac Ninh needs a more transparent and professional housing market to accommodate its growing international workforce and strengthen its competitiveness in attracting high-quality foreign direct investment (FDI), speakers said at a conference held in the city on October 12.
The conference, “Housing for Foreigners Living and Working in Bac Ninh City,” was organized by Tap chi Kinh te Viet Nam / Vietnam Economic Times / VnEconomy in coordination with the People’s Committee of Bac Ninh City at the Bac Ninh City Convention Center in Bac Giang Ward.
The event brought together local government representatives, real estate associations, foreign investors, FDI enterprises, residential developers, property consultants and legal experts to discuss housing demand among international professionals and ways to improve the local market’s capacity to meet their needs.
Opening the conference, Mr. Pham Van Thinh, Vice Chairman of the People’s Committee of Bac Ninh City, emphasized that housing for foreign nationals should be viewed as part of the infrastructure supporting economic development and investment attraction, rather than simply as a niche segment of the property market.
“A factory may be decided based on investment indicators. But for a specialist to choose to bring their family to live here long-term, they also care about housing, schools, healthcare, transportation, commerce, green spaces, management services, community and the ability to access information transparently and conveniently,” he said.
Growing demand amid industrial expansion
Bac Ninh’s housing requirements have become increasingly important as its industrial parks expand and international investment continues to drive demand for skilled personnel.
According to figures cited by Professor Dr. Hoang Van Cuong, Vice President of the Vietnam Economic Association, 41,416 foreign nationals had registered for temporary residence across the city as of October 1, 2026, representing 63 countries and territories. Approximately 85 per cent had entered Vietnam primarily for work.
Meanwhile, the Bac Ninh Industrial Zones Management Board reported that nearly 25,000 foreign experts, managers, engineers and highly skilled workers were employed in local industrial parks as of the end of September this year.
The two figures cover different populations and should not be combined, Professor Cuong noted. More importantly, the number of foreign residents does not directly translate into demand for homes for purchase.
An engineer assigned to Vietnam for 18 months may prefer a rented apartment, while a manager relocating with a family for several years may prioritize access to schools, healthcare, transportation and other essential services. Only a proportion of international residents will seek to purchase property.
This distinction has important implications for developers and policymakers. Rather than focusing solely on the number of apartments available for sale, Bac Ninh needs a clearer understanding of demand for rental housing, serviced apartments and homes suitable for longer-term family residence.
Under the city’s master zoning plan and industrial park expansion strategy through 2030 and beyond, the city’s international community of specialists and technical personnel is projected to grow by 10 to 15 per cent annually over the next three to five years, supported by industrial park expansion and the local development strategy through 2030 and beyond. The resulting demand could provide a positive impetus for the local real estate market, provided housing products are developed in line with actual requirements.
Housing as a competitive advantage
In his opening remarks, Mr. Thinh linked the housing issue to Bac Ninh’s new administrative status and its ambitions to improve urban quality, governance and the living environment.
Bac Ninh became a centrally governed city following the entry into force of National Assembly Resolution No. 39/2026/QH16 on September 20, 2026. By mid-2026, the city had approximately 3,631 FDI projects with total registered capital exceeding $50.6 billion, the opening remarks noted.
As competition for investment increasingly shifts from attracting capital to attracting higher-quality projects and talent, residential conditions are becoming an important part of the local business environment.
Mr. Thinh argued that the ability to attract and retain highly skilled personnel is itself a component of a locality’s competitiveness. Beyond industrial infrastructure and investment incentives, international specialists need a suitable living environment if they are to work in Bac Ninh over the longer term and bring their families with them.
Although the city has residential projects with integrated amenities that meet the conditions for foreign ownership, it still faces a shortage of systematically planned residential ecosystems capable of meeting the expectations of international executives and specialists.
The challenge is therefore not simply to increase the number of available homes, but to ensure that their locations, quality, management standards and surrounding services match the needs of different groups of foreign residents.
Improving transparency and access to housing
One of the key issues identified during the seminar was the need to make the process of finding and purchasing eligible housing more accessible to foreign nationals.
According to Mr. Thinh, land registration authorities had issued 498 housing ownership certificates to foreign organizations and individuals across the city. He noted that all complete applications eligible for processing at the registration stage had been handled within the stipulated administrative timeframe of eight working days.
The figures suggest that the issuance of housing ownership certificates is not necessarily the principal bottleneck. Instead, difficulties may arise earlier, when prospective buyers try to identify eligible projects, check remaining foreign ownership quotas, understand legal requirements and prepare transaction documents.
Professor Cuong emphasized the importance of distinguishing between properties legally available for foreign ownership, those already purchased and those for which ownership certificates have been issued.
Under the current legal framework, the Law on Housing 2023 regulates the eligibility, forms, limits and duration of foreign ownership. Eligible foreign individuals and organizations may own apartments and certain landed houses in qualifying projects and areas, subject to applicable conditions and quotas. Foreign ownership in an apartment building is generally capped at 30 per cent of its total units.
Decree No. 95/2024/ND-CP also requires relevant information on eligible properties and ownership quotas to be made public. However, publishing project lists alone may not provide prospective buyers with all the information they need to make informed decisions.
To address this gap, Professor Cuong proposed developing an accessible online housing information platform, initially through a Vietnamese-English page on an existing government website rather than a costly standalone system.
The platform could provide standardized information on eligible residential projects, available units, remaining ownership quotas, transaction conditions, required documentation and relevant contact points. Information would need to be regularly updated, with clearly assigned responsibilities for verification.
A multilingual housing portal could also help foreign residents compare rental and purchase options while enabling FDI enterprises to identify suitable accommodation for incoming employees.
Five priorities for a more responsive market
Professor Cuong outlined five areas for further action to help Bac Ninh build a housing market aligned with its economic development objectives.
First, quantify actual housing demand. The city should conduct annual surveys of FDI enterprises to identify the residential requirements of foreign employees, distinguishing between short-term assignments, long-term employment and families relocating with children. Information on preferred locations, rental or purchase needs, budgets and service expectations would provide a stronger basis for planning and investment. Such assessments should draw on aggregated data from industrial park authorities, residence management agencies and housing departments while protecting personal information.
Second, develop a professional rental market. Given that many foreign specialists work in Vietnam on fixed-term assignments, demand for rental housing may be more frequent than demand for homeownership. The city could pilot serviced apartments and professionally managed long-term rental housing near industrial parks with high concentrations of international personnel. These developments should offer convenient transport connections, reliable property management and multilingual support. FDI enterprises could contribute demand forecasts or enter into group rental agreements, while public authorities focus on planning, transportation and social infrastructure.
Third, turn public information into practical market data. Beyond publishing lists of eligible projects, authorities should provide information that prospective residents can use directly when evaluating properties and preparing transactions. Accurate data, clear update schedules and designated agencies responsible for verification would help reduce uncertainty for buyers, developers and property intermediaries.
Fourth, standardize the transaction process. Foreign buyers need clear, multilingual guidance covering eligibility checks, deposits, payments, contract signing, handover, ownership registration and subsequent property rights. A standardized legal information sheet supplied by developers before transactions could identify official information sources, applicable conditions and the date on which the details were verified.
Fifth, address regulatory issues with specific evidence.

articles.title: Foreign securities firms lag behind in the race to expand capital in Vietnam - Theinvestor
articles.summary: Foreign securities firms lag behind in the race to expand capital in Vietnam  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
While many domestic securities firms have been steadily increasing their charter capital, foreign-owned brokerages have been slower to expand in recent years, raising questions about their ability to maintain a competitive edge as Vietnam’s financial market continues to grow.
Domestic securities firms step up capital expansion
Techcom Securities Joint Stock Company (TCBS, HoSE: TCX) has completed the issuance of nearly 555 million shares to pay its 2025 dividend. The move increased its charter capital from over VND27.74 trillion to more than VND33.29 trillion ($1.28 billion), making it the securities firm with the largest charter capital in Vietnam.
Over roughly five years, the securities firm within the Techcombank ecosystem has increased its charter capital from VND1.12 trillion ($43.22 million) to VND33.29 trillion, nearly 30-fold.
Similarly, SSI Securities (HoSE: SSI) has completed a capital increase from approximately VND25.03 trillion to VND30.03 trillion ($1.16 billion) through a bonus share issue funded by equity.
One of the earliest securities firms established in the market, SSI began operations in 1999 with initial charter capital of VND6 billion ($231,520). Its capital base has expanded rapidly in recent years, rising from approximately VND6.03 trillion in 2020 to more than VND30 trillion ($1.16 billion) currently, nearly fivefold.
The past six years have also marked a period of substantial capital expansion for Ho Chi Minh City Securities Corporation (HoSE: HCM). Its charter capital has increased from just over VND3 trillion to VND13.73 trillion ($529.8 million). The company is implementing a plan to offer an additional 200 million shares to nine professional securities investors, which is expected to raise its charter capital to VND15.73 trillion.
Vietcap Securities (HoSE: VCI) has also expanded its capital base from VND1.64 trillion to VND11.52 trillion ($444.5 million), approximately sevenfold. Meanwhile, VIX Securities (HoSE: VIX) has charter capital of VND25.73 trillion ($992.82 million), around 4.4 times its level at the end of 2022. VPS Securities (HoSE: VCK) has approximately VND24.35 trillion ($939.59 million), more than four times the VND5.7 trillion it maintained from the end of 2021 before embarking on major capital increases from late 2025.
Among securities firms backed by banks, ACB Securities (ACBS) has also received additional resources from its parent, Asia Commercial Bank (ACB), increasing its charter capital from VND1.5 trillion to VND13 trillion ($501.72 million) over the 2021-2026 period. In May 2026, Vietcombank Securities (VCBS) raised its charter capital to VND8.5 trillion ($328.05 million), 3.4 times its previous level of VND2.5 trillion, with additional support from its parent, Vietcombank.
These developments show that the capital race among domestic securities firms is being driven not only by independent businesses but also by banking groups. A larger financial base enables firms to expand margin lending, invest in technology, develop products and attract customers.
Foreign brokers slow pace of capital increases
Between 2016 and 2021, several South Korean-backed securities firms, including Mirae Asset and KIS Vietnam, significantly increased their capital. Since 2021, however, the pace of expansion at some foreign-owned firms has slowed considerably.
Mirae Asset Vietnam Securities (MAS) stood out in the capital race after receiving several capital injections between 2016 and 2021. Its charter capital reached VND6.59 trillion ($254.4 million) at the end of 2021 and has remained at that level since.
At KIS Vietnam Securities, charter capital rose from approximately VND1.11 trillion to VND3.76 trillion ($145.11 million) between 2015 and 2021. The company did not undertake another capital increase until early 2026, when its charter capital reached VND4.55 trillion ($175.6 million). Similarly, KB Vietnam Securities (KBSV) has maintained charter capital of around VND3.03 trillion ($116.94 million) since the end of 2021.
Among Taiwan-backed securities firms, Yuanta Vietnam Securities increased its charter capital from VND300 billion ($11.58 million) to VND2.5 trillion ($96.48 million) between 2018 and 2023. The company has continued to signal its intention to raise capital to strengthen its competitiveness, but since 2023 it has not publicly announced the scale or timing of another capital increase.
Meanwhile, Maybank Securities Vietnam (MSVN), a member of Malaysia’s Maybank Investment Banking Group, maintained charter capital of VND2.2 trillion ($84.9 million) from 2022. In June 2026, it completed a capital increase of VND1.3 trillion ($50.17 million), bringing its charter capital to VND3.5 trillion ($135.08 million), an increase of nearly 59%.
Overall, capital growth among foreign securities firms has varied. Some have injected additional capital in recent years, but the scale and frequency of their increases have generally failed to keep pace with the expansion seen at many domestic brokers.
Competitive pressures intensify
Vietnam’s stock market continues to expand in terms of market capitalization, liquidity and the number of investors. Demand for margin lending, trading technology, investment products and customer services is also rising, placing greater demands on securities firms’ financial capacity.
Capital size and the ability to mobilize resources can affect a firm’s capacity to expand margin lending, invest in technology and broaden its customer base. As domestic firms continue to increase their capital, foreign-owned brokers that expand more slowly could face mounting competitive pressure unless they also improve operational efficiency and service quality.
Another notable development is the divergence between domestic capital flows and foreign investor trading. Between 2023 and 2025, foreign investors recorded cumulative net sales of approximately VND250 trillion ($9.65 billion) in Vietnam’s stock market. In the first nine months of 2026, net selling continued at around VND100 trillion ($3.86 billion), even as FTSE Russell upgraded Vietnam from a frontier market to a secondary emerging market, effective September 21, 2026.
Foreign securities firms have distinct advantages, including international institutional client networks and connections with overseas investors. However, these strengths do not necessarily translate into large domestic brokerage market shares when foreign capital is flowing out of the market. By contrast, many domestic firms benefit from established local customer bases, access to retail investors, and support from their parent banking groups.
Data on stock brokerage market shares on the Ho Chi Minh Stock Exchange (HoSE) show that leading firms include several with large charter capital bases, such as SSI, TCBS and VPS. Notably, TCBS increased its market share from around 4.6% in 2021 to 10.03% in the third quarter of 2026, crossing the 10% threshold for the first time.
Among foreign-owned brokers, Mirae Asset is a notable case, with its brokerage market share declining substantially from previous levels. On the HoSE, the company ranked fourth in the third quarter of 2022, with a 5.85% share of stock brokerage transactions. By the third quarter of 2026, its share had fallen to 3.03%, placing it ninth. On the Hanoi Stock Exchange (HNX), the company ranked seventh in 2022 with a 3.16% market share but no longer featured in the top 10 for listed-stock brokerage in the third quarter of 2026.
KIS Vietnam is the second foreign-owned firm represented in the HoSE’s top 10 brokerage rankings. Its market share declined in 2024 but recovered in 2026. In the third quarter of 2026 alone, KIS recorded a market share of 3.72%, up 0.73 percentage points from the previous quarter and above Mirae Asset’s 3.03% in the same period.
These developments indicate that brokerage market shares are shifting among firms, with some well-capitalized domestic securities companies expanding their positions. Charter capital is not the only factor determining market share, but it plays an important role in creating room to expand margin lending, invest in technology, and compete through fees, interest rates and customer incentives.
When capital growth fails to keep pace with business expansion needs, securities firms may have to rely more heavily on borrowed funds to finance their operations. However, as borrowing costs are no longer as low as they once were, funding expenses may rise, narrowing the scope for competition on margin lending rates and fee incentives designed to attract customers.

articles.title: Vietnam Removed from EU Tax Blacklist: Implications for Businesses - Vietnam Briefing
articles.summary: Vietnam Removed from EU Tax Blacklist: Implications for Businesses  Vietnam Briefing
articles.full_text:
Vietnam EU tax blacklist developments took a significant turn on October 9, 2026, when the Council of the European Union removed Vietnam from its list of non-cooperative jurisdictions for tax purposes. While the move is likely to improve investor confidence and reduce some tax-related concerns for cross-border transactions, Vietnam remains under monitoring through its placement in Annex II.
Key development
On 9 October 2026, the Council of the European Union (EU) decided to remove Vietnam from the EU list of non-cooperative jurisdictions for tax purposes, commonly referred to as the EU tax blacklist. Vietnam had been added to the list in February 2026 following an assessment by the OECD Global Forum that identified shortcomings in Vietnam’s framework for the exchange of tax information upon request.
The removal reflects Vietnam’s subsequent reform efforts. However, Vietnam has been moved to Annex II, which covers jurisdictions that have made commitments to implement international tax governance standards but remain subject to monitoring. Vietnam is awaiting an in-depth review by the OECD Global Forum of its exchange-of-information framework.
Review EU Tax Exposure
Assess whether existing withholding tax, reporting, or compliance requirements still apply to your business.
What does this mean?
1. Improved international tax standing
Removal from Annex I represents progress in Vietnam’s cooperation with the EU on tax transparency and international tax governance. It may also support investor confidence and Vietnam’s efforts to attract foreign investment, particularly from European businesses.
2. Potential implications for cross-border transactions
The EU blacklist can influence the tax treatment of transactions involving listed jurisdictions, including certain defensive tax measures adopted by individual EU Member States. Vietnam’s removal from Annex I may therefore reduce concerns associated specifically with its former listing.
However, the actual impact will depend on the domestic tax rules of the relevant EU Member State, the nature of the transaction and the applicable effective dates. Businesses should not assume that all additional tax requirements or restrictions will automatically cease following the announcement.
3. Continued focus on tax transparency and BEPS compliance
Vietnam remains under monitoring in Annex II. The EU has also noted Vietnam’s commitment to address recommendations concerning parts B(1) and B(2) of the OECD’s Country-by-Country Reporting (CbCR) terms of reference, with a view to reflecting progress in the Action 13 peer review report in autumn 2027.
Strengthen Tax Compliance
Review your transfer pricing, CbCR, and reporting processes to stay ahead of regulatory changes.
Recommended actions for businesses
Companies with Vietnam–EU cross-border operations should consider the following:
- Review EU tax exposure: Check whether the previous listing affected withholding tax, deductibility, reporting obligations or other defensive measures under the relevant EU Member State’s domestic legislation.
- Reassess transaction documentation: Review cross-border payments, related-party arrangements and supporting tax documentation where the former listing was identified as a compliance risk.
- Monitor further developments: Track the outcome of Vietnam’s OECD Global Forum review and future updates to the EU list.
- Maintain robust tax compliance: Continue to meet applicable transfer pricing, CbCR, tax reporting and information-disclosure requirements. Removal from the EU blacklist does not exempt businesses from these obligations.
Our perspective
Vietnam’s removal from the EU tax blacklist reflects the country’s continued efforts to strengthen its tax transparency framework, improve its regulatory environment and align with international tax governance standards. This development also demonstrates Vietnam’s commitment to constructive cooperation with the EU and the international community in addressing tax transparency concerns and promoting a fairer, more transparent global tax environment.
While this marks an important step forward, Vietnam remains subject to further monitoring and review. Businesses engaged in Vietnam–EU transactions should continue to monitor regulatory developments and assess the implications for their cross-border operations, taking into account the applicable tax rules in the relevant EU Member States.

articles.title: Mainstay of national economic development - Vietnam Economic Times
articles.summary: Mainstay of national economic development  Vietnam Economic Times
articles.full_text:
Over the more than four decades of the “Doi Moi” (Economic Renewal) process, Vietnam’s shift from a centrally-planned, subsidized economy to a market-based system has transformed State-owned enterprises (SOEs). While their numbers have declined, their scale and efficiency have continued to improve. Beyond the pursuit of profit, SOEs have retained an irreplaceable role in carrying out critical economic and social missions and in serving as a firm backbone for the broader economy.
According to data from the National Statistics Office at the Ministry of Finance, in the 1975-1985 period, prior to Doi Moi, Vietnam had more than 10,000 State-owned economic entities operating in most economic sectors. As Vietnam entered the Doi Moi era and began reducing subsidies and restructuring its State apparatus, the number of SOEs fell sharply, from 3,020 in 1989 to 2,170 in 1994. Yet through proactive innovation and comprehensive restructuring, the State-owned sector quickly adapted and regained strong growth momentum.
At constant 2010 prices, the value-added generated by the State-owned sector stood at just VND174.33 trillion ($6.7 billion) in 1986. By 2025, it was estimated to have reached VND1,353.15 trillion ($52.04 billion), or 8.72-times the 1986 level and representing average annual growth of 5.71 per cent during the 1987-2025 period.
Laying the foundations
Though the State-owned sector’s share of GDP declined from 36.58 per cent in 1986 to an estimated 20.89 per cent in 2025, reflecting the rapid expansion of the private and foreign-invested sectors, its absolute scale has continued to grow. The sector has also become increasingly concentrated in backbone industries that remain critical to Vietnam’s economy.
SOEs are no longer spread across small-scale services or wholesale and retail trade as they once were. Rather, they are increasingly focused on opening up new areas of development, shouldering infrastructure investment, and creating the conditions for other economic sectors to grow. The resilience of SOEs in strategic industries has been a key factor in helping Vietnam’s economy maintain stability amid geopolitical shifts and global economic crises.
In energy security, leading State-owned groups such as Vietnam Electricity (EVN), the Vietnam Oil and Gas Group (PetroVietnam), and the Vietnam National Coal and Mineral Industries Holding Corporation Limited (TKV) ensure the stable and continuous supply of energy and fuel for the production and business activities of millions of enterprises as well as for household consumption.
Regarding connectivity infrastructure and telecommunications, the Vietnam Posts and Telecommunications Group (VNPT) and the Viettel Group have played leading roles in developing nationwide telecommunications networks. They have also served as pioneers in the country’s digital transformation and e-government development. The information and communications sector has steadily increased its contribution to GDP from 1.22 per cent to 3.26-4.39 per cent in recent years.
In banking and finance, State-owned commercial banks (SOCBs) such as Agribank, Vietcombank, VietinBank, and BIDV play a leading role in supplying capital to the economy. They have helped raise the contribution of financial, banking, and insurance activities from 1.22 per cent of GDP in 1986 to an estimated 4.8 per cent in 2025. SOCBs not only effectively implement preferential credit policies but also serve as instruments for interest rate management and maintaining stability across the national financial and monetary system.
Importantly, SOEs do more than pursue profits: they also serve as effective instruments of macro-economic regulation. During periods of volatility in global energy and raw material prices, SOEs have taken the lead in stabilizing prices of essential goods and limiting the adverse effects of inflation.
At the same time, they have pioneered the provision of public services, extending electricity and telecommunications networks, and building roads in remote, mountainous, border, and island areas - locations where costs are high and profitability is limited, making them difficult for private businesses to reach. These efforts also contribute to national security and poverty reduction.
By maintaining a dominant position in these key sectors, SOEs provide essential technical infrastructure and services, helping reduce input costs for other economic sectors and creating favorable conditions for private and foreign-invested businesses to grow.
Strategic priorities
In terms of resource efficiency, though SOEs account for only a small share of the total number of operating businesses, they control substantial assets and capital and make significant contributions to the national budget.
Every year, State-owned groups and corporations contribute hundreds of trillions of VND to the State budget through taxes, fees, and after-tax profits. These revenues provide strategic financial resources for the government to invest in transport infrastructure and expand public services, including education and training, which accounted for about 3.88 per cent of GDP in 2025, and healthcare and social assistance, which accounted for some 2.95 per cent. The SOE sector also provides stable employment and implements comprehensive welfare and occupational safety policies for millions of employees.
In the era of Industry 4.0, SOEs are also transforming into drivers of technology and innovation. Major groups such as Viettel, VNPT, and PetroVietnam have stepped up investment in R&D, taken greater control of advanced technologies, produced telecommunications equipment and management software, developed renewable energy and green solutions, and expanded their investments into international markets.
However, viewed objectively, the State-owned sector continues to face significant barriers and challenges. The equitization and restructuring of SOEs remain slow, reaching only about 16 per cent of the target during 2021-2025. Divestment from non-core investments has also progressed slowly at some enterprises, while the use of capital and land resources in some areas has yet to match their potential. In several fields, the sector’s role in opening up new areas of development, providing leadership, and creating spillover effects for other economic sectors has also fallen short of expectations.
To address these bottlenecks and create new growth momentum, Politburo Resolution No. 79-NQ/TW, issued on January 6, 2026, on developing the State-owned economic sector, sets out core objectives and a clear development roadmap.
First, reforming governance models and improving operational efficiency. By 2030, all State-owned groups and corporations are expected to complete the adoption of modern governance models based on international standards, including Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) standards, while fundamentally resolving weak and persistently loss-making projects.
Second, concentrating resources on strategic industries. Restructuring is to focus State capital rather than spread it thinly, directing resources toward strategic infrastructure, new energy, high technology, semiconductors, digital transformation, and foundational industries where the private sector does not yet have sufficient capacity to invest.
Third, strengthening the sector’s role in opening up new areas and providing leadership. The goal is to develop large-scale State-owned economic groups with strong financial capacity and international competitiveness, serving as leaders that connect, support, and encourage domestic private enterprises to participate more deeply in global value chains.
Fourth, improving the institutional framework for managing State capital. Management processes will be restructured to clearly separate the State’s ownership - representation function from government management and corporate governance, while granting enterprises maximum autonomy alongside open and transparent inspection and oversight mechanisms.

articles.title: The bank has allocated over 400 trillion VND in preferential loans to small and medium-sized enterprises. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: The bank has allocated over 400 trillion VND in preferential loans to small and medium-sized enterprises.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
(Dan Tri Newspaper) - The banking sector is implementing a credit package of over 400,000 billion VND for small and medium-sized enterprises, with interest rates 1-2 percentage points lower, accompanied by requirements for financial transparency.
This information was shared by Mr. Nguyen Duc Lenh, Deputy Director of the State Bank of Vietnam, Region 2 branch, at the seminar "Capital Paves the Way - Businesses Accelerate" organized by Dan Tri newspaper on October 12th, in response to Vietnamese Entrepreneurs' Day on October 13th.
Mr. Leinh stated that in the first nine months of the year, the total outstanding credit balance in Ho Chi Minh City was estimated at approximately 5.8 million billion VND, an increase of 11.4% compared to the end of last year. This is a positive sign as credit capital continues to focus on production, business, and sectors that are the driving force of economic growth.
Khám phá thêm
Tìm hiểu lịch sử
Đọc Mẹo Du Lịch
Khám phá ĐNA
Credit capital is concentrated in sectors that account for a large proportion and contribute to Ho Chi Minh City's GRDP. In particular, the processing and manufacturing industries recorded good growth rates; outstanding loans in the logistics, construction, real estate, wholesale and retail sectors also showed positive results.
According to Mr. Leinh, to alleviate capital difficulties for businesses, the banking sector is implementing three key groups of solutions.
First, the banking sector continues to maintain stable interest rates and support businesses through preferential credit packages. In particular, the credit package for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) has a scale of over 400,000 billion VND, with lending interest rates approximately 1-2 percentage points lower than the average lending interest rates of credit institutions.
The banking sector also continued to disburse credit packages for the forestry and fisheries sectors, with outstanding loans reaching VND 154,000 billion, supporting interest rate reductions of 1.5-2 percentage points for businesses. Banks prioritized interest rates for five industry groups: exports, small and medium-sized enterprises, supporting industries, high-tech enterprises, and agriculture and rural areas.
To effectively access these policies, Mr. Leinh suggested that businesses need to be transparent in their finances, improve their management capabilities, and prepare complete documentation, thereby ensuring that the funds are used effectively and targeted at the right recipients.
You may also like
The second solution is to further strengthen the connection between banks and businesses. The banking sector in Ho Chi Minh City will receive information about specific cases facing difficulties in accessing capital, connect them with lending banks, and directly resolve these issues.
"Credit activities are conditional activities, so lending must comply with regulations. Any obstacles related to administrative procedures and specific cases will be received and processed through the channels of the State Bank of Vietnam," Mr. Leinh said.
Associations and businesses can submit feedback in writing or provide information via email at tonghop@sbv.gov.vn and hotline 028.8211230. If difficulties in accessing capital stem from administrative procedures, the State Bank of Vietnam will provide support and resolve them.
The third solution is to continue strengthening policy communication, helping businesses understand credit programs and conditions for accessing capital.
Focus on disbursing funds in the final months of the year.
According to Mr. Leinh, in the last months of the year, the demand for capital to serve production, business, trade, and services is expected to increase. Therefore, the banking sector in Ho Chi Minh City will focus on three core tasks.
Firstly, we will continue to maintain stable interest rates and the monetary market to support economic growth, while also creating favorable mechanisms, policies, and administrative reforms for production and business activities. The banking sector in Ho Chi Minh City will strengthen management and guidance for credit institutions to improve operational efficiency, labor productivity, and reduce costs to contribute to maintaining stability and reducing lending interest rates for businesses.
You may also like
Secondly, we will accelerate the disbursement of preferential credit packages, including those for small and medium-sized enterprises with interest rate reductions of 1-2 percentage points. Loan programs for forestry products, fisheries, social housing, and the application of science and technology will also continue to be implemented.
For the bank-business connection program, the total registered amount since the beginning of the year is 591,000 billion VND. To date, banks have disbursed 416,000 billion VND to 218,000 customers.
Thirdly, effectively implement credit programs, including the market stabilization loan program. Towards the end of the year, the demand for consumer goods and essential items for holidays and Tet (Lunar New Year) increases significantly. The banking sector, in coordination with the Ho Chi Minh City Department of Industry and Trade, is implementing a market stabilization loan program to support the entire supply chain from production to distribution, contributing to ensuring the supply of essential goods, stabilizing prices, and directly supporting manufacturing businesses.
“All the mechanisms and policies of the Government , the Central Bank, and the Ho Chi Minh City People's Committee aim to create a favorable investment and business environment for enterprises to develop. However, enterprises must also proactively and flexibly respond and effectively utilize borrowed capital,” Mr. Leinh shared.
On the occasion of Vietnamese Entrepreneurs' Day on October 13th, Mr. Leinh stated that the banking sector always stands alongside businesses, aiming to support their sustainable development.

articles.title: Foxconn's northern Vietnam subsidiary more than doubles registered capital to $710 mln - Theinvestor
articles.summary: Foxconn's northern Vietnam subsidiary more than doubles registered capital to $710 mln  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
Fukang Technology, a Vietnam-based subsidiary of Foxconn, has more than doubled its registered capital to nearly $710.4 million, reflecting the Taiwanese electronics giant’s continued investment in its local operations.
According to a business registration update issued late last month, Fukang Technology increased its registered capital from VND8.35 trillion to nearly VND17.47 trillion, or $710.4 million, up over 109%, according to its business registration records.
The company’s new capital base is classified as foreign capital, with contributions made in freely convertible foreign currencies, the registration update shows.
Established on January 20, 2021, Fukang Technology is based at Lot I in Quang Chau Industrial Park, Nen ward, Bac Ninh city, northern Vietnam. Yao Chang-Hao serves as the company’s legal representative, chairman of its members’ council, and general director.
The registration update also revised the amounts of capital represented by three authorized individuals. Yao represents nearly VND13.97 trillion, equivalent to 80% of the registered capital, while Huang Yu-Ching and Huang Shih-I each represent approximately VND1.75 trillion, or 10%.
Fukang Technology is wholly owned by Foxconn Singapore Pte. Ltd., placing it within the corporate structure of Hon Hai Precision Industry, the Taiwanese group’s legal name. Hon Hai confirmed the ownership relationship in a disclosure dated August 18, 2026. Fukang Technology manufactures electronic products including tablets, laptops, smart speakers, and motherboards.
According to the disclosure, Foxconn Singapore invested a total of $358.4 million in additional capital in Fukang Technology between October 14, 2025 and August 18, 2026. Following the transaction, Foxconn Singapore’s cumulative investment in the subsidiary reached $710.4 million, while its ownership remained at 100%.
Hon Hai said the transaction was intended as a long-term investment through a capital increase at its subsidiary.
According to the provincial statistics office, in the first nine months of 2026, Bac Ninh city recorded 264 newly registered foreign-invested projects totalling $1.67 billion and 219 foreign-invested projects having their capital expanded totalling $2.3 billion.

articles.title: What Thailand stands to gain from hosting IMF–World Bank meetings - Thai PBS World
articles.summary: What Thailand stands to gain from hosting IMF–World Bank meetings  Thai PBS World
articles.full_text:
Amid uncertainty in the global economy, Thailand finds itself interestingly placed to share its views and experiences with finance authorities from around the world.
Thailand hosts the 2026 IMF–World Bank Group Annual Meetings from October 12–18 at the Queen Sirikit National Convention Center in Bangkok.
“Finance ministers and central bank governors of the IMF’s 191 member countries will come together to assess the direction of the world economy at a time of high uncertainty and rapid change. It is vital that they do, and Thailand is just the right host to have—another open and dynamic country at the heart of a vibrant region,” Kristalina Georgieva, managing director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), said recently in Singapore on her way to Bangkok.
“Since Thailand last hosted our annual meetings 35 years ago, in 1991, Asia-Pacific’s share of global GDP has gone up from 25 per cent to 43 per cent.”
For a change, Thailand will be in the global headlines for the right reasons after weeks of negative images of Bangkok being swamped by unprecedented flooding. The capital is just recovering after being brought to a standstill for nearly a week late last month. Several provinces were still under water as of October 9, damaging farms, industry, tourism, and logistics and retail trade.
The flood catastrophe was a bolt from the blue when the country already faced numerous other long-term economic challenges. The government has come under sharp criticism from local people and experts for lack of flood disaster preparedness, and they are hoping that weather conditions will not disrupt the important seven-day meeting.
“In addition to policy makers from around the world attending the IMF-World Bank annual meeting, global business leaders will also be coming to attend side events. This opens opportunities to gain economic benefit and build business connections,” says Pipat Luengnaruemitchai, managing director and chief economist at Kiatnakin Phatra Financial Group.
Pipat revealed that he himself had scheduled several meetings with people from global businesses.
Since the host country is allowed to set some of the agenda, Thailand has proposed the theme: “New Horizons: Empowering People and Building Resilience”.
“If there is a Bangkok initiative or consensus that comes out of the event, it would be beneficial for Thailand and other countries,” says Pipat.
When Thailand hosted the IMF-World Bank meeting 35 years ago, the country was considered one of Asia’s high-growth tiger economies. But times have changed and a decade of sluggish economic growth, eroding competitiveness, an aging society and high corruption have earned it the label of the “Sick Man of Asia” from some international media and critics.
“This time the Thai economy has to be mature and adopt artificial intelligence [AI] technology to improve productivity and overcome the challenge of an aging society,” says Pipat.
On the positive side, Thailand’s stock market has recently recovered from a severe downturn. The global AI rush has contributed to rising exports of electronics goods related to AI. The country has also drawn in investments in data centers and some higher-value industries.
Thailand and the World Bank have long collaborated in a bid to drive the country toward a high-income economy by promoting high-value and new industries and building human capital and workforce capacity. A relatively small and open economy, Thailand, apart from facing local challenges, also faces uncertainty from external factors.
Key takeaways from IMF chief’s statement
In her curtain-raiser statement in Singapore prior to the Bangkok meetings, Kristalina outlined a stern assessment of the global economy pulled in opposite directions: a positive demand shock from AI and negative supply shocks from energy prices and geopolitical conflicts.
While global growth remains steady overall, regional hits stem from ongoing wars—including the war in Ukraine in its fifth year and conflict in the Gulf in its eighth month—and severe El Niño weather impacts.
Georgieva emphasized three primary global crosscurrents:
1. AI boom and disruption: AI investment is surging, with hardware and tech products now exceeding 10 per cent of global goods trade. Top Asian exporters (of microprocessors, memory chips, robotics) benefit immensely alongside net hardware importers like the US, China and India.
However, non-participating economies risk falling into wider global inequality. IMF research indicates that AI adoption could add up to 0.5 percentage points annually to world GDP growth over time, but requires strong AI preparedness, digital infrastructure, labor safeguards, and strict governance to mitigate job market fallout and cyber risks.
2. High energy prices and inflation: Geopolitical tensions near the Strait of Hormuz keeps crude oil hovering around 100 dollars per barrel, compounded by another $100 per barrel crack spread due to limited global refining capacity. High energy, fertilizer, and food costs push inflation up while benchmark sovereign yields (US, Germany, Japan) hit multi-decade highs. Georgieva cautioned central banks to maintain a prudently hawkish monetary policy stance to keep inflation expectations firmly anchored.
3. Record public debt and fiscal deficits: Global public debt approaches post-WWII highs and is on track to surpass 100 per cent of GDP. Advanced economies face heavy gross debt loads, while emerging and low-income markets struggle with elevated funding costs and volatile capital flows. Georgieva urged policymakers to execute credible medium-term fiscal consolidation plans, protect vulnerable populations, slash red tape, and pursue structural reforms to unlock long-term productivity.
Strategic benefits and vision
Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas emphasized that hosting over 15,000 international delegates for the 2026 Annual Meetings serves as a pivotal opportunity to position Thailand as a key regional financial leader and a neutral, trusted “global connector”.
The Thai government envisions four core outcomes from hosting the gathering:
1. Attracting high-quality investment and infrastructure capital: Thailand aims to leverage the global stage to showcase its stability amid a fragmented world economy. The summit will act as a gateway to secure international foreign direct investment, technical expertise, and long-term financing for vital infrastructure—specifically clean energy, data centers, advanced manufacturing, and water resource management.
2. SME integration and market expansion: High-level interactions with world corporate executives and financial organizations directly connect Thai small-and-medium enterprises to global value chains while opening new export destinations for local industries.
3. Showcasing national potential and sustainable models: Thailand is highlighting its physical infrastructure, digital readiness, public health, tourism, and soft power (such as Thai identity and cuisine). Through displays like the Royal Pavilion exhibition, the country is presenting its sustainable development practices, the Sufficiency Economy Philosophy, and royal water retention frameworks (such as the Kaem Ling or “monkey cheek” approach) to demonstrate climate resilience.
4. Re-establishing global economic leadership: Thailand intends to leave a lasting footprint on global economic policy by proposing host initiatives like the “Bangkok Blueprint”, “Bangkok Dialogue”, and “Bangkok Declaration”. These frameworks aim to guide international consensus on digital finance, climate adaptation, and sustainable growth long after the meetings conclude, restoring Thailand’s standing as a central leader in global financial cooperation.
Opposition MP plays down hype
Anusorn Tamajai, a member of Parliament of the opposition People’s Party, says that hosting the meetings may boost investor confidence in financial markets to some extent, but not significantly, unless capital market governance is urgently established and the issue of the Thai financial sector being used for money laundering is addressed.
He estimates the meeting would generate spending no more than 8 billion baht in the economy, directly benefiting hotels, restaurants, and tourism.
“While holding the summit serves as a useful platform for Thailand’s international image, it is not a decisive factor in elevating Thailand into a regional financial hub. For Thailand to become a financial hub, major economic and financial sector reforms are required, driven by clear, committed political goals and strategies,” he adds.
By Thai PBS World’s Business Desk

articles.title: The Chairman of the Board of Directors and General Director of Geleximco was honored as an Outstanding Vietnamese Entrepreneur - Saint Giong Cup 2026. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: The Chairman of the Board of Directors and General Director of Geleximco was honored as an Outstanding Vietnamese Entrepreneur - Saint Giong Cup 2026.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
The ceremony to honor and award the title of Outstanding Vietnamese Entrepreneur - Saint Giong Cup 2026, organized by the Vietnam Chamber of Commerce and Industry (VCCI), was held on the evening of October 11th in Hanoi , on the occasion of the Vietnamese Entrepreneurs' Day on October 13th.
The Chairman of the Board of Directors and General Director of Geleximco was honored as an Outstanding Vietnamese Entrepreneur - Saint Giong Cup 2026.
The title of Outstanding Vietnamese Entrepreneur - Saint Giong Cup 2026 is not only a recognition of the contributions of the Chairman of the Board of Directors and General Director of Geleximco Group, Vu Van Hau, in the journey of building and developing Geleximco, but also a testament to the spirit of innovation, creativity, and responsibility for the common prosperity of the country.
Initiated by VCCI in 2006, the Saint Giong Cup enters its 10th selection round in 2026. This year, the program will select 100 outstanding entrepreneurs from over 260 applications submitted by ministries, departments, localities, and business associations.
At the ceremony, VCCI Chairman Ho Sy Hung stated that the evaluation process was based not only on scale, revenue, or profit, but also on considering the business's performance and leadership capabilities over the past five years, starting from 2021; its ability to maintain competitiveness, overcome difficulties, and contribute to the country's development.
Speaking at the awards ceremony, Deputy Prime Minister Pham Gia Tuc emphasized the need for a change in management thinking towards a constructive, service-oriented approach, with people and businesses at the center. The Deputy Prime Minister also expressed his hope that the business community would continue to demonstrate resilience, self-reliance, innovation, and responsibility towards the country, contributing to the realization of development goals in the 2026-2030 period.
The awarding of the "Outstanding Vietnamese Entrepreneur - Saint Giong Cup 2026" to Mr. Vu Van Hau is a significant milestone for him personally and for Geleximco Group. Established in 1993, after more than three decades of development, Geleximco has become one of the leading multi-sector private economic groups in Vietnam. Under the leadership of Mr. Vu Van Hau and the management team, Geleximco continuously strengthens its development foundation, improves its management, control, and operational capabilities, and affirms its brand position.
Geleximco's operations focus on core business areas, which are also key sectors of the national economy, such as industry, real estate, finance, banking, commercial services, and transportation infrastructure. In all business areas, Geleximco has made significant achievements and received cooperation from many large economic and financial corporations in the region.
Geleximco not only aims for economic development but also links corporate interests with community interests, actively implementing charitable programs, building schools, awarding scholarships, supporting disaster-stricken areas, and organizing annual social welfare activities, spreading the spirit of compassion and community responsibility…
With outstanding achievements in production and business activities, along with positive contributions to the country and the community, Geleximco has been honored and awarded important certificates and prizes by the People's Committees of provinces and cities, as well as domestic and international organizations.
The recognition given to Mr. Vu Van Hau further spreads Geleximco's development journey, while affirming the significance of long-term vision, innovative spirit, and collective strength in building a business. This achievement also demonstrates the inherent strength of Vietnamese businesses – daring to think and act for the common prosperity of the country, moving forward together in the era of global integration.
